Multivariable multinomial logistic regression, with the Low-Fear Declining class as the reference, indicated that a longer diagnosis-to-treatment interval and higher baseline anxiety and depression scores each independently increased the likelihood of belonging to the Moderate-Fear Declining or High-Fear Declining class. Positive nodal status further increased the likelihood of belonging to the Moderate-Fear Declining class, and total thyroidectomy further increased the likelihood of belonging to the High-Fear Declining class, whereas older age and stronger social support were protective. Conclusion FCR after PTC surgery follows heterogeneous trajectories that differ in initial level and rate of decline. These trajectories are associated with baseline psychological and clinical factors that are routinely assessable before surgery. They may inform the future development of risk-stratified psychosocial care for patients with PTC, pending prospective validation.

title: Performance of the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index in Predicting Mortality in Acute Pulmonary Embolism at a Kenyan Tertiary Referral Hospital: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background Pulmonary embolism is a leading cause of cardiovascular hospitalization and death. The Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) is recommended for risk stratification, but evidence on its performance in Sub-Saharan Africa is limited. This study assessed the association between observed 30-day mortality and PESI-predicted mortality in patients with acute pulmonary embolism at a Kenyan tertiary referral hospital. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults admitted between January 2020 and December 2024 with acute pulmonary embolism confirmed by computed tomography pulmonary angiography or ventilation-perfusion scan. PESI scores were calculated at admission, and patients were assigned to risk classes I to V. Classes I and II were grouped as low risk and classes III to V as high risk. The primary outcome was all-cause 30-day mortality. Logistic regression, adjusted for age and sex, was used to estimate the association between PESI risk group and mortality. Results Of 500 patients screened, 386 were included. Median age was 51.6 years and 41.5% were male. Cancer was the most common comorbidity (15.3%), followed by chronic lung disease (9.8%), heart failure (4.1%) and HIV infection (2.8%). The distribution across PESI classes I to V was 44.0%, 19.4%, 17.4%, 11.1% and 8.0%. In-hospital mortality rose from 0% in Class I to 22.6% in Class V, and 30-day mortality from 0% to 30.8% (p < 0.001). High-risk patients were older, more often male, stayed longer in hospital and carried a greater comorbidity burden. Thirty-day mortality was 10.9% in high-risk and 1.7% in low-risk patients (adjusted odds ratio 9.4, 95% confidence interval 2.4–37.3). Anticoagulation was given to 97.9% of patients and thrombolysis to 2.1%. Conclusions PESI stratified short-term mortality effectively in this younger African cohort with a high cancer burden. The findings support routine use of PESI for risk stratification in resource-limited settings and point to the need for multicentre validation across diverse African healthcare environments.

title: Beyond natriuresis: NAPE-PLD as an emerging molecular target of NCC-inhibiting diuretics—mechanistic hypothesis and translational agenda in Hypertension
abstract: Natriuresis through inhibition of the renal sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) is the established initiating mechanism of hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, and indapamide, but chronic blood-pressure lowering also reflects reduced systemic vascular resistance and drug-specific extrarenal actions. Recent structural and preclinical work identified N-acyl phosphatidylethanolamine phospholipase D (NAPE-PLD), a membrane zinc hydrolase that generates anandamide and other N-acylethanolamines, as a binding target of hydrochlorothiazide and of the chemically distinct NCC-inhibiting diuretics chlorthalidone and indapamide. Importantly, this evidence does not yet establish that clinically used doses increase anandamide in humans or that NAPE-PLD explains cardiovascular outcome benefits. Rather, it provides a testable molecular hypothesis that can be integrated with established renal and vascular mechanisms. We therefore distinguish three evidence layers: (i) clinically established NCC inhibition and natriuresis; (ii) experimentally supported drug-specific vascular effects involving potassium channels, calcium handling and Rho/Rho-kinase signaling; and (iii) the emerging NAPE-PLD/endocannabinoid hypothesis. We review the molecular architecture of NAPE-PLD, its regulation by membrane substrates and bile acids, the drug-binding interface described for hydrochlorothiazide, and the downstream biology of anandamide at CB1, CB2, TRPV1 and PPAR-related pathways. Particular attention is given to endothelial nitric oxide signaling, blood-brain barrier biology, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and sympathetic regulation. We also propose a precision-pharmacology research framework based on drug structure, low-renin/salt-sensitive phenotype, kidney function, lipidomic endocannabinoid signatures and NAPE-PLD pharmacodynamic biomarkers. The central conclusion is deliberately conservative: NAPE-PLD is a credible newly identified molecular target of NCC-inhibiting diuretics, but the clinical importance of this interaction remains unproven and requires independent replication, human pharmacodynamic studies and prospective outcome-oriented investigation. Clinical trial registration: Not applicable.

title: Is somatosensory tinnitus confined to the craniocervical region: Diagnostic pitfalls, manual therapy and safety considerations
abstract: Somatosensory tinnitus is tinnitus that is triggered or modulated by somatic input, and current diagnostic criteria locate that input in the cervical spine and temporomandibular region. This minireview, based on a structured narrative search of PubMed (January 2015 to October 2026), grades the evidence for somatic modulation by body region and examines diagnosis, conservative management and safety. Evidence is strongest for the jaw, face and neck, where auditory-somatosensory convergence in the dorsal cochlear nucleus is anatomically established and small randomized trials of cervical and temporomandibular manual therapy report short-term benefit with a high risk of bias. Modulation by limb contractions is documented but preliminary. Evidence for a lumbosacral contribution is indirect, consisting of confounded spinal neuromodulation case reports, a cross-sectional association with low back pain and uncontrolled observations; no anatomical projection has been demonstrated, and no controlled study has tested lumbar-directed treatment for tinnitus. One author-managed patient, whose tinnitus began with acute lumbosacral pain during use of a percussive massage device, is used only to frame four diagnostic pitfalls; this uncontrolled observation cannot establish causation, a lumbosacral mechanism or a treatment effect, and no recommendation depends on it. We compare manual therapy with guidelines that recommend cognitive behavioural therapy, summarise published massage-device adverse events, which are case reports that cannot establish causation or incidence, outline practical suicide screening tools and recommend validated outcome measures. An expanded somatic examination can be considered when specific history clues are present, but its yield is unknown, and we define research priorities to test it.

title: Association between kinesiophobia and poor short-term postoperative outcomes in elderly patients undergoing lung cancer surgery
abstract: Objective To explore early postoperative kinesiophobia and its associated factors among elderly patients undergoing lung cancer surgery, and examine associations between kinesiophobia and short-term postoperative outcomes. Methods A consecutive sampling strategy was adopted to recruit 135 patients receiving thoracoscopic radical lung cancer surgery between May and December 2025. All eligible patients admitted to the Department of Thoracic Surgery within this period were included. Data were collected via face-to-face interviews using a general information questionnaire, the Chinese version of the Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia (TSK), and the MD Anderson Symptom Inventory. Additional clinical data, including chest tube indwelling time, early ambulation distance, and postoperative complications, were extracted from medical records and telephone follow-up. Patients were categorized into a kinesiophobia group (n = 66) and a non-kinesiophobia group (n = 69) according to postoperative TSK scores. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were conducted to identify factors associated with short-term prognosis, and ROC curve analysis was performed to assess the discriminative performance of the indicators. Results Univariate analysis showed that age, smoking history, history of chemotherapy, comorbidities, pain level, surgical approach, and physical activity status were associated with kinesiophobia (P < 0.05). Compared with the non-kinesiophobia group, patients in the kinesiophobia group had higher postoperative symptom scores, a higher incidence of subcutaneous emphysema, and lower rates of early ambulation within 6 hours after surgery (P < 0.05). Multivariate logistic regression demonstrated that age, smoking history, comorbidities, and TSK scores were associated with greater postoperative symptom burden; age, pain level, chemotherapy history, and kinesiophobia were associated with postoperative complications (P < 0.05). The nomogram yielded an AUC of 0.661 (95% CI: 0.624–0.698), showing acceptable discriminative ability for poor short-term outcomes. Calibration curves indicated favorable agreement between observed and predicted probabilities. Conclusion Early postoperative kinesiophobia is associated with short-term outcomes in elderly patients with lung cancer. Age, smoking history, comorbidities, and kinesiophobia are associated with short-term prognosis. These findings may help identify patients with kinesiophobia in clinical practice.

title: Cost-Benefit Study of Febrile Neutropenia Prophylactic Treatment with Pegfilgrastim vs. Filgrastim in Pediatric Patients with Solid Tumors
abstract: Background: Febrile neutropenia is one of the main complications in cancer patients that exponentially increases treatment costs.Pegfilgrastim is a pegylated form of filgrastim, and it might reduce the severity and duration of febrile neutropenia, as well as costs.Objective: To analyze the cost-benefit ratio of febrile neutropenia prophylactic treatment with pegfilgrastim vs. filgrastim in pediatric patients with solid tumors.Methods: A cost-benefit study was carried out, where complete medical records of pediatric patients with solid tumors and febrile neutropenia who received prophylactic treatment with pegfilgrastim vs. filgrastim were analyzed.Clinical-demographic variables, febrile neutropenia events, and days of hospital stay were considered, as well as related complications and global related cost, looking for differences by means of Student's t-test and the chi-square test.Results: Twenty-six patients with a total of 106 chemotherapy courses were included.Fourteen patients (52.8%) were administered filgrastim and 12 patients (46.1%) received pegfilgrastim.There were 57.6% of males.Mean hospital days of stay and costs were significantly higher in the filgrastim versus the pegfilgrastim group (p < 0.001).Conclusion: The use of pegfilgrastim reduced the number of neutropenia and fever events, days of hospital stay, and costs by up to 30%.(creativecommons.org/

title: Clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula after pancreaticoduodenectomy within a standardized multimodal preventive pathway: a descriptive single-center cohort benchmarked against ISGPS risk classes
abstract: Background/aims Clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF) remains the principal driver of morbidity after pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD). This study describes CR-POPF incidence, severity and associated outcomes in consecutive patients managed within a standardized multimodal preventive pathway (perioperative pasireotide, piperacillin–tazobactam prophylaxis and duct-to-mucosa pancreaticojejunostomy), benchmarked against International Study Group of Pancreatic Surgery (ISGPS) class-specific reference rates. Methods Prospectively collected data from 63 consecutive patients undergoing PD at a single hepatopancreatobiliary unit between January 2018 and April 2026 were retrospectively analyzed. Patients were stratified into ISGPS risk classes A–D based on intraoperative pancreatic texture and main pancreatic duct (MPD) diameter. The primary outcome was CR-POPF (ISGPS grade B or C). Observed CR-POPF was compared with the number expected from ISGPS validation-cohort rates. Exploratory univariable associations were estimated with Firth penalized-likelihood logistic regression. Results CR-POPF occurred in 6 of 63 patients (9.5%; 95% CI 3.6–19.6; all grade B). Applying ISGPS class-specific rates, 7.24 events were expected [observed/expected 0.83 (95% CI 0.30–1.80)]. Half of the cohort was ISGPS class A (32/63), in which CR-POPF occurred in 3/32 (9.4%) against a 3.5% reference, and 60.3% had pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), a lower-risk case mix than the ISGPS reference cohort. All 6 events occurred in 2018–2022 (6/31) and none in 2023–2026 (0/32; p = 0.011), while the proportion of PDAC rose from 48% to 72% (p = 0.07). CR-POPF occurred in 1/38 patients with PDAC and 5/25 with other histology. Clavien–Dindo ≥ IIIa complications occurred in 4 patients (6.3%), all grade IIIa. There was no 90-day mortality (upper 95% confidence limit 5.7%). Median length of stay was 6.5 vs. 6 days with and without CR-POPF (p = 0.24). Conclusions In this small descriptive cohort from a low-volume unit managed within a multimodal preventive pathway, the CR-POPF rate was consistent with, but not demonstrably lower than, ISGPS benchmark expectations, and the favorable case mix and the concentration of events in the early years preclude attributing outcomes to the pathway. Comparative studies are required to establish whether such pathways reduce CR-POPF.

title: Efficacy of seven 5-HT3 receptor antagonists in reducing postoperative nausea and vomiting following general anesthesia for laparoscopic gynaecological surgery: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
abstract: Background 5-HT 3 receptor antagonists are commonly used for the prophylaxis of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) following general anesthesia for laparoscopic gynaecological surgery. However, no consensus has been reached regarding the optimal agent among them. Objective To compare the efficacy and safety of 5-HT 3 receptor antagonists for the prevention of PONV using a Bayesian network meta-analysis. Methods We searched PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science for eligible randomised controlled trials (RCTs). The primary outcomes were the incidences of acute nausea, late nausea, overall nausea, acute vomiting, late vomiting, and overall vomiting after laparoscopic gynaecological surgery. Risk ratios with 95% credible intervals (RR, 95%CrI) for dichotomous data were estimated using a Bayesian random-effects model, and SUCRA values and rankograms were used to rank the pharmacological interventions. Results A total of 38 eligible RCTs involving 4,415 patients undergoing gynaecological laparoscopic surgery were included, comparing seven 5-HT 3 receptor antagonists and placebo. Bayesian models converged well; node-splitting tests showed no significant inconsistency. For acute nausea, palonosetron (RR = 0.44, 95%CrI 0.28–0.68), ramosetron (RR = 0.55, 95%CrI 0.31–0.91), and ondansetron (RR = 0.71, 95%CrI 0.58–0.87) significantly reduced acute nausea risk vs. placebo; palonosetron had the highest SUCRA value. For late nausea, ramosetron (RR = 0.38, 95%CrI 0.19–0.76), palonosetron (RR = 0.43, 95%CrI 0.25–0.73), and ondansetron (RR = 0.60, 95%CrI 0.41–0.87) outperformed placebo. For acute vomiting, granisetron, palonosetron and ondansetron were superior to placebo, and granisetron had the top SUCRA value. For late vomiting, granisetron (RR = 0.21, 95%CrI 0.03–0.81), palonosetron (RR = 0.25, 95%CrI 0.13–0.48), ondansetron (RR = 0.42, 95%CrI 0.28–0.60) reduced late vomiting risk versus placebo; granisetron had the top SUCRA value. No 5-HT 3 receptor antagonist significantly increased the risk of headache. Conclusions Ondansetron, palonosetron, and ramosetron were effective in reducing nausea, while granisetron, ondansetron, and palonosetron were effective in reducing vomiting after laparoscopic gynaecological surgery. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the risk of chance findings from multiple comparisons and incomplete adverse event data. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261442904, identifier: CRD420261442904.

title: LoS estimator: Robust deconvolution of patient length of stay distributions in intensive care units during epidemic scenarios
Dog Boarding Wisconsin Rapids WI
abstract: When you need to be away, your dog can stay with us in our comfortable, secure boarding facility. We provide personalized care and extensive amounts of playtime to ensure they feel relaxed and at home. Our state-of-the-art air exchange systems combined with UV sanitizers ensure that your dog is breathing air that exceeds the standards of a hospital patient room.

title: Robotic pancreaticoduodenectomy without nasogastric tube placement
journal: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association
abstract: BACKGROUND: Nasogastric (NG) tube placement has been standard practice in pancreatoduodenectomy, but also questioned. This study evaluated the feasibility and safety of foregoing a NG tube in robotic pancreatoduodenectomy (RPD). METHODS: Patients undergoing RPD or open pancreatoduodenectomy (OPD) at Taipei Veterans General Hospital were included in this study for propensity score matching. The surgical outcomes including surgical mortality, morbidity and length of stay were compared between the study group of RPD without a NG tube and the control groups of RPD with a NG tube and OPD with a NG tube. RESULTS: A total of 906 patients were included. After propensity score matching, each arm comprised 100 patients. The RPD groups without and with NG tube had less intraoperative blood loss compared to the OPD group, with a median of 155 vs. 200 vs. 500 cc (p < 0.001) and a higher lymph node yield, with a median number of 18 vs. 15 vs. 12 (p < 0.001). The surgical outcomes including surgical mortality and postoperative complications were comparable among the RPD without NG tube, RPD with NG tube, and OPD with NG tube groups, except for delayed gastric emptying and length of hospital stay. The incidence of delayed gastric emptying was significantly lower in the RPD without and with NG tube groups than in the OPD with NG tube group (3% vs. 4% vs. 18%, p < 0.001). The length of hospital stay was also shorter in the RPD without NG tube group, with a median of 17 days, compared to the other two groups with NG tube, 22 days and 26 days (p < 0.001). Only operation type, OPD, remained an independent risk factor for predicting the occurrence of delayed gastric emptying. CONCLUSION: RPD groups were associated with lower delayed gastric emptying and shorter length of hospital stay, as compared to OPD with NG tube. There appears to have no significant difference in the outcomes between RPD with and without NG tube. It is feasible to forego a NG tube in RPD cases without negatively impacting safety.

title: Nutritional Interventions in Older Adults Undergoing Hip Fracture Surgery or Elective Hip Arthroplasty: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Background: Nutritional vulnerability may compromise recovery after hip surgery in older adults. We reviewed nutritional interventions after hip fracture surgery and elective hip arthroplasty. Methods: We searched PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science in July 2026. The systematic review covered oral, enteral and parenteral strategies; principal meta-analyses were restricted to oral protein and/or energy support in hip-fracture populations. We used inverse-variance common-effect models for in-hospital complications and random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood and modified Knapp–Hartung inference for length of stay. Sensitivity analyses excluded trials rated at high overall risk of bias. Results: We included 37 reports. Four trials involving 371 participants evaluated protein-containing oral supplements, with or without additional energy, including individually tailored supplementation. The complication RR was 0.731 (95% CI 0.565–0.945; p = 0.017; I2 = 50.2%). After exclusion of one high-risk trial, the RR was 0.760 (95% CI 0.580–0.996; p = 0.047; I2 = 61.2%). Estimates for acute hospital stay (five trials; MD −0.70 days, 95% CI −2.39 to 0.98) and rehabilitation stay (three trials; MD −3.52 days, 95% CI −10.44 to 3.40) remained inconclusive. Excluding high-risk trials left two rehabilitation trials, which were not pooled. Conclusions: Oral protein and/or energy support was associated with fewer in-hospital complications under the common-effect model, but heterogeneity, the small evidence base and post hoc model selection make this finding exploratory. No particular formulation was established as superior. Absolute benefit depends on baseline risk, and effects on length of stay remain uncertain.

title: Efficacy of sivelestat sodium for patients with acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: To minimize the influence of language bias and methodological heterogeneity, this study systematically integrated English and Japanese databases, restricting inclusion to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials (quasi-RCTs), to re-evaluate the efficacy and safety of sivelestat sodium for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and acute lung injury (ALI). English databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library) and Japanese databases (Ichushi Web, J-STAGE) were searched to December 31, 2025. RCTs or quasi-RCTs comparing sivelestat sodium with a control group (placebo or standard treatment) in adult patients with ALI/ARDS were included. The primary outcome was 28–30-day mortality; secondary outcomes included duration of mechanical ventilation, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio, and incidence of adverse events. A total of 14 RCTs and quasi-RCTs were included. The meta-analysis suggested that sivelestat sodium may reduce 28–30-day all-cause mortality in patients with ALI/ARDS compared with the control group (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65–0.97, p = 0.02 ), with minimal heterogeneity ( I 2 = 1%). However, the statistical significance of this finding was sensitive to the exclusion of individual studies in leave-one-out analyses. Regarding secondary outcomes, sivelestat significantly shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation and ICU length of stay. Significant improvements in the PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio were noted on days 3, 5, and 7. No statistically significant differences were found between the groups regarding the incidence of adverse events. Sivelestat sodium may reduce 28–30-day all-cause mortality, shorten the duration of mechanical ventilation and ICU length of stay, and improve oxygenation in patients with ALI/ARDS. The potential mortality benefit requires confirmation in adequately powered, multicenter randomized controlled trials. PROSPERO CRD420251067146.

title: The use and impact of community Care (Education) and Treatment Reviews (C(E)TRs) in people with intellectual disability and autistic people: a cohort and case-control study using electronic health records
abstract: Background Care (Education) and Treatment Reviews (C(E)TRs) were introduced in 2015 to prevent unnecessary hospital admissions amongst people with intellectual disability and autistic people. Little is known about people who receive community C(E)TRs or the effectiveness of community C(E)TRs in reducing admissions. Aims To estimate the causal effect of community C(E)TRs on psychiatric hospital admission, and compare length of hospital stay between patients who did and did not have a pre-admission community C(E)TR. Method We conducted a retrospective observational study using de-identified electronic health record data from 2,495 patients. We characterised the sociodemographic and clinical profiles of people with intellectual disability and autistic people who received a community C(E)TR between 2015 and 2025. We used propensity score weighting and a difference-in-differences analysis to compare changes in psychiatric hospital admissions in the six months before and after community C(E)TRs, with changes over corresponding periods in matched controls. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to compare lengths of hospital stay between patients who had a pre-admission C(E)TR and those who did not. Results 446 community C(E)TRs were identified in the intellectual disability group and 382 in the autistic group. The intellectual disability group had a median age of 21 years and were predominately male (60.7%) whereas the autistic group were younger (median age 16 years) with a higher proportion of females (55.2%). Community C(E)TRs reduced the odds of psychiatric hospital admission over six months compared with controls (pooled OR = 0.47, 95% CI 0.26-0.85) but there was no difference over 12 months (pooled OR = 0.81, 95% CI 0.48-1.35). Length of hospital stay did not differ between those with and without a pre-admission C(E)TR. Conclusions These findings suggest that C(E)TRs may delay rather than prevent admissions and highlight the need for adequately resourced, sustainable community services to support people at high risk of admission.

title: Perioperative complications after unilateral total joint arthroplasty in elderly patients receiving general versus non-general anesthesia: a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study
abstract: Elderly patients undergoing unilateral total joint arthroplasty (TJA) are particularly vulnerable to anesthetic-related outcomes due to age-related physiological decline and high comorbidity burden, yet the optimal anesthetic technique in this population remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of general anesthesia (GA) versus non-GA on the postoperative length of stay (PLOS) and other secondary outcomes in patients undergoing unilateral TJA. This single-center, retrospective observational cohort study included patients treated at the First Medical Center of the Chinese PLA General Hospital between January 2014 and December 2021. Ethical approval was granted by the Research Ethics Committee of the Chinese PLA General Hospital (S2024-094-02). The GA group comprised patients who underwent general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation and controlled mechanical ventilation. Non-GA included neuraxial anesthesia (spinal or epidural) and peripheral nerve block anesthesia. The primary outcome was PLOS, and secondary outcomes included postoperative complications such as delirium, surgical site infection, stroke, myocardial infarction, acute kidney injury (AKI), myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery (MINS), ICU admission, and one-year mortality. Univariate, multivariate, propensity score matching (PSM) at a 1:1 ratio, and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) analyses were performed to assess the effect of anesthetic techniques. The study included 4518 patients, with 2708 receiving GA and 1810 receiving non-GA. GA was associated with a shorter hospital stay than non-GA (-0.43 days, 95% CI: -0.71 to -0.14, P = 0.003). After PSM, 1647 matched pairs were included and the length of hospital stay was reduced in the GA group compared to that in the non-GA group (-0.61, 95%CI: -0.93 to -0.29, P < 0.001). This finding was consistent with the IPTW( -0.52, 95%CI: -0.79 to -0.25, P < 0.001). There were no significant differences between the two groups in terms of other postoperative complications or mortality after unilateral TJA. General anesthesia was associated with a shorter the postoperative hospital stay for elderly patients undergoing unilateral TJA with no statistically significant differences in postoperative complications​. These findings offer valuable insights for anesthesiologists, surgeons, and patients in anesthesia decision-making.

title: Admission Vitamin B12 and in Hospital Outcomes in Adults with Acute Hepatitis and Acute Liver Injury
abstract: Background/Objectives: Elevated serum vitamin B12 accompanies liver injury, but its relationship with outcomes in acute hepatitis remains uncertain. We evaluated admission vitamin B12 and an exploratory B12–ferritin index (BFI). Methods: This retrospective study included 186 adults hospitalized with acute hepatitis or acute liver injury (2018–2025). Outcomes included ward length of stay, transplantation, and in-hospital mortality; exploratory endpoints were ICU admission, encephalopathy, and an ICU-inclusive composite. Discrimination was assessed using ROC AUC, including comparison with MELD 3.0. Eight B12 values exceeded the assay limit of 4000 pg/mL and were top-coded in numerical analyses. Results: Nine (4.8%) patients died, one (0.5%) underwent transplantation, and 20 (10.8%) met the ICU-inclusive composite; all 20 were admitted to the ICU. Encephalopathy occurred in 11 (5.9%). Vitamin B12 AUCs were 0.935 (95% CI 0.891–0.979) for mortality, 0.944 (0.904–0.984) for death or transplantation, and 0.938 (0.897–0.980) for the composite. B12 was unrelated to ward length of stay (Spearman ρ = 0.017; p = 0.818). BFI did not improve discrimination over B12. In an exploratory model adjusted for age and MELD 3.0, the B12 association persisted (adjusted OR per 1000 pg/mL, 7.67; 95% CI 3.38–17.44). Conclusions: Admission B12 was associated with adverse in-hospital outcomes, but limited event counts, uncertain sampling–event timing, and assay censoring prevent clinical prediction claims. Prospective validation is needed.

title: Clinical outcomes following the incorporation of a geriatric nurse practitioner into diabetic foot ulcer management: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Introduction Diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) are a leading cause of prolonged hospitalization and lower-limb amputation, and their inpatient management depends on multidisciplinary care. The contribution of geriatric nursing expertise to the surgical DFU team has not been described. We compared clinical outcomes of DFU admissions before and after the integration of a geriatric nurse practitioner (NP) into the multidisciplinary team of an orthopedic DFU unit. Methods In this retrospective before-and-after cohort study, all admissions to the DFU unit of a tertiary medical center between 2021 and 2025 were reviewed (1,556 admissions of 934 patients; 1,266 before and 290 after NP integration). The primary outcome was length of stay (LOS); secondary outcomes were in-hospital mortality, minor and major amputation, and 30- and 90-day readmission. Results Admissions after NP integration were of older patients (mean age 64.2 vs 62.0 years), with more insulin use (48.3% vs 41.7%) and higher admission glucose (median 196 vs 188 mg/dL). LOS did not differ significantly (median 11 vs 12 days, p = 0.28), nor did in-hospital mortality (2.1% vs 2.8%; difference -0.8%, 95% CI -2.7 to 1.1) or major amputation (20.3% vs 18.2%; difference 2.1%, 95% CI -3.0 to 7.2). Minor amputation was more frequent (38.6% vs 25.4%), without more major amputations within 90 days (5.6% vs 5.6%). Vascular workup (70.0% vs 46.4%), angioplasty (22.1% vs 15.3%) and antibiotic treatment (92.1% vs 85.9%) were more frequent after integration, and 30-day readmission was similar (10.9% vs 10.7%). Conclusion The integration of a geriatric NP into the DFU team was associated with more frequent vascular workup and antibiotic treatment and a higher proportion of minor amputations, with no significant difference in length of stay, mortality or major amputation. Since the before-and-after design does not allow causal inference, prospective comparative studies are needed.

title: ASSESSMENT OF ADMISSION OXIDATIVE STRESS MARKERS IN EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PATIENTS WITH CT-CONFIRMED, TRAUMATIC AND NON-TRAUMATIC SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE
journal: Eskisehir Medical Journal Eskisehir City Hospital
abstract: Introduction: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is a life-threatening neurological condition associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Oxidative stress is thought to contribute to the pathophysiology of both traumatic and non-traumatic SAH. This study aimed to evaluate admission oxidative stress markers in emergency department patients with CT-confirmed, traumatic and non-traumatic SAH and to explore their associations with selected clinical severity indicators. Methods: This prospective case–control study included 41 patients with SAH and 47 healthy controls. Total oxidant status (TOS), total antioxidant status (TAS), oxidative stress index (OSI), and ischemia-modified albumin (IMA) levels were measured at admission. Clinical data, including Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score, intensive care unit requirement, and hospital length of stay, were recorded. Functional outcome at hospital discharge was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale. Associations between oxidative stress markers and clinical variables were analyzed. Results: TOS, OSI, and IMA levels were significantly higher in patients with SAH than in healthy controls (all p<0.001), whereas TAS levels did not differ significantly (p=0.395). TOS demonstrated a significant negative correlation with GCS score (r=-0.329, p=0.036). OSI showed a weak positive correlation with hospital length of stay (r=0.323, p=0.039). No significant associations were observed between oxidative stress markers and presenting symptoms. TAS and TOS levels were significantly higher in patients with an unfavorable functional outcome (p=0.002 and p=0.015, respectively). Among non-survivors, TAS was significantly higher (p=0.001), whereas the association between TOS and mortality did not reach statistical significance (p=0.076). Conclusion: Patients with CT-confirmed, traumatic and non-traumatic SAH demonstrated increased oxidative stress at admission, reflected by elevated TOS, OSI, and IMA levels. Selected oxidative stress markers were associated with certain clinical severity indicators, as well as with short-term hospital outcomes. These findings suggest a potential relationship between oxidative stress and disease burden in acute SAH; however, further studies are required to clarify the clinical significance of these biomarkers.

title: Preoperative Body Composition and Inflammatory-Nutritional Status as Prognostic Determinants in Adults with Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer Undergoing Curative-Intent Anatomical Pulmonary Resection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Background and Objectives: Preoperative skeletal muscle depletion and inflammatory-nutritional indices have each been associated with survival after resection of non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Registered primary outcomes were overall survival (OS), complications and length of stay; we asked whether the muscle association persists when both enter one multivariable model (integrated phenotype), and mapped the evidence in patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy. Materials and Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL and Scopus were searched from inception to 18 May 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420261401871) for adults undergoing curative-intent anatomical resection for stage I–III NSCLC. Multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for dichotomised exposures were pooled (restricted maximum likelihood, Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman) where ≥3 estimates were compatible; the remainder were presented narratively. QUIPS and GRADE were applied. Results: Of 179 studies, 34 entered the quantitative synthesis. Muscle depletion modelled with an inflammatory-nutritional marker, a comparison we identified in no previous synthesis, remained associated with OS (5 cohorts, 3934 patients; HR 1.82, 95% CI 1.17–2.82; low certainty). Elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (1.54, 1.39–1.71; very low certainty, funnel-plot asymmetry), low prognostic nutritional index (1.71, 1.36–2.16), low lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (1.75, 1.19–2.57) and plain muscle depletion (1.93, 1.43–2.59) were each associated with worse OS. For recurrence-free survival, the estimate from the same cohorts was heterogeneous and imprecise (1.96, 0.81–4.75; very low certainty). Complications and length of stay were not poolable. Most thresholds were cohort-derived; no pooled comparison supplied an estimate for patients treated before surgery, and we identified no mutually adjusted study reporting incremental discrimination. Conclusions: The muscle association with OS was not accounted for by the inflammatory-nutritional markers measured alongside it. Based on low-certainty, retrospective, mostly East Asian evidence, this supports a prognostic association, not added prediction or decision rule. Prospective studies should measure both domains before induction and again before resection, enter them continuously with any threshold pre-specified, and report incremental discrimination in the neoadjuvant setting, where we identified no mutually adjusted estimate.

title: Evaluating the prognostic and safety outcomes of awake extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in cardiogenic shock patients: A meta-analysis
abstract: Objective: This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the association between awake extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and clinical outcomes in patients experiencing cardiogenic shock. Methods: Chinese (CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP) and English (PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane) databases were searched for retrospective observational studies on awake ECMO support in patients with cardiogenic shock. Outcomes included survival rate, length of intensive care unit (ICU) stay, duration of ECMO support, blood lactic acid level after 24 hours of ECMO support, and incidence of adverse events. The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed using the Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tool. RevMan 5.3 was used to perform a meta-analysis of the included studies. Results: Eight studies involving 973 patients, with a mean age of 49.94 years, were included. The results indicated that patients undergoing awake ECMO exhibited a higher survival rate, reduced duration of intensive care unit stay, lower blood lactic acid levels, and decreased incidence of adverse events related to the nervous system and renal function than those receiving conventional nonawake ECMO. However, no significant differences were observed between the two groups in terms of ECMO support duration, pulmonary complications, bleeding, embolism, hemolysis, or bacteremia. Conclusion: Awake ECMO was associated with potentially favorable clinical outcomes in patients with cardiogenic shock. However, because all included studies were observational and had a moderate-to-high risk of bias, these findings should be regarded as exploratory hypothesis-generating associations rather than as definitive evidence of clinical benefit. Awake ECMO can cause psychological stress and anxiety in patients. Large, well-designed prospective studies and randomized controlled trials are required to validate our findings.

title: Association of electronic versus paper-based documentation with completeness of prehospital emergency physician reports in suspected acute coronary syndrome: a retrospective cohort analysis
abstract: Background Complete prehospital documentation supports safe handover, continuity of care, quality assurance, and secondary data use in emergency medical services. This study examined the association between documentation format and record completeness in a physician-staffed prehospital cohort of patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS), with particular attention to information relevant to hospital handover. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort analysis of 2,787 prehospital emergency physician reports for suspected ACS, recorded in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2018. Six records with implausible dates were excluded before primary analysis. The final analytic cohort therefore comprised 2,781 reports: 2,120 from paper-based documentation (PBD) and 661 from electronic-based documentation (EBD). The primary endpoint was complete documentation of a predefined record set comprising hospital destination, prehospital length of stay, initial and handover systolic and diastolic blood pressure, initial and handover peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO 2), documentation of a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), and a numeric pain score (NRS). A sensitivity analysis repeated the endpoint without the NRS. Completeness rates were compared using chi-square tests, and adjusted associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression including age, sex, calendar year, and ACS subtype. Results Overall record completeness was higher in the EBD group than in the PBD group (90.9% vs. 48.2%; p < 0.001), an absolute difference of 42.7% points. The largest between-group differences involved handover blood pressures, handover SpO 2, prehospital length of stay, and 12-lead ECG documentation. In the adjusted model, EBD remained associated with higher odds of a complete record (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 10.48, 95% confidence interval [CI] 7.58–14.48; p < 0.001). When the NRS was excluded from the endpoint, completeness remained higher in the EBD group (94.9% vs. 75.6%; aOR 4.40, 95% CI 3.44–5.62; p < 0.001). Conclusion Electronic documentation was associated with more complete prehospital emergency physician reports in suspected ACS, particularly for handover-relevant variables. However, documentation modality was structurally confounded with treatment site, precluding isolation of an independent technology effect. As this study assessed a process metric rather than clinical outcomes, prospective multicentre studies should determine whether structured electronic documentation improves handover quality, workflow reliability, treatment timeliness, guideline adherence, and patient-centred outcomes. Trial registration German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00036944 (MONAH1 study).

title: Short-term efficacy analysis of uni-portal non-coaxial spinal endoscopic surgery with ligamentum flavum preservation combined with manual annular suture for lumbar disc herniation
abstract: Objective To preliminarily evaluate the technical feasibility and short-term clinical outcomes of ligamentum flavum preservation combined with manual annular suture under uni-portal non-coaxial spinal endoscopic surgery (UNSES) for the treatment of lumbar disc herniation (LDH). Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on 35 patients with LDH who underwent UNSES with ligamentum flavum preservation and manual annular suture between January 2024 and May 2025. Perioperative parameters, including operative time, intraoperative blood loss, and length of hospital stay, were recorded. Pain intensity was assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for low back and leg pain, and functional status was evaluated using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) preoperatively and at 1 week, 3 months, and 6 months postoperatively. Results All procedures were successfully completed. The mean operative time was 101.3 ± 32.4 min, mean intraoperative blood loss was 43.4 ± 23.1 mL, and mean hospital stay was 9.4 ± 1.5 days. VAS scores for low back and leg pain and ODI scores at all postoperative time points showed statistically significant improvement compared with preoperative values (P < 0.05). During a mean follow-up of 8.5 months, no serious complications or recurrent disc herniation occurred. The complication rate was 0% (95% CI 0%–10.0%, calculated by the Clopper–Pearson exact method). Conclusion UNSES with ligamentum flavum preservation combined with manual annular suture for LDH preliminarily demonstrates technical feasibility, significantly relieves pain, improves short-term function, and shows good short-term safety. However, this single-center, retrospective, non-controlled small-sample exploratory case series has selection bias and relatively short follow-up; the findings are insufficient to support widespread clinical application. Larger prospective controlled multicenter studies with at least 2 years of follow-up are needed to further clarify long-term efficacy.

title: Out of hospital cardiac arrest following low voltage electrical injury with complete neurological recovery
abstract: Low voltage electrical injuries are generally associated with minimal or no external burns but may cause severe injury, fatal cardiac arrhythmias and respiratory arrest depending on length of exposure, size of individual, environmental humidity and the cross-sectional area in contact with electrical source. Complete neurological recovery after prolonged resuscitation is uncommon. We report a case of 22 years old male who sustained low voltage electrical injury culminating in out of hospital cardiac arrest. He brought to the emergency department within 10 min after the incident. With initial rhythm of asystole. High quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation started immediately according to advanced cardiac life support guideline; the rhythm converted from asystole to ventricular fibrillation after third cycle of resuscitation requiring three defibrillation attempts. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved at the end of eighth cycle of resuscitation. Subsequently the patient admitted to intensive care unit and post cardiac arrest care were continued which includes mechanical ventilatory support, hemodynamic support, seizure management, fever prevention. The patient showed progressive neurological improvement and discharged home after three days of stay in intensive care unit with complete neurological recovery. This case shows the critical importance of immediate transport to the hospital, early high-quality CPR and comprehensive post cardiac arrest care for patient survival.

title: Palliative Extubation and De-Escalation of Life-Sustaining Treatments in the Emergency Department
journal: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians Open
abstract: An aging, increasingly multimorbid population, coupled with challenges in bed availability and staffing, is increasing emergency department (ED) boarding of admitted patients, including those admitted to intensive care units (ICUs). This increase shifts aspects of care traditionally performed in the inpatient setting into the ED, which may include palliative extubation and de-escalation of other life-sustaining treatments when they no longer align with the patient's goals of care. Very little guidance exists in emergency medicine journals or textbooks regarding the care of these patients, and the limited data in the literature focuses primarily on the ICU setting. An expert panel of dual-certified physicians in emergency medicine and hospice and palliative medicine, working in both academic and community settings, convened to perform a narrative review and develop an evidence-based framework for the ethical and procedural aspects of de-escalation of life-sustaining treatment and palliative extubation in the ED, supporting emergency medicine physicians to provide compassionate, patient-centered, goal-concordant care.

title: From Infection to Resistance: Clinical Predictors and Outcomes of Antimicrobial-Resistant Infections in Hospitalized Patients
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: A Simple Four-Factor Predictive Model for Same-Day Discharge After Elective Total Hip Arthroplasty
abstract: Background/Objectives: Same-day discharge (SDD) after Total Hip Arthroplasty (THA) is an important outcome in modern arthroplasty, yet no simple, reliable pre-operative prediction tool exists. This study aimed to develop and temporally validate a bedside scoring tool to estimate SDD probability for patients electively undergoing THA. Methods: A retrospective cohort of all elective primary unilateral THAs performed at a single orthopaedic National Treatment Centre between 2023 and 2024 (n = 1119) was analysed. SDD was defined as length of stay of zero days. Predictors included demographics, frailty, comorbidity, anaesthetic type and knife-to-skin time. Variable selection used complete-case LASSO (n = 804) followed by multiply-imputed pooled logistic regression (20 datasets). A simple 4-factor score of sex, age, anaesthetic type and knife-to-skin time was derived. Temporal validation was performed on an independent dataset from 2025 (n = 547). Results: The final 4-factor scoring system demonstrated excellent discrimination—AUC 0.83. Calibration was good across both cohorts (Hosmer–Lemeshow p > 0.5). Decision curve analysis showed a net benefit across clinically relevant thresholds. The optimal threshold was identified using Youden’s J (−2 points; sensitivity 0.86; specificity 0.64). The strongest indicators of SDD were general anaesthetic, and an earlier knife-to-skin time. Conclusions: This simple 4-factor scoring system gives clinicians an accurate, well-calibrated and clinically useful method for the pre-operative prediction of SDD in elective unilateral THAs. Temporal validation supports its robustness. This scoring system has potential to alter clinical practice, inform list planning, and optimise resource allocation to maximise SDD potential.

title: Abdominal wall abscess and long-term incisional hernia after loop ileostomy reversal: a 12- year analysis of 749 procedures
abstract: Loop ileostomy reversal carries a substantial long-term incisional hernia risk, but the contribution of modifiable surgical factors remains unclear. We hypothesised that wound-related factors would be more strongly associated with hernia than anastomotic technique. This retrospective single-centre study included 749 consecutive loop ileostomy reversals (2007–2018). The primary endpoint was incisional hernia at the ileostomy site at 3 years. Secondary endpoints included hernia at 1 year, anastomotic leak, abdominal wall abscess, length of stay, and bowel-function recovery. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent correlates of hernia; mediation analysis assessed the skin-closure–abscess–hernia pathway. Hernia occurred in 50/630 patients (7.9%) at 1 year and 71/470 (15.1%) at 3 years. On multivariable analysis ( n = 460, 68 events), two independent correlates of hernia at 3 years emerged: abdominal wall abscess (odds ratio (OR) 3.89, 95% CI 1.56–9.46; p = 0.003), and emergency original surgery (OR 4.35, 1.79–11.49; p = 0.002). Anastomotic technique was not independently associated; other technical factors were not associated on univariate analysis. The association between complete skin closure and hernia was statistically accounted for by abscess (bootstrap average causal mediation effect 0.016, bias-corrected 95% CI 0.004–0.039, p = 0.007; Sobel p = 0.034). Model fit was acceptable (Hosmer–Lemeshow p = 0.478; C -statistic 0.723). Abdominal wall abscess was the strongest potentially modifiable factor associated with long-term incisional hernia after loop ileostomy reversal and statistically accounted for the association between complete skin closure and hernia. Wound management may therefore deserve comparable attention to anastomotic technique, although these observational findings require prospective confirmation.

title: Initial Experience with the Implementation of Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Inpatient Care
abstract: Introduction: High glycemic variability during hospitalization is associated with an increased risk of complications, prolonged hospital stay, higher costs, and mortality. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) enables ongoing measurement of interstitial fluid glucose concentration and reduces the incidence of hypo- and hyperglycemic episodes, glycemic variability, and the need for repeated capillary blood sampling in hospitalized patients. Aim To evaluate the implementation of CGM telemonitoring in the hospital setting, the indications for its use, the duration of monitoring in hospitalized patients with diabetes mellitus (DM), and to compare the economic aspects of CGM with standard monitoring using capillary blood sampling. Methodology: This retrospective observational study included 47 hospitalized patients with DM and non-diabetic hypoglycemia in whom a FreeStyle Libre 2 sensor was applied. The indications for CGM application, monitoring duration, economic costs, and the proportion of patients who continued using CGM after discharge home were analyzed. Given the retrospective and descriptive nature of the study, no formal statistical hypothesis testing was performed. Results CGM was implemented in 47 patients, of whom 43 were included in the analysis. The most common indication was metabolic decompensation of type 2 diabetes (43%). The mean monitoring duration was 8.5 ± 4.8 days, and 38% of patients continued using CGM after discharge. Although the direct costs of CGM are higher than those of capillary sampling, the difference decreases with longer monitoring duration and measurement frequency. Conclusion The use of CGM telemonitoring represents a safe supplementary method of glycemic monitoring in hospitalized patients with glycemic variability and differentiation of hypoglycemic states. Despite the higher direct costs, when the length of hospitalization and indirect benefits are taken into account, it may be a potentially cost-effective solution. In addition to increasing safety and individualization of glycemic management, its use was also associated with continued monitoring after discharge to home care in a significant proportion of patients.

title: Effect of Chlorhexidine Oral Care on Ventilator-Associated Events in 4 ICU Populations: A Retrospective Study
Risk of severe dengue in immunocompromised adults in Thailand: A multi-centre retrospective cohort study
abstract: Background Case reports suggest severe outcomes in immunocompromised patients, but large cohort comparisons are lacking. We compared dengue outcomes between immunocompromised and non-immunocompromised patients. Methods A retrospective multicenter cohort study of patients with laboratory-confirmed dengue infection between January 2023 and June 2024 was conducted. People living with HIV (PLWH) with CD4 < 350 cells/µL, recipients of solid organ transplantation, hematopoietic stem cell transplant within 2 years, active malignancy, splenectomy or asplenia, and conditions requiring immunosuppressive agents were classified as immunocompromised. Severe dengue based on WHO 2009 criteria, hospitalization, length of stay, and 30-day mortality were primary outcomes. Findings A total of 894 dengue patients were included, including 59 were immunocompromised. Immunocompromised patients were older (median [interquartile range] age 47.0 [30.0-59.0] vs 33.5 [26.0-49.0] years) and had greater comorbidity burden (Charlson index 1 [0–3] vs 0 [0–1]). Clinical presentation was similar, although absence of fever was more common (10.2% vs 1.1%). Laboratory findings were comparable at presentation, but immunocompromised patients had lower nadir platelet counts and prolonged thrombocytopenia. Severe dengue was more frequent in immunocompromised patients (22% vs 4.9%), with higher hospitalization rates, longer stays, and mortality. In multivariable analysis, immunocompromised status (OR 3.43, 95% CI 1.61–7.31) and comorbidity index (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.16–1.52) were independently associated with severe dengue. Interpretation This study adds to the current evidence of higher risk of severe dengue outcome in immunocompromised highlighting the need for improved strategies for prevention and treatment in this patient population.

title: Early outcome trade-offs and radiographic placement surrogates after CCS versus cannulated screw fixation of femoral neck fractures
abstract: Background Angular-stable constructs are increasingly used for femoral neck fracture fixation, but their early clinical advantages must be interpreted alongside operative burden, cost, and the uncertain value of radiographic placement metrics. We compared early outcomes, treatment burden, and radiographic placement surrogates between an angular-stable composite compression system (CCS) and conventional cannulated screws (CS). Methods We retrospectively reviewed 82 adults with femoral neck fractures treated with CCS (n = 41) or CS (n = 41) at a single centre between June 2022 and July 2025. Clinical outcomes, operative time, length of stay, total cost, and complications were compared in the full cohort. Post-operative anteroposterior radiographic placement surrogates (tip-apex surrogate and screw-shaft angle) were explored in multivariable models of the Harris Hip Score in 79 matched patients. Results CCS was associated with higher Harris Hip Scores (90.2 vs 87.6; P = 0.011) and faster union (12.7 vs 14.7 weeks; P = 0.045) but required longer surgery (61.0 vs 49.4 min; P = 0.001) and higher total cost (44,630 vs 30,461 CNY; P < 0.001). Osteonecrosis and screw back-out were numerically less frequent after CCS but did not differ significantly. In exploratory regression, neither the tip-apex surrogate (P = 0.623) nor the screw-shaft angle (P = 0.848) predicted the Harris Hip Score, whereas CS remained associated with a lower score (base-model beta = -3.20; 95% CI, -4.79 to -1.61; P < 0.001). Conclusions CCS fixation may offer better early function and faster union than cannulated screws, but at greater operative and economic cost. Simple anteroposterior radiographic placement surrogates did not explain the observed functional difference and should be interpreted cautiously across structurally different implants.

title: Early prediction of acute kidney injury in traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage: a machine learning model using admission laboratory variables
abstract: Background Traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage (tICH) represents a severe subtype of traumatic brain injury, with reported mortality rates ranging from 20% to 60%. Among tICH patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in approximately 7.6% to 24% of cases and is associated with increased mortality, prolonged ICU length of stay, and greater healthcare burden. Early identification of AKI risk using admission laboratory parameters may facilitate timely renal protective strategies. This study aimed to develop a machine learning model for early AKI prediction in this population. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort study included 539 ICU patients with tICH admitted between January 2024 and December 2025. Patients with chronic kidney disease or AKI at ICU admission were excluded. All predictor variables were collected within the first 24 h following ICU admission. Feature selection was performed using the Boruta algorithm and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression. Seven machine learning algorithms were compared; the final model was selected based on cross-validated performance within the training set, with comparable discriminative performance among top models confirmed by DeLong tests. Model interpretability was assessed using Shapley Additive Explanations analysis. Results Five variables were retained: serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, platelet count, bicarbonate, and prothrombin time activity. The XGBoost model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.901 (95% confidence interval: 0.838–0.953), sensitivity of 0.784, specificity of 0.902, F1 score of 0.744, and Brier score of 0.098 in the validation set. Decision curve analysis demonstrated positive net clinical benefit. Conclusions This five-variable laboratory-based model showed promising internally validated performance for early AKI risk prediction in ICU patients with tICH. However, it is hypothesis-generating and requires external multicenter validation before any clinical application.

title: Evaluation of the ACS Trauma Quality Improvement Program benchmark for intracranial pressure monitoring across trauma centers
journal: The Journal of Trauma: Injury, Infection, and Critical Care

title: Expanding use of continuous glucose monitoring beyond COVID in critical care: study protocol for a hybrid implementation trial
abstract: Over the last 2 decades, continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to improve glycemic control and patient outcomes in the outpatient setting, yet these technologies are not approved for inpatient use. Both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, which are common in the inpatient setting, are associated with increased morbidity, mortality, length of stay, and hospital costs. Point-of-care (POC) glucose monitoring has been the standard of care in the hospital setting since the late 1980’s, yet POC glucose monitoring implementation remains insufficient with frequent missed testing and missed timing of testing. Capabilities inherent to CGM (e.g., continuous measurement, hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia threshold alarms, predictive hypoglycemia alarms, trend data) hold the promise of improving glycemic control, patient outcomes, and nursing burden in the inpatient setting, yet ongoing research is needed to examine both outcomes and implementation of CGM in the inpatient environment. This mixed methods hybrid II effectiveness-implementation study will examine patient outcomes and the feasibility of CGM implementation using a CGM plus (+) POC protocol among 100 patients on IV insulin in a single Midwest academic medical center’s medical intensive care unit (MICU). In this single arm clinical trial, we are pursuing 4 research questions (RQ): RQ 1. Establish the clinical utility, fidelity, and adoption of Dexcom G6 CGM as a tool for making dosing decisions within a CGM + POC protocol among medical intensive care unit (MICU) patients; RQ2. Assess the effects of CGM implementation on nursing workload and factors influencing nursing care delivery through surveys administered to MICU nurses and through a MICU staff nurse focus group ( N = 10); RQ3. To assess glycemic control among patients receiving CGM in the CGM enabled MICU compared to historical control patients who received POC glucose monitoring in the MICU; RQ4. (exploratory) To assess hospitalization outcomes and conduct economic evaluation of the costs of delivering CGM implementation in the MICU. This trial that combines elements of effectiveness and implementation research will provide valuable data simultaneously evaluating patient outcomes and feasibility to enable more rapid adoption of CGM as standard of care. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05571397; Registered on 13 June 2018.

title: Laparoscopic-assisted versus ultrasound-guided transversus abdominis plane block in laparoscopic colorectal surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract: Transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block is widely used as part of multimodal analgesia in laparoscopic colorectal surgery. Laparoscopic-assisted TAP block (LTAP) is an alternative to ultrasound-guided TAP block (UTAP), but comparative effectiveness remains uncertain. We compared LTAP versus UTAP for postoperative analgesia, opioid use, and perioperative recovery after laparoscopic colorectal surgery. We conducted a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in accordance with PRISMA 2020. PubMed/MEDLINE (native PubMed interface), Scopus (Elsevier), Web of Science Core Collection, Embase (Elsevier), and Google Scholar were searched from inception to April 1, 2026 without language restrictions. Cochrane RoB 2 was used for risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE for certainty of evidence. The primary outcome was 24-hour morphine-milligram-equivalent (MME) opioid consumption. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261376522). Six RCTs involving 760 patients were included. For 24-hour MME consumption (5 RCTs; 585 patients), the pooled estimate did not show a statistically significant difference (MD − 4.47 mg, 95% CI − 10.16 to 1.23; p = 0.12), but heterogeneity was extreme (I²=96%; Tau²=38.64), making the magnitude of this estimate highly uncertain. Reviewer-requested exploratory sensitivity analyses showed that exclusion of Zaghiyan et al. reduced heterogeneity (I²≈75%) without changing the non-significant direction of effect; exclusion of studies at high overall RoB 2 risk also did not materially change the conclusion. Pain scores were not significantly different at assessed time points. LTAP shortened block completion time (MD − 6.81 min, 95% CI − 8.91 to − 4.70), while operative time, length of stay, and postoperative nausea and/or vomiting were not significantly different. Certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low across outcomes. LTAP may shorten block completion time and appear to provide postoperative analgesia broadly like UTAP; however, certainty varies by outcome and the pooled estimate for 24-hour opioid consumption is highly uncertain because of extreme heterogeneity and limited study numbers. Technique selection should therefore consider workflow, resources, and expertise rather than an expectation of superior analgesia.

title: Medication Safety and Quality of Care on an Interprofessional Training Ward vs Conventional Care in Gastroenterology and Hepatology: A 2-Year Cohort Study
abstract: Background Drug-related problems (DRPs) are a leading cause of preventable inpatient harm. Interprofessional training wards prepare future physicians and nurses for collaborative practice, but whether they also provide safe medication management is unknown. We therefore compared the need for clinical pharmacist interventions and the characteristics of DRPs between an interprofessional training ward and a conventional ward. Methods This retrospective cohort study analyzed prospectively documented pharmacist-led medication reviews from weekly interprofessional ward rounds on 2 gastroenterology and hepatology wards of a German university hospital (June 2024 to June 2026), including all adult inpatients with at least 1 review. On the interprofessional training ward A-STAR, final-year medical students and nursing trainees treat patients under supervision. The primary outcome was the rate of pharmacist interventions per prescribed drug; secondary outcomes were interventions per review and DRP characteristics according to the ATC, PCNE and NCC MERP classifications. Results A total of 946 medication reviews were analyzed (interprofessional training ward, 540 reviews in 351 patients; conventional ward, 406 reviews in 344 patients). Age, sex and length of stay were comparable, and liver cirrhosis was the leading diagnosis on both wards. Although more drugs were prescribed per review on the interprofessional training ward (mean, 13.8 vs 12.7; P = .006), fewer pharmacist interventions were required (11.8 vs 15.0 per 100 prescribed drugs; adjusted incidence rate ratio [IRR], 0.80; 95% CI, 0.72–0.90; P < .001), robustly across sensitivity analyses. Affected drug classes, DRP causes, acceptance of recommendations (58.6% vs 55.2%), problem resolution (98.9% vs 99.1%) and DRP severity were similar. Only excessive treatment duration, mainly of anti-infectives, was more frequent on the interprofessional training ward (6.8% vs 3.5% of causes; q = .03). Conclusions In this cohort study, care on an interprofessional training ward was associated with fewer pharmacist interventions and a DRP profile comparable to that of conventional care. Interprofessional training wards with embedded clinical pharmacists combine medication safety and high-quality care with the interprofessional education of future physicians; antimicrobial stewardship is a priority learning target. Trial registration Not applicable (retrospective observational study; approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Regensburg, No. 26-4816-104).

title: Comparison of one-stage triple-incision versus two-stage quadruple-incision unilateral biportal endoscopic decompression for two-level degenerative lumbar canal stenosis: A retrospective cohort study
abstract: Background Unilateral biportal endoscopy (UBE) is increasingly used for degenerative lumbar canal stenosis (DLCS), yet the optimal surgical strategy for two-level involvement remains unclear. This study compared the clinical outcomes, safety, and cost-effectiveness of one-stage triple-incision UBE versus two-stage quadruple-incision UBE for two-level DLCS. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 155 consecutive patients who underwent UBE decompression for two-level DLCS between January 2023 and February 2025. Patients were divided into Group A (one-stage triple-incision UBE, n = 82) and Group B (two-stage quadruple-incision UBE, n = 73). Perioperative parameters, clinical outcomes (VAS for back and leg pain, JOA scores, ODI, modified MacNab criteria), and radiographic outcomes (CSDA, facet joint preservation rate, segmental stability, disc height) were compared. The minimum follow-up was 12 months. Results Group A demonstrated significantly shorter total operative time, total fluoroscopy time, less blood loss, shorter total incision length, reduced hospital stay, and lower total hospital costs (all P < 0.001). Both groups achieved significant improvements in all clinical parameters (all within-group P < 0.01). Group A showed superior outcomes in VAS back pain, JOA scores, and ODI at all postoperative time points (all P < 0.05), while VAS leg pain scores were comparable between groups (all P > 0.05). The excellent/good rates were 90.24% and 89.04%, respectively (P > 0.05). CSDA increased significantly in both groups (P < 0.001) with comparable increase rates (P > 0.05). Facet joint preservation rates were similar between groups (all P > 0.05). Although no patient in either group developed clinical instability, Group B showed significantly greater progression in vertebral translation distance and range of motion at the L4/5 level (P < 0.05). Complication rates were comparable between groups (9.76% vs. 9.59%, P > 0.05). Conclusions One-stage triple-incision UBE achieves comparable neural decompression efficacy and safety to two-stage UBE for two-level DLCS, while offering superior perioperative efficiency, better functional recovery, and reduced healthcare costs, with a more favorable profile of paraspinal muscle protection and segmental stability preservation. These findings support the one-stage approach as a safe and cost-effective alternative for appropriately selected patients.

The Hospital Frailty Risk Score in hip fracture measures documented illness burden, not frailty: an external validation study
abstract: Background. In hip fracture, geriatric co-management and discharge planning are directed at patients judged frail, and the Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS) is increasingly used to make that judgement. Whether it measures frailty has never been tested: every validation has scored the same admission whose outcome it predicts. We therefore scored it twice, at the index and earlier admissions. Methods. Retrospective cohort from MIMIC-IV v3.1 (2015–2019): 1,594 hospitalizations (1,445 patients) aged ≥ 65 years with hip fracture (ICD-10 S72.0–S72.2). We compared the HFRS with the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) and Elixhauser indices, quantified incremental value over comorbidity and routine admission laboratory values, classified its 109 codes as acute, chronic or geriatric, and compared the pre-admission score (n = 558) with a Charlson index built from the same prior codes. Results. The HFRS discriminated 30-day mortality similarly to the CCI (0.726 vs. 0.693, p = 0.19) and added to it (ΔAUC + 0.026 to + 0.041) and to laboratory values (+ 0.078). It correlated with the number of coded diagnoses (ρ = 0.76), added nothing beyond it at 30 days (ΔAUC − 0.000) and was worse for prolonged stay (0.837 vs. 0.881, p = 0.001). Two-thirds of its points (65.6%) came from acute events and complications; the acute component alone reproduced its discrimination (30-day AUC 0.726; chronic 0.606), and removing acute codes left none of the 322 admissions above 15. It flagged 20.2% of admissions yet captured 44.5% of 30-day deaths and 65.9% of prolonged stays. Net benefit for prolonged stay was higher with the HFRS at every threshold (20%: 0.028 vs. 0.007). Before the fracture, the score was at chance at 30 days (0.551), inferior to a Charlson index from the same prior codes (0.649, p = 0.018), and correlated only weakly with the index score (ρ = 0.28). Conclusions. At discharge the HFRS can flag the patients whose admission went badly—one in five, yet nearly half of 30-day deaths and two-thirds of prolonged stays—for geriatric follow-up. It summarises what was documented during the admission, not the vulnerability that preceded it, and should not guide surgery or baseline risk adjustment.
