Routine Versus Selective Nasogastric Decompression After Bariatric and Abdominal Surgery: A Structured Narrative Evidence Review — Randomised Trials, Meta-Analyses, Procedure-Specific Evidence, Tube Reinsertion, Patient Burden and Perioperative Guidelines
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Background: For most of the twentieth century a nasogastric tube was left in place after abdominal surgery until bowel function returned. The aims were to prevent vomiting, gastric distension and aspiration, to protect anastomoses and to shorten ileus. From the 1980s onwards, randomised trials began to test whether routine postoperative decompression achieves these aims, and enhanced recovery pathways later made omission of the tube a standard item. Bariatric surgeons face the same question, with the added concern of protecting long staple lines and new anastomoses in patients with obesity. This review summarises the clinical evidence on routine versus selective (or no) postoperative nasogastric decompression across abdominal operations, with a separate look at bariatric surgery and at the operations where the answer may differ. Methods: Five PubMed/MEDLINE searches were run through the NCBI E-utilities on 25 November 2026, limited to publication dates from 1 January 1980 to 31 October 2026. They covered nasogastric decompression after surgery in general, randomised trials and systematic reviews, bariatric surgery, guidelines and surveys, and tube-related complications. Records were filtered by rule-based criteria and screened by hand, and a few guidelines were added through targeted look-ups. Numbers were taken only from retrieved abstracts or open-access full texts. Every reference was checked against PubMed and Crossref. Studies of tube placement verification, enteral feeding and bowel obstruction were outside the scope. Results: The searches returned 3056 records (1821 unique); the synthesis cites 123 publications. The pooled evidence across abdominal surgery is consistent. In the largest Cochrane review (33 trials, 5,240 patients), patients managed without a routine tube had earlier return of bowel function and fewer pulmonary complications, with no difference in anastomotic leak; vomiting was somewhat more frequent without a tube. Procedure-specific meta-analyses in colorectal surgery, gastrectomy, hepatectomy and pancreatoduodenectomy reached similar conclusions, and the only randomised trial of routine decompression after pancreatoduodenectomy found no difference in complications of Clavien–Dindo grade II or higher. The cost of omission is a need for tube insertion in a minority of patients. Reported rates were mostly 2% to 15% after colorectal, gastric and hepatic surgery and 15% to 22% after pancreatoduodenectomy, and reinsertion was strongly associated with an underlying major complication. Oesophagectomy is the main exception. A 2025 multicentre randomised trial of 448 patients could not show that omitting the tube was non-inferior for anastomotic leak (22.1% without versus 15.2% with five days of decompression). In bariatric surgery the direct evidence is small: one randomised trial of 145 sleeve gastrectomies and one cohort of 1,067 gastric bypasses found no benefit from routine postoperative decompression. Intraoperative orogastric tubes carry their own risk of being stapled or sutured into the pouch or sleeve. Current enhanced recovery guidelines advise against routine postoperative tubes in colorectal, liver and bariatric surgery, recommend individual assessment in emergency laparotomy, and still recommend decompression after oesophagectomy. Conclusions: After elective abdominal and bariatric surgery, routine postoperative nasogastric decompression does not reduce leak, pulmonary complications or length of stay, and it causes discomfort. Selective use, with prompt insertion for persistent vomiting, distension or a developing complication, is supported by the trial evidence. Oesophagectomy, and probably some emergency operations, are different and need their own evidence. The bariatric evidence base is thin and is mostly extrapolated from other abdominal operations. Manufacturer website: https://sybariatric.com

title: A Novel Left‐Hand Tool Control System for Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection: Technical Description and Initial Clinical Experience (With Video)
abstract: In conventional endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), the operator's right hand alternates between stabilizing the endoscope shaft and manipulating the treatment device. We developed a left‐hand tool control system, assembled from a polytetrafluoroethylene tube, fixation tape, two plastic one‐touch clips serving as a movable device grip, and a sterile adapter cap, that relocates the accessory‐channel inlet into the left‐hand control field so that the knife is advanced and withdrawn with the left hand while the right hand maintains continuous scope control. Unlike existing left‐hand techniques, the grasping point lies only a short distance from the relocated inlet, which prevents the sheath from buckling during advancement. We report the initial experience in 41 consecutive ESD procedures (three esophageal, 13 gastric, and 25 colorectal) performed between June 2025 and April 2026. In every procedure, the operator maintained shaft torque and moved the knife simultaneously and without assistance. En bloc and R0 resection were each achieved in 39 procedures (95.1%), with no muscle injury or intraprocedural perforation. Within 3 weeks, one colorectal procedure was followed by delayed bleeding treated endoscopically and another by an unscheduled 3‐day prolongation of hospital stay. In an exploratory comparison adjusted for specimen area, fibrosis, age, and organ, ESD time was not shorter than in conventional procedures by the same operator during the preceding 2 years (time ratio 1.23, 95% confidence interval 1.00–1.52). The system was feasible in this single‐operator series; its effect on procedural efficiency and its safety require prospective evaluation.

title: Editorial: Advances in bioelectrical impedance analysis for clinical nutrition
abstract: for trunk impedance; one showed a measurement uncertainty of approximately 1.4% at the 95% confidence level, whereas the other exhibited greater deviations. These findings indicate that measurements obtained from different devices should not be assumed to be interchangeable and underscore the need for calibration, quality control, transparent reporting of measurement uncertainty and standardized measurement conditions in both research and clinical practice.Population-specific validity is equally important. In patients receiving maintenance haemodialysis, Wang et al. showed that dialysis-specific anthropometric equations improved agreement with Appendicular Skeletal Muscle Mass (ASMM) estimated by multi-frequency BIA under standardized post-dialysis conditions, compared with equations developed in the general population (10). The model combining height-weight and height-circumference variables showed the most consistent performance across internal validation and analyses stratified by ultrafiltration volume. These findings support the importance of population-specific calibration when assessing muscle mass in patients with diseaserelated alterations in body composition and fluid balance.Several contributions show that body mass index (BMI) alone does not fully capture clinically relevant differences in body composition. Li Y. et al. demonstrated that masked obesity can occur among young adults with a normal BMI and that the muscle-to-fat ratio may provide additional information for identifying this phenotype (11). In children and adolescents with multifactorial dyslipidaemia, Hamou et al. found that adiposity and the balance between muscle and fat were associated with cardiometabolic markers, particularly blood pressure, beyond the information provided by body weight alone (12). Zhang et al. reported sex-specific differences in adipose and skeletal muscle compartments among adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus and age-, sex-and BMI-matched controls, whereas phase angle did not differ significantly between the groups (13). These observations support the complementary use of body-composition phenotyping alongside BMI and emphasize the importance of interpreting BIAderived measures according to age, sex and disease context.The study by Khazrai et al. evaluated the potential role of BIA in monitoring body-composition changes during nutritional interventions (14). After 28 days of Very Low-Energy Ketogenic Therapy (VLEKT) with standardized meal replacements, participants showed reductions in body weight, BMI, waist circumference and fat mass (FM) percentage, together with an increase in the relative proportion of fat-free mass. However, absolute FFM decreased slightly, indicating that the change in its percentage primarily reflected a proportionally greater reduction in FM. PhA, body cell mass and hydration-related parameters remained stable. The intervention also coincided with changes in faecal microbial composition and stool-derived metabolites. This study provides preliminary evidence of short-term changes in body composition, gut microbiota and stool-derived metabolites during VLEKT and warrants confirmation in larger, controlled studies with longer follow-up and integration of microbiome data with biochemical and clinical outcomes.The relationship between bioelectrical parameters, nutritional status and physical functions was explored in rehabilitation and hospital settings. In 87 subacute post-stroke patients admitted to a rehabilitation setting, Bertoncini et al. found that Nutrigram®, a novel BIA-derived index, was associated with the Mini Nutritional Assessment Short Form and the Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index and that lower values were observed in patients with malnutrition diagnosed according to the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition criteria (15). Higher Nutrigram® values remained independently associated with lower odds of malnutrition, supporting its potential as a rapid and objective adjunct to nutritional assessment in post-stroke rehabilitation. A complementary perspective was provided by Zhong et al. in 998 hospitalized patients with cancer (16). Although extracellular water-to-total body water ratio increased across higher Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 (NRS2002) categories, single-time-point measures of skeletal muscle index, visceral fat area, PhA and extracellular water-to-total body water ratio were not independently associated with nutritional risk after adjustment. By contrast, albumin and C-reactive protein showed more consistent associations in the adjusted analyses. In this setting, BIA-derived parameters may therefore complement validated nutritional screening and clinical assessment by providing additional information on body composition and fluid distribution.The clinical relevance of PhA across nutritional, functional and prognostic domains was examined in respiratory, oncological and metabolic populations. In 235 older patients with respiratory diseases (17), Li C. et al. found that sarcopenia modified the association between PhA and GLIM-defined malnutrition: lower PhA was associated with malnutrition among patients with sarcopenia, but not among those without sarcopenia. By contrast, lower PhA was associated with impaired physical performance across the entire cohort, independently of sarcopenia status. In oncology, Mei et al. synthesized 10 observational studies involving 1,439 patients with colorectal cancer and found that lower PhA was repeatedly associated with poorer nutritional status, less favorable body-composition and muscle-related measures, adverse short-term outcomes and reduced survival (18). This prognostic perspective was also supported by Yanxin et al. in a prospective cohort of patients with newly diagnosed nasopharyngeal carcinoma undergoing chemoradiotherapy, in whom higher baseline PhA was independently associated with longer overall survival after adjustment for age and tumour stage (19). Finally, Hao et al. examined the longitudinal dimension of PhA in 90 patients undergoing esophagectomy for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (20). A greater perioperative decline in PhA was associated with postoperative sarcopenia after adjustment for preoperative sarcopenia and nutritional risk, whereas preoperative PhA alone was not associated with postoperative sarcopenia, postoperative complications or length of stay. In a different metabolic context, Sabuncular et al. found that adults with hepatic steatosis defined by controlled attenuation parameter had higher whole-body and segmental PhA than those without steatosis, consistently across age and obesity strata (21). PhA remained independently associated with steatosis alongside waist circumference and age, although its discriminative performance was moderate when considered alone and improved when combined with simple anthropometric variables. Rather than supporting a universal interpretation of PhA, these findings emphasize that its clinical meaning depends on the outcome assessed, the underlying bodycomposition phenotype and the disease context.Taken together, the contributions in this Research Topic highlight the complementary value of BIAderived measures in clinical nutrition. Beyond BMI alone, BIA can provide information on adiposity, muscle-related characteristics and body-composition patterns that may be relevant to nutritional and cardiometabolic assessment. The studies also emphasize the importance of using populationappropriate equations and reliable measurement procedures, particularly in patients with altered body composition or fluid balance. Among raw bioelectrical parameters, PhA was associated with nutritional status, physical performance, sarcopenia and clinical outcomes across several populations, while its interpretation varied according to the disease setting, underlying muscle phenotype and timing of assessment.BIA should therefore be considered as complementary tool in nutritional assessment, alongside anthropometry, dietary information, laboratory findings, muscle function and clinical evaluation, rather than a stand-alone diagnostic method.The contributions to this Research Topic highlight the need to move beyond the simple estimation of body composition towards a more comprehensive and context-specific interpretation of bioelectrical parameters. title: Financial Performance Moderates Fiscal Independence and Priority Expenditure on Human Development Index
abstract: Massive intergovernmental transfers to newly autonomous regencies in Papua consistently fail to accelerate human development amidst fragile local tax bases and volatile budget execution. This study evaluated how regional financial performance moderated the effects of fiscal independence, education expenditure, and health expenditure on the Human Development Index across twenty newly autonomous Papuan regencies from 2018 to 2024. A balanced census panel of 140 observations was analyzed using Fixed Effects Moderated Regression Analysis. Empirical estimates demonstrate that education expenditure exerts a strong positive direct effect on human development, whereas fiscal independence and health expenditure show statistically insignificant effects because subsistence economies limit local taxation and extreme alpine transport costs erode healthcare purchasing power. Although standalone financial performance negatively affects human development due to conservative revenue target setting, financial performance significantly moderates and strengthens the positive effect of education expenditure. These novel contingency findings prescribe enforcing educational earmarks alongside subsidized highland logistics.

title: Increased body mass index correlates with the development of posttraumatic complications and an altered extracellular vesicle profile in the plasma following severe traumatic injury
abstract: Introduction Polytrauma triggers a pronounced systemic thromboinflammatory response, during which immunoregulatory extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as biomarkers for identifying patients at risk for post-traumatic complications. Obesity and an elevated body mass index (BMI) influence both baseline and stress-induced systemic inflammation. However, their impact on the post-traumatic EV profile has not yet been systematically characterized. This study aimed to investigate BMI-stratified plasma EV profiles and evaluate their associations with post-traumatic clinical course and outcomes. Methods Adult trauma patients (≥18 years) with a severe multiple injury (injury severity score (ISS) ≥16) underwent blood sampling immediately upon admission to the emergency department at a level 1 trauma center. Circulating EVs were isolated from plasma via size-exclusion chromatography and analyzed with a bead-based multiplex panel to assess the EV surface protein profiles. Clinical data and the occurrence of complications were assessed retrospectively. Patients were stratified according to BMI using a cutoff of 25 kg/m². Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was performed to assess associations between BMI and clinical variables, laboratory parameters, and EV populations. Results We included 85 patients with a median BMI of 24.8 (Interquartile range (IQR) 23.3-27.8) kg/m2, ISS of 24 (IQR 18-33), and in-hospital mortality rate of 13.8%. Despite comparable injury severity, patients with BMI ≥ 25 (n=39) had significantly higher rates of acute kidney injury (17.9% vs. 2.2%; p = 0.021) and pneumonia (28.2% vs. 8.7%; p=0.024) than patients with BMI < 25 (n=46). In-hospital mortality did not differ significantly between groups (10.3% vs. 17.4%; p=0.53). BMI correlated positively with increased C-reactive protein levels on days 5, 6, and 8 (r=0.26–0.36; p< 0.05) and creatinine levels on days 3 to 7 (r = 0.26–0.34; p< 0.05). In contrast, BMI correlated negatively with three EV populations: platelet-associated CD42a + (r=-0.23; p=0.033), immune-cell associated CD40 + (r =-0.22; p=0.043), and endothelial/leukocyte-associated CD31 + (r =-0.23; p=0.036) EVs. Discussion This study provides the first systematic observation suggesting that BMI may influence circulating EV profiles in severely injured patients. Higher BMI was associated with prolonged late-phase systemic inflammation and increased rates of pulmonary and renal complications, but not with increased mortality, consistent with the ‘obesity paradox’ described in trauma. The concurrent reduction in mainly platelet-, immune cell-, and endothelial-derived EVs with increasing BMI suggests a BMI-dependent modulation of the EV response to trauma, which may contribute to the mechanisms underlying this paradox.

title: The feasibility of positive expiratory pressure device on lung expansion and shoulder range of motions in thoracotomy patients
abstract: Background: Thoracic surgery leads to respiratory muscle injury and a decrease in lung expansion and shoulder joint movement. Positive expiratory pressure (PEP) breathing with conventional chest physical therapy techniques may improve lung volume. Objectives: To evaluate the effects of PEP breathing on lung expansion and shoulder range of motion after training in thoracotomy patients. Materials and methods: Eighteen thoracotomy patients (ages between 31 and 83 years) who met inclusion criteria received PEP breathing at 15 cmH2O loadings, 15 breaths/set, 12 sets/day with conventional chest physical therapy. Comparisons of slow vital capacity (SVC), chest wall expansion, and shoulder ranges of motion at pre-, post-operative, and before discharge from the hospital were used the statistics repeated measure ANOVA and post hoc tests were used TukeyHSD. Results: The result shows significant improvement in SVC (p < 0.001) and chest wall expansion (p < 0.01). Shoulder range of motion was a significant increase in flexion (p < 0.001) and abduction (p < 0.001) when compared to pre-operative, post-operative, and before discharge from the hospital. Conclusion: PEP breathing combined with conventional chest physiotherapy treatment could improve lung expansion, and shoulder motion in thoracotomy patients. Randomized control trials should be conducted in a further study.

title: Comparative Analysis of Multielectrode Mapping Catheter Designs in Scar‐Related Ventricular Tachycardia Ablation
abstract: BACKGROUND: High-density (HD) electroanatomical mapping is routinely used for scar-related ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation. The performance of multielectrode mapping catheters with different array designs has not been directly compared. OBJECTIVE: To compare the procedural performance of two different multielectrode mapping catheter designs-a flexible spline catheter (SC) and a fixed paddle catheter (PC) in scar-related VT ablation. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 104 consecutive patients who underwent left ventricular scar-related VT ablation (SC, n = 44; PC, n = 60). The primary endpoint was acute procedural success, defined as non-inducibility of the clinical VT after ablation. Secondary endpoints included procedural efficiency, VT inducibility, VT morphology burden, and procedural and in-hospital adverse events. RESULTS: Acute procedural success was achieved in 95.5% of SC and 98.3% of PC procedures (p = 0.57). Procedure duration, LV mapping time, mapping point count, fluoroscopy time, and adverse-event rates were comparable between groups. Overall VT inducibility (mechanical or programmed induction) was similar (81.8% vs. 76.7%; p = 0.63); however, ≥3 distinct inducible VT morphologies were significantly more frequent with the spline catheter than with the paddle catheter (38.6% vs. 11.7%; p = 0.002). During follow-up, rates of VT recurrence (34.5% vs. 20.0%; p = 0.19) and repeat ablation (13.8% vs. 7.3%; p = 0.44) did not differ significantly between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Both catheter designs achieved comparable acute procedural success, procedural efficiency, and safety in scar-related VT ablation. Procedures with the spline catheter were associated with a higher inducible VT morphology burden; this hypothesis-generating finding, which may partly reflect differences in substrate location, warrants prospective evaluation.

title: Glucose-to-albumin ratio predicts major adverse cardiovascular events after non-cardiac surgery: a two-cohort study with external validation of machine learning models
abstract: Background The glucose-to-albumin ratio (GAR) has emerged as a novel prognostic biomarker in various clinical settings, but its association with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) after non-cardiac surgery and its value in machine learning (ML) prediction have not been validated. Methods This retrospective study included patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery from the MOVER and INSPIRE cohort. The primary outcome was MACE occurring within 30 days after surgery during the index hospitalization. The association between GAR and MACE was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. Six ML models were developed by 5-fold stratified cross-validation internally (MOVER) and subsequently validated externally (INSPIRE). SHAP analysis was applied to the best-performing model to interpret the contribution of each predictor to the outcome prediction. Results Among 8,098 patients in the MOVER cohort, MACE occurred in 394 (4.9%), while among 75,971 patients in the INSPIRE cohort, it occurred in 902 (1.2%). Multivariable analyses indicated that per SD increase in GAR significantly correlated with MACE in both MOVER (OR = 1.15, 95% CI = 1.06–1.25) and INSPIRE (OR = 1.12, 95% CI = 1.07–1.18) cohorts. As a categorical variable, high GAR level remained associated with MACE in both MOVER (OR = 1.69, 95% CI = 1.32–2.17) and INSPIRE (OR = 1.30, 95% CI = 1.08–1.56) cohorts. Among 6 ML models, CatBoost achieved the highest AUC for MACE in both internal (AUC = 0.842) and external (AUC = 0.868) validation. In two cohorts, adding GAR to the RCRI score improved the AUC (from 0.631 to 0.713 in MOVER and from 0.796 to 0.839 in INSPIRE). Moreover, incorporating GAR provided a modest improvement in discrimination over the base model in two cohorts (all P < 0.05). SHAP analysis ranked ASA classification and GAR as the two most important predictors of MACE in MOVER cohort. Conclusions GAR is independently associated with MACE occurring within 30 days after surgery during the index hospitalization in two cohorts. ML models incorporating GAR achieved good, externally validated discrimination, and GAR added a modest improvement in discrimination over a base model, supporting its potential as a readily available biomarker for perioperative cardiovascular risk stratification.

title: Benchmarking Pancreaticoduodenectomy in Australia Using Clinical Quality Registry Data: Preliminary Benchmarks and a Need for Data Expansion
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Benchmarking surgical outcomes using local data is a key component of healthcare quality improvement. International groups have outlined a range of benchmarks for pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) but there are currently no benchmarks using Australian data. This study aimed to use existing Australian registry data to develop benchmarks for PD. METHODS: Retrospective cohort study based on existing data from two pancreatic cancer registries in Australia-the Upper Gastrointestinal Cancer Registry and the Pancreatic Cancer: Understanding Routine Practice and Lifting End Results Registry. Established methodologies were used to develop benchmarks for surgical outcomes for patients undergoing PD for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) for each registry, de-identified to Registry A and B. RESULTS: Registry A included 602 PDAC patients from 18 hospitals, and Registry B included 496 patients from 15 hospitals. The surgical outcomes available to benchmark for Registry A were lymph node yield and microscopically positive surgical margin (R1) status. Registry B had these outcomes in addition to inpatient mortality, readmission rate (within 30 days), and survival. Results were similar to international comparisons. CONCLUSION: This study presents the first published benchmarks for PD in Australia, representing the best currently available data and showcasing the substantial work of existing Australian registries, while also highlighting that there are substantial opportunities for dataset expansion. Locally developed benchmarks for the outcomes specified as core indicators by international bodies should be the minimum goal, with collection of other key outcomes providing richer data.

title: Low skeletal muscle mass increases the risk of perioperative myocardial injury in older patients with hip fractures: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Background Perioperative myocardial injury (PMI) is a frequent complication after surgical treatment of hip fractures and is linked to elevated mortality rates, especially in older patients. While low skeletal muscle mass (LSMM) is a widespread and potentially reversible condition in this demographic, its specific contribution to PMI remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between preoperative LSMM and the occurrence of PMI in older patients undergoing surgical treatment of hip fractures. Methods A retrospective cohort design was employed, enrolling patients aged 65 years or older who received surgical treatment of hip fractures between January 2021 and July 2025. LSMM status was determined using the preoperative skeletal muscle index derived from an axial chest computed tomography slice at the T12 vertebral level. Propensity score matching (PSM) was utilized to create comparable cohorts of patients with and without LSMM. The incidence of PMI was evaluated and compared across cohorts and multivariable logistic regression was performed to determine independent predictors. Subsequently, a exploratory prediction model for PMI was constructed and evaluated using a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Results Among 1,165 patients, the overall incidence of PMI was 9.1%. Following PSM, each group comprised 190 participants. The PMI rates for the LSMM group versus non-LSMM group were: 13.7% versus 3.2% (P < 0.001). multivariable logistic regression identified LSMM as an independent predictor of PMI (odds ratio: 6.475; 95% CI: 2.351–17.829; P < 0.001). ROC curve analysis showed an AUC of 0.850 (95% CI: 0.794–0.907), indicating strong predictive ability. Conclusions Independent of other clinical variables, LSMM is significantly associated with a heightened risk of PMI in older patients undergoing surgical treatment of hip fractures. Further interventional research is required to examine whether perioperative LSMM strategies can be integrated into surgical protocols to prevent PMI.

title: Case Report: Sacubitril/valsartan-induced refractory hypotension after 48-hour discontinuation: a case highlighting prolonged washout need in hypothyroidism
abstract: Background Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI) are established first-line antihypertensive agents that exert their effect by dual inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and neprilysin. The recommended preoperative discontinuation period for these drugs is generally 24–36 h. We report a case of refractory hypotension occurring during the general anaesthesia in a hypothyroid patient, despite a 48-hour discontinuation of sacubitril/valsartan. Clinical presentation A 65-year-old female patient with hypothyroidism was scheduled for abdominal aortic stent-graft implantation and aortography. The patient had discontinued sacubitril/valsartan 48 h preoperatively. Following admission to the operating room and the induction of anaesthesia, her blood pressure decreased from 200/100 mmHg to 60/35 mmHg. The administration of vasoactive agents, including norepinephrine and dopamine, failed to improve her blood pressure, leading to the suspension of the procedure. A second surgery was performed after a continuous drug-free interval of approximately 7 days, during which sacubitril/valsartan had not been reintroduced following the first procedure. The procedure was completed successfully without recurrence of refractory hypotension. Conclusion We encountered a case of refractory hypotension following anaesthesia induction, which was likely attributable to an insufficient preoperative washout period of the ARNI and the patient's co-existing hypothyroidism. Despite the drug being withheld for over 48 h, this case underscores the necessity for a comprehensive preoperative evaluation and the implementation of proactive preventive strategies in patients on long-term ARNI therapy, particularly those with additional comorbidities.

title: Predictive value of elevated preoperative serum syndecan-1 and myeloperoxidase-DNA complex for aortic adverse events after endovascular repair of Stanford type B aortic dissection: a prospective cohort study
abstract: Objective To investigate the predictive value of preoperative serum syndecan-1 and myeloperoxidase-DNA complexes (MPO-DNA) for aortic adverse events (AAEs) after thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) in patients with Stanford type B aortic dissection (TBAD). Methods A total of 211 patients with TBAD who underwent TEVAR between January 2020 and January 2023 were prospectively enrolled. Preoperative serum levels of syndecan-1 and MPO-DNA were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). All patients were scheduled for follow-up of at least 3 years. Cox regression analysis was used to identify independent risk factors. Nested models and inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis were applied to evaluate predictive performance and incremental value. A combined prediction model was constructed based on the two biomarkers. Results AAEs occurred in 56 patients (26.54%). Preoperative serum levels of syndecan-1 (3.38 ± 0.82 vs. 2.34 ± 0.94 ng/mL, P < 0.001) and MPO-DNA (2.77 ± 0.85 vs. 2.03 ± 0.86 ng/mL, P < 0.001) were significantly higher in the AAE group than in the non-AAE group, and both were identified as independent risk factors for postoperative AAEs. In the IPCW time-dependent ROC analysis, the combined model yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.784, 0.790, and 0.835 for predicting AAE at 12, 24, and 36 months after surgery, respectively, with an integrated AUC (iAUC) of 0.800. Harrell's C-index was 0.774, and the model showed good calibration and clinical net benefit. According to the median risk score, patients were divided into a low-risk group (n = 105) and a high-risk group (n = 106); the cumulative incidence of AAEs differed significantly between the two groups (log-rank χ 2 = 50.56, P < 0.001). Conclusions Preoperative serum syndecan-1 and MPO-DNA are independent predictors of AAEs after TEVAR in patients with TBAD. The combined score of the two biomarkers can be used for preoperative risk stratification. However, its incremental value over single biomarkers and conventional clinical and imaging factors requires validation in multicenter external studies.

title: Later abortion care, practice, and service delivery in New York after Dobbs
journal: Frontiers in Global Women s Health
abstract: Introduction In 2022, Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health removed federal protections for abortion access. We describe efforts to expand access after Dobbs in New York, a state with legal protections for abortion. Methods Cross sectional survey (November-December 2024) with descriptive statistics of New York State practices identified through an email database maintained by reproductive health advocates, and semi-structured interviews with survey respondents (October-November 2025). We used a rapid qualitative assessment with thematic analysis to identify cross-cutting themes. Results Nine of 41 practices that provided abortion ≥13 weeks responded. All offered care to at least 22 weeks. A formal New York City-managed referral hub directed patients to practices best suited to their needs. Sites reported increased labor induction for later abortion, which was impacted by institutional culture. Most reported heightened attention to legal risks for out-of-state patients and undertook privacy and security precautions. New York's strong pro-choice position and state funding grants targeted to respond to the federal Dobbs legislation enabled sites to increase capacity, purchase equipment, and align institutional policies and practices. Staff hiring was limited by the time constraints of the grants. Several programs reported that institutional endorsement of abortion care was not reflected in resource allocation or was impacted by bureaucratic processes that impeded access. Conclusion New York-based abortion practices undertook multiple measures to expand access; however, site-specific structural and leadership barriers limited implementation. Funding opportunities, regional collaboration, and coordinated referral pathways are avenues for continued increased access for persons seeking abortion care in New York.

title: The effects of TIVA and combined intravenous–inhalational anesthesia (CIVIA) on early recovery parameters: a prospective randomized controlled trial
abstract: Background This study aimed to compare early recovery profiles and emergence agitation (EA) between propofol-based total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) and two combined intravenous–inhalational anesthesia (CIVIA) techniques incorporating desflurane and sevoflurane. Methods In this prospective, randomized, controlled trial, 238 adult patients undergoing elective spine surgery were enrolled and randomized. Patients were assigned to three BIS-guided maintenance strategies: propofol–remifentanil TIVA (n = 82), CIVIA–desflurane (0.5 age-adjusted MAC) (n = 78), or CIVIA–sevoflurane (0.5 age-adjusted MAC) (n = 78). Thirteen patients were excluded due to extreme perioperative bleeding or intraoperative monitoring difficulties, leaving a final analyzed cohort of 225 patients (n = 75 per group). The primary outcome was extubation time, assessed by an independent investigator blinded to group allocations. Secondary outcomes included postoperative recovery time, eye-opening time, pain scores, anesthetic consumption, and emergence agitation (Richmond Agitation–Sedation Scale > + 1). Results There were no statistically significant differences among the three groups in recovery time, extubation time, eye opening time and postoperative pain scores (p > 0.05). The incidence of emergence agitation did not differ significantly among groups (TIVA 18.7%, CIVIA–desflurane 25.3%, CIVIA–sevoflurane 24.0%; p = 0.587). Intraoperative propofol and remifentanil consumption were significantly higher in the TIVA group compared with both CIVIA groups (p < 0.05). Hemodynamic parameters and perioperative complication rates were similar between groups. Conclusions In elective spine surgery, CIVIA with desflurane or sevoflurane showed no significant differences in early recovery outcomes or emergence agitation compared with TIVA, while significantly reducing intravenous anesthetic consumption.

title: Biomedical waste management in health facilities in Uganda: a mixed-methods cross- sectional study of performance, enablers and barriers
abstract: Background Healthcare facilities generate general and hazardous waste that requires safe handling throughout the management process. Weaknesses at any stage, from segregation to final disposal, can expose healthcare workers, patients, waste handlers and surrounding communities to avoidable risks. This study assessed biomedical waste management (BMWM) performance across health facilities in Uganda and explored the operational factors that enabled or constrained implementation. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional mixed-methods study in 23 of 24 health facilities targeted across four regions of Uganda. One facility in the Eastern Region could not participate because of COVID-19-related access restrictions. Assessors used the East, Central and Southern Africa Health Community and East African Public Health Laboratory Networking Project checklist (version 1.2) to assess eight BMWM domains through document review and direct observation. Each indicator was scored as 0 (non-compliance), 1 (partial compliance) or 2 (full compliance). Descriptive statistics summarised facility and domain performance. An 80% threshold was applied as a study-defined satisfactory-performance benchmark. Key-informant interviews (KIIs) and focus-group discussions (FGDs) explored implementation experiences, enablers and barriers. Quantitative and qualitative findings were integrated during interpretation. Results The study included 242 participants, performance profile varied by domain and region. Waste generation had the highest regional score in Central Uganda (73.3%), whereas segregation and collection had the highest scores in Eastern (61.1%), Northern (85.5%) and South-Western Uganda (54.8%). Disposal was weakest in Central (9.1%) and Northern Uganda (22.0%); treatment was weakest in Eastern (17.0%) and South-Western Uganda (10.8%). Across facilities, median scores were highest for segregation and collection (65.8%) and waste generation (65.0%). Five of 23 facilities reached the 80% threshold for segregation and collection, and seven of 23 did so for waste generation. No facility reached the threshold for management and documentation, storage and transportation, treatment or disposal. Median treatment and disposal scores were 10.0% and 18.2%, respectively. Gulu Regional Referral Hospital had the highest overall score (67.9%), followed by Apac General Hospital (53.6%); Ndejja Health Centre III and Nsangi Health Centre III had the lowest scores (7.1% each). Reported enablers included oversight committees, staff training, colour-coded bins, personal protective equipment and contracted waste collection. Shortages of supplies, space and funding, irregular collection, non-functional treatment infrastructure and limited verification of final disposal constrained performance. Conclusions Biomedical waste management performance was stronger in upstream activities than in treatment and final disposal. Improvement efforts should address the entire waste-management process through clear facility accountability, dependable supplies, safe interim storage, reliable collection, functional treatment systems, verified final disposal and continuing staff training.

title: Dermatological care, training systems and care pathways for people with albinism in five sub-Saharan African countries in 2025–2026: a mixed-methods assessment
authors: Grâce – Alice Enam Bladavi Gumedzoe – Hoseto
abstract: Introduction Dermatological diseases are a major public health burden in sub-Saharan Africa, yet remain systematically under-prioritized. People with albinism (PWA) face compounded risk and melanin deficiency predisposes to life-threatening skin cancers while stigma and fragmented health systems impede care. Materials and methods We conducted a multi-country comparative assessment of dermatological care and training across Côte d'Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Madagascar, Niger, and Uganda. We conducted a mixed-methods cross-sectional evaluation in all five countries between November 2025 and March 2026. Data collection comprised documentary review, structured facility questionnaires, and key informant interviews with policymakers, dermatologists, training leaders, and civil society representatives. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively; qualitative data were interpreted thematically. Results All five countries share consistent deficits. No country has a dedicated dermatology policy or integrates dermatological or albinism indicators into its health information system. Specialist shortages are severe (1:369,000 in Côte d'Ivoire to 1:4,783,000 in DRC; benchmark 1:50,000–100,000), compounded by extreme urban concentration that leaves rural populations and PWA without specialist access. Postgraduate training capacity is critically insufficient, essential equipment is largely absent from public facilities, and government procurement and routine public provision of sunscreen were largely absent with public provision documented at only one of the six assessed sites in Niger. PWA consistently present at advanced stages with ulcerated lesions and inoperable cancers, driven by interlocking barriers of cost, geography, stigma, and provider knowledge gaps. Civil society organizations are the primary, and often sole, source of structured care for PWA across all five countries. Conclusion Dermatology is systematically neglected across all five health systems. To close these gaps, governments should implement coordinated actions across five domains: national dermatology policy, postgraduate training capacity, essential equipment at regional hospitals, integration of dermatological and albinism indicators into HMIS, and public procurement of sunscreen as an essential medicine. Regional cooperation and teledermatology offer strategic pathways to accelerate equitable access.

title: Immigration Enforcement and Appointment Attendance at an Urban Federally Qualified Health Center: An Interrupted Time Series Analysis
abstract: Immigration enforcement operations are hypothesized to deter immigrant-origin populations from seeking healthcare, a phenomenon termed the "chilling effect." However, quantitative evidence from electronic health record (EHR) data at Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) is limited, particularly using methods capable of detecting gradual trajectory changes. We conducted a retrospective interrupted time series (ITS) analysis using 109 weeks of scheduling data (January 2024 to January 2026) from a Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC) in the Midwest, a 12-site FQHC serving a large immigrant-origin population in Chicago, Illinois. Three immigration enforcement events served as interruptions: Enhanced Targeted Operations (January 26, 2025), Operation Midway Blitz (September 8, 2025), and a national immigration enforcement surge (January 19, 2026). Outcomes were weekly cancellation rate, no-show rate, and attendance rate. ITS regression with Newey-West heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) standard errors was the primary analysis, supplemented by Welch pre/post comparisons and a calendar-week-matched year-over-year comparison of 2025 versus 2024. A secondary ethnicity analysis used individual-level records (n = 563,502) stratified by patient OMB ethnicity. A significant level increase in cancellation rate was detected at Event 1 (+ 1.66 pp; p = 0.009); no other level changes reached significance at Events 1 or 2. The ITS identified significant slope changes: after Event 1, the no-show rate trajectory reversed from declining to rising (+ 0.073 percentage points [pp]/week; p < 0.001). After Event 2, this slope reversed again (− 0.10 pp/week; p < 0.001) while the cancellation rate slope increased (+ 0.18 pp/week; p = 0.004). Year-over-year analysis showed that the first weeks of 2025 were improving relative to the same weeks in 2024 (cancellation rate − 1.6 pp lower; attendance + 3.8 pp higher), reversing after Event 1. Site-level analysis identified a significant no-show increase at Auburn Gresham (+ 3.1 pp; p < 0.001), which remained significant after correction for multiple site-level comparisons. Hispanic patients had consistently lower cancellation rates than non-Hispanic patients (gap: 1.9 to 3.6 pp). A step-change in attendance at Event 3 (-1.27 pp; p = 0.047) was not robust to modeling choices and should not be read as a confirmed finding. Immigration enforcement events were associated with gradual trajectory changes in appointment attendance at an urban FQHC, rather than acute single-week disruptions. Enforcement appears to shift healthcare avoidance behavior over weeks to months, and the mechanism evolves across events. These findings support the need for longitudinal EHR-based surveillance of enforcement impacts at safety net providers.

title: An intervention for healthcare professionals to offer an adapted proactive referral for online smoking cessation treatment in a health check-up setting: a single-arm feasibility study (N-EQUITY2301)
abstract: Background Proactive referral, in which healthcare staff connect smokers to smoking cessation services, is an effective implementation strategy for increasing service uptake. A health check-up is an optimal setting in which to provide proactive referral to a large number of smokers. This study evaluated the feasibility of conducting a definitive trial by examining the fidelity of a proactive referral adapted to the health check-up setting. Methods A single-arm feasibility study was conducted from January to April of 2024 at a health check-up center in Japan. The Brief Tobacco Intervention with Proactive Referral (BTI-PR) was developed as a proactive referral adapted to the health check-up setting. In the BTI-PR, healthcare professionals encourage smokers to schedule an appointment for online smoking cessation treatment while at the health check-up center. A provider-level intervention for the BTI-PR included a training session on the brief tobacco intervention, a BTI-PR guide, a BTI-PR checksheet, a flyer on the online treatment, and an instructional session on the BTI-PR. Healthcare professionals delivered the BTI-PR over a two-month period to smokers aged 20 years or older. Primary outcome was healthcare professionals' fidelity to the BTI-PR, defined as the proportion of smokers who were delivered the BTI-PR in accordance with the guide. Secondary outcomes included the proportion of smokers who received the online treatment and perceived acceptability and appropriateness of the BTI-PR by healthcare professionals and smokers. Results The BTI-PR was provided as described in the guide by four healthcare professionals to 42 of 49 eligible smokers (85.7%). Subsequently, one smoker (2.0%) received the online smoking cessation treatment. The BTI-PR was perceived as highly acceptable and appropriate by both healthcare professionals and smokers. Conclusion Following provision of a multi-component intervention for healthcare professionals, the BTI-PR was implemented with high fidelity. These findings do not establish BTI-PR effectiveness but inform the planning of a future definitive trial to evaluate its effectiveness, and also inform the development of context-adapted implementation strategies for delivering high-fidelity proactive referral in health check-up settings. Clinical Trial Registration: https://center6.umin.ac.jp/cgi-open-bin/ctr_e/ctr_view.cgi?recptno=R000060819, identifier UMIN000053290.

title: Economic toxicity due to nomadism of the radiotherapy patient of the Regional Institute of Neoplastic Diseases of the Center, 2021
abstract: Background: The knowledge of the expenses generated by the cancer patient at the Latin American level is scarce, and null in radiotherapy.Objective: To demonstrate the relationship between transfer costs and the start of radiotherapy.Method: Quantitative, observational, retrospective, cross-sectional and analytical study.From a sample of 126 patients with cancer diagnosis who received radiotherapy in 2021.The sampling was for convenience, collecting data through medical records and expense files.To confirm or rule out the correlation of variables, Spearman's Rho test was performed.Results: There is a positive correlation between transportation costs and the start of radiotherapy; the average weekly expense is 320.26 soles ($84.28);there is a positive correlation between weekly monetary transfer costs and distance of origin; and there is a positive correlation between time to start radiotherapy and remoteness of origin.Conclusion: The relationship between transfer cost and the start of radiotherapy is demonstrated; as well as the relationship of the time to start from the indication of irradiation with the distance of origin of the patients.

title: Economic evaluation of denosumab in patients with solid tumors with bone metastasis at the IMSS
abstract: Objective: To evaluate denosumab economically compared with a mixed scenario of zoledronic acid or no treatment if there is contraindication to such agent due to severe kidney impairment (Mix ZA/No Trt) in patients with solid tumors (ST) with bone metastasis.Method: It is a cost-effectiveness analysis based on a Markov model with a lifetime horizon, under the IMSS perspective.We evaluated the frequencies of skeletal-related events (SRE) as well as the costs associated to drug acquisition, intravenous infusion of ZA, routine patient management, medical attention of SRE, and treatment of serious adverse events.Results: In the base-case, denosumab resulted dominant over Mix ZA/No Trt, with mean savings of $2,494 Mexican pesos and 0.781 SRE avoided per patient.If ZA is given every 12 weeks, denosumab would not be dominant, but cost-effective.Denosumab was either dominant or cost-effective in 74.7% of the simulations.Conclusions: In patients with ST with bone metastasis, denosumab represents a dominant or at least a cost-effective intervention in comparison with Mix ZA/No Trt.

title: Implementing a trauma-informed mindful mental health service in a community mental health setting: a 10-year program description and preliminary evaluation
abstract: Introduction Mindfulness-based programs (MBPs) have demonstrated efficacy for reducing anxiety, depression, and stress, yet implementation in community mental health settings serving trauma-exposed, low-income, and racially/ethnically diverse populations remains limited. Service-level trauma-informed delivery models are largely undescribed. Methods We conducted a retrospective quality improvement evaluation of the Mindful Mental Health Service (MMHS), a trauma-informed, insurance-reimbursable MBP clinical service at Cambridge Health Alliance, a safety-net public health system, using administrative records spanning 2019-2026 and voluntary pre-post questionnaires. MMHS offers four group types with co-facilitation, multilingual programming, and trauma-informed adaptations across referral, intake, delivery, and supervision. Six abbreviated measures assessed anxiety, depression, perceived stress, self-compassion, emotion dysregulation, and interoceptive awareness. Results MMHS delivered 148 group cohorts with 1,796 enrollments and a 72% completion rate; an estimated 40% of enrollments were from participants who were racially or ethnically minoritized, had a primary language other than English, or attended Spanish- or Portuguese-language groups, and more than half of referred patients had federally funded or subsidized insurance. In participants who completed all six measures on both voluntary questionnaires (n = 114), self-compassion, emotion regulation, and interoceptive awareness improved significantly (| d | = 0.23–0.24); among those with elevated baseline symptoms, all six outcomes improved significantly (| d | = 0.45–1.29). Discussion These findings suggest preliminary feasibility and clinical utility of this service within a safety-net community mental health system. Results should be interpreted considering the retrospective observational design and small matched outcome subsample. MMHS represents a replicable model for equity-centered, trauma-informed mindfulness care in safety-net settings.

title: Nurse Staffing Ratios and Patient Mortality in Hospitals
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Whether the number of registered nurses on a ward changes the chance that a patient dies has been studied for more than two decades, and the answer is still contested. This paper combines a synthesis of secondary evidence with an analytical model and an original panel regression. The synthesis rests on 101 sources retrieved and checked in November 2026: multi-country surveys, single-system cohorts, systematic reviews, staffing laws and guidance in the United States, Australia, Britain, Ireland, and Germany, and studies from Kenya and Nigeria. Effect sizes are given as the original authors report them, and nothing is pooled. Observational studies from Europe, England, New Zealand, and the United States consistently link fewer patients per nurse, more registered-nurse time, and a larger registered-nurse share with lower mortality, though the reported odds ratios are modest. A Queensland panel study reports lower 30-day mortality after ratios were introduced, an analysis of California's mandate found no causal effect on patient safety, and a Cochrane review found no eligible studies of staffing levels. Turning to the new work, a competing-hazards model of rescue after a complication implies that each added patient per nurse does less additional harm as workloads rise, a prediction that bears on hospitals with 14 to 25 patients per nurse. A pre-specified two-way fixed-effects regression on 255 state-quarters of U.S. hospital reports, January 2021 to March 2022, finds no association between the share of hospitals declaring a critical staffing shortage and in-hospital COVID-19 deaths per 100 patient-days once state and quarter effects are removed (coefficient −0.0017, p = 0.821), although a small positive association appears across states. Evidence from low- and middle-income countries is thin. The record supports a protective association and a plausible causal link. It does not fix a safe ratio. Keywords: nurse staffing; patients per nurse; hospital mortality; failure to rescue; skill mix; mandated ratios; evidence synthesis

title: Invisible at the Interface: Nurses’ Hidden Labour in Sustaining Access to Digitally Mediated Care
Ensuring Nursing Expertise Continuity in Hospitals: Distribution, Accessibility and Substitutability — A Scoping Review
abstract: Nursing expertise is an essential organisational resource that contributes to patient safety, quality of care, clinical decision-making and continuity of healthcare services. Although existing approaches to nursing workforce management predominantly focus on staffing levels, skill mix, professional competence and workforce retention, less attention has been directed towards how hospitals ensure the continuous availability of appropriate nursing expertise across organisational units, clinical settings and working shifts. This scoping review aims to map and synthesise existing evidence on the distribution, accessibility and substitutability of nursing expertise in hospitals. The review will identify relevant organisational models, management strategies, assessment instruments, barriers and facilitators, as well as reported implications for nursing practice, patient safety, continuity of care and organisational resilience. The review will encompass all hospital nursing specialties, professional roles and levels of clinical experience, without geographical restrictions. It will be conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and reported following the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The expected outcome is a comprehensive mapping of the available evidence and the identification of research gaps related to nursing expertise continuity. The findings may provide an evidence-informed foundation for the subsequent development of a Nursing Expertise Continuity Framework (NECF), supporting hospital-wide nursing expertise management, competency-based workforce planning, professional collaboration and organisational resilience.

title: A scalable leadership development model for advanced practice providers
Centralized Perioperative Transition‐to‐Practice Program: Restructuring Orientation to Support Multiple Units
Occupational Health Hazards and Safety Protocol Compliance among Clinical Staff across Tertiary and Secondary Healthcare Facilities in Gombe State, Nigeria: A Multi-Center Cross-Sectional Analysis
abstract: Background Healthcare practitioners routinely confront diverse biological, physical, ergonomic, chemical, and psychological hazards. Sustained adherence to Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) guidelines and personal protective equipment (PPE) protocols remains central to preventing occupational injuries, controlling nosocomial infections, and safeguarding workforce capacity. However, baseline empirical data regarding safety compliance and hazard distribution across different health facility tiers in North-Eastern Nigeria are limited. Objective This study evaluated occupational safety practices, institutional safety policy awareness, and hazard exposure patterns among clinical personnel across five major public healthcare facilities in Gombe State. Methods We conducted a multi-center cross-sectional quantitative survey across seven clinical professions (Nursing/Midwifery, Medicine, Medical Laboratory Science, Pharmacy, Physiotherapy, Radiography, and Dentistry). A multi-stage stratified proportionate random sampling framework was applied to a regional clinical workforce of N pop = 1,450 across five hospitals (Federal Teaching Hospital Gombe, State Specialist Hospital Gombe, Federal Medical Centre Kumo, General Hospital Bajoga, and General Hospital Kaltungo). To achieve adequate statistical power and preserve an Events Per Variable ratio > 25 for multivariable modeling, 575 questionnaires were distributed. We retrieved n = 502 valid questionnaires (87.3% response rate; covering 34.6% of the regional clinical workforce). Data were gathered using a validated tool adapted from the Weymouth Portland Health and Safety Self-Assessment Questionnaire (α = 0.83, Content Validity Index = 0.88). Chi-square tests (ꭓ 2), Cramér’s V effect sizes, and multivariable binary logistic regression models (reporting Adjusted Odds Ratios [aOR] and 95% Confidence Intervals [95% CI]) were performed (p < 0.05). Results Ergonomic strain emerged as the dominant hazard, with 76.5% (n = 384) of participants experiencing work-related musculoskeletal disorders primarily low back pain (51.2%) and neck/shoulder discomfort (25.3%) followed by high workload-related psychological stress (69.7%). Biological exposures were frequent: 56.4% reported mucosal or skin contact with blood and body fluids, while 43.2% sustained percutaneous needle-stick or sharps injuries within the preceding 12 months. PPE adherence varied widely: standard glove utilization was high (93.2%), whereas use of facial protection (68.1%), protective gowns (47.4%), specialized safety footwear (31.5%), and protective eyewear or face shields (23.1%) was limited. Supply chain deficits and institutional stock-outs were identified by 80.5% of respondents as the primary obstacle to compliance, with secondary state hospitals reporting significantly higher stock-out frequencies than the federal tertiary center (p < 0.001). Hazard patterns differed significantly across professions (ꭓ 2 = 82.45, df = 6, p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.30). Multivariable logistic regression revealed that ≥ 5 years of clinical experience (aOR = 2.68, 95% CI: 1.82–3.95, p < 0.001) and completion of formal institutional OSH orientation (aOR = 3.42, 95% CI: 2.28–5.13, p < 0.001) independently predicted high PPE compliance. Conversely, nurses and physicians faced greater odds of percutaneous injury compared to allied health controls (aOR = 3.38, 95% CI: 2.21–5.17, p < 0.001). Conclusion Healthcare workers across public tertiary and secondary facilities in Gombe State experience notable ergonomic strain, psychological stress, and biological exposures. Although basic barrier practices are common, widespread compliance with comprehensive PPE protocols is hampered by supply deficits especially within secondary general hospitals and incomplete safety onboarding for early-career staff. Institutional safety management, mandatory orientation programs, ergonomic workspace adjustments, and stable supply procurement are needed to protect clinical personnel. Clinical Trial Registration Not applicable.

title: Nurse academics' experiences and perceptions of artificial intelligence in education, research, clinical practice and nursing management: a qualitative descriptive study
abstract: Background Nurse academics educate future nurses and nurse managers and often hold managerial roles, yet existing research has examined artificial intelligence (AI) in education, research, clinical practice and nursing management separately and mostly through surveys. This study aimed to explore nurse academics' experiences, perceptions and expectations regarding AI across academic work, nursing education, clinical practice and nursing management. Methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted with 17 nurse academics in Türkiye selected by criterion sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analysed in MAXQDA using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis. Coded segments were descriptively quantitized and code saturation was assessed. The study is reported according to the COREQ checklist. Results Nine themes and 47 codes (405 coded segments) were identified. Participants positioned AI as an assistant rather than a replacement for the nurse. AI was used most intensively in academic work, whereas clinical experience remained limited. In nursing management, use for duty rostering, in-service training planning and documentation stood out, and AI-generated rosters were reported to strengthen perceived fairness among nurses. Reliability, ethical and security concerns formed the most extensive theme, and verifying AI outputs against sources was the most frequently coded strategy. Although almost all participants used AI, 14 did not feel ready or competent and requested structured training. Participants emphasised that the final decision must remain with the nurse; most showed opportunity-oriented but conditional adoption. Conclusions Nurse academics adopt AI as a supportive tool under human oversight. Perceived lack of competence and concerns about the reliability of information are the main barriers to adoption. Nursing schools and healthcare organisations should provide structured AI literacy training, develop guidelines on output verification and data protection, and transparently pilot AI-assisted rostering in which the final decision remains with the nurse manager.

title: Effect of Surgical Instrument Availability on Operating Theatre Efficiency in Tertiary Care Hospitals
abstract: Background: Operating theatres are resource-intensive units whose workflow depends in part on complete, functional surgical instrument sets. Local evidence linking instrument availability to theatre efficiency remains limited.Objective: To evaluate surgical instrument availability among operating theatre staff in selected hospitals and its association with perceived operating theatre efficiency.Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted over four months among 43 operating theatre staff recruited by convenience sampling from THQ Depalpur, Surgical Hospital Mian Channu, Ihsan Mumtaz Hospital, and Iffat Anwar Medical Complex. A structured self-administered questionnaire collected demographics, five yes/no availability items, and five Likert-scale efficiency items. Data were analyzed in SPSS 27 using descriptive statistics, the chi-square test, and Spearman correlation (p ≤ 0.05).Results: Of 43 participants, 53.5% were male and 46.5% female; 55.8% were nurses and 44.2% OT technicians; 37.2% had less than one year of theatre experience. Availability was adequate in 51.2% (22/43) and inadequate in 48.8% (21/43). Perceived efficiency was moderate in 69.8%, high in 16.3%, and low in 14.0%. Mean availability and efficiency scores were 1.50 ± 0.23 and 2.99 ± 0.69. The association was not statistically significant (χ² = 4.751, df = 2, p = 0.093); 66.7% of cells had expected counts below 5. Spearman correlation was also non-significant (r = −0.299, p = 0.051).Conclusion: Staff reported mixed instrument availability and predominantly moderate perceived theatre efficiency. In this small convenience sample, a statistically significant association between instrument availability and operating theatre efficiency was not demonstrated. Larger studies with probability sampling and objective time-motion measures are needed.BS Operation Theater Technology thesis, Department of Emerging Allied Health Technologies, Faculty of Allied Health Sciences, Superior University, Lahore, Pakistan (2026). Supervisor: Mr. Umair Shafique.

title: Standardizing care in the community: Clinical flowcharts for common paediatric conditions in a Quebec school-based health centre
Management of an outbreak of central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) in patients with sickle cell disease at a tertiary care center in Brussels, Belgium
abstract: Patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) are at increased risk of central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs). We conducted a retrospective, observational, pre-post study of a 21-month long CLABSI outbreak in SCD patients at a tertiary care center, during which infection control measures were implemented. We identified cases from January 2023 to September 2024 through surveillance, calculated CLABSI rates, and used Poisson regression to compare them pre- and post-interventions. To assess routes of transmission, we audited catheter-associated factors. Catheter type distribution across periods was evaluated using chi-squared test. We identified 19 CLABSIs among 8 SCD patients. Baseline CLABSI rate was 0.17 per 1,000 patient-days, compared with 3.12 CLABSIs per 1,000 patient-days during the epidemic period ( p = 0.005), confirming the outbreak. Outbreak management involved comprehensive sets of measures including hand hygiene compliance audits, standardized catheter-related care protocols, communication strategies, patient education, equipment enhancements, algorithm-based catheter prescription, catheter placement assessments, staff training, a catheter referent nurse, and a root cause analysis. Following interventions, CLABSI rates decreased from 3.12 per 1,000 patient-days to 0.54 per 1,000 patient-days ( p = 0.024), and from 20.83 per 1,000 central-line days to 4.37 per 1,000 central-line days ( p = 0.034). Adjusting for monthly variations in central catheter types, the reduction in CLABSI incidence persisted ( p = 0.036). The proportion of peripheral catheters increased compared with central lines ( p < 0.001). Catheter protocol compliance reached 100% by 5 months after first interventions. Outbreak control involved open communication between patients and healthcare workers, and patients actively monitoring their catheters and dressings. Appropriate catheter prescribing was central to control efforts. SCD patients require specialized care, equipment, and follow-up to prevent CLABSIs.

title: Midwife‐Performed Point‐of‐Care Ultrasounds in a Community Birth Center Setting: A Program Evaluation
journal: Journal of Midwifery & Women s Health

title: Implementation research to improve compliance with iron-folic acid and calcium tablets in pregnant and lactating women in select states of India- findings from qualitative formative research
journal: Frontiers in Global Women s Health
abstract: Background Anemia remains a significant public health challenge, affecting over 57% of Indian women despite national intervention programs. Objective The formative research (as part of an implementation research) aimed to critically examine health systems to improve compliance with Iron-Folic Acid (IFA) and calcium supplementation among pregnant and lactating women. Methods Design: To understand and assess the strengths, opportunities and implementation challenges, formative research using exploratory qualitative methods was used. Building blocks of World Health Organization’s health systems framework was used as a reference. Thematic analysis was done guided by the WHO health systems building blocks. Settings: Two districts from two states in India. Participants: 52 in-depth interviews and 65 focus group discussions with stakeholders were conducted during 2021-22. The stakeholders included state level officials (from Government, bilateral agencies), service providers (Medical officers, field level functionaries) and community (pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls, and family members). Results The states have a structured procurement policy, logistics and supply chain, human resources and financing in place to support Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) program. Despite strong political commitment and structured frameworks for anemia control, significant implementation gaps were identified: unclear guidelines at peripheral facilities, inconsistent testing methodologies, inadequate counseling, occasional supply disruptions, overburdened staff with insufficient training, and limited mechanisms for tracking actual consumption. Sociocultural factors and side effects significantly impacted compliance. Digital interventions for monitoring showed promise but remained at nascent stages. Conclusion Effective anemia control requires exploring health systems comprehensively to identify context specific factors. Implementation strategies should aim to involve stakeholders to identify local solutions for supply-side constraints such as standardized protocols and improved monitoring systems. It should also unravel demand side factors like targeted counseling and community mobilization to achieve meaningful impact on maternal health outcomes.

title: Healthcare professionals’ experiences of weight and exercise management in UK adult cystic fibrosis services in the CFTR modulator era: a qualitative study
abstract: Background Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a life limiting inherited disease that primarily effects the respiratory and gastrointestinal systems. Patients with CF have complex healthcare needs requiring multidisciplinary specialist centre care, as this is associated with improved health outcomes. Recent introduction of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator therapy has significantly improved the health and life expectancy of this population. This study aimed to explore CF healthcare professionals experience of the impact of CFTR modulator therapies on specialist services. Methods Qualitative semi-structured online focus groups (n = 5) and individual (n = 8) interviews were conducted with 10 dietitians, 6 physiotherapists,4 clinical nurse specialists and 3 doctors working in adult CF centres. Interview data were analysed using the framework method. Themes and subthemes were mapped to Bronfenbrenner’s socio-ecological model to characterise the individual and interpersonal (micro), organisational (meso) and policy levels (macro) and chrono (time) influence of CFTR modulator therapies on the CF healthcare service model. Results Five main themes were identified; existing challenges (timeline -chrono), generalist vs. specialist (individual - micro), relationships and roles (interpersonal - micro), model of care (organisational – meso), normalising amid uncertainty (CF culture and society - macro). Conclusions Since the introduction of CFTR modulator therapies, specialised CF multidisciplinary teams have experienced a change in the healthcare needs and life expectancy of their patients due to fewer respiratory exacerbations, improved lung function, and weight gain. Services are now transitioning from acute care to the management of a chronic condition. As people with CF live longer and experience co-morbidities increasingly similar to the general population, services will need to incorporate approaches that prevent and manage co-morbidities associated with overweight, obesity and ageing. Targeted training, role development, and a change to infrastructure will be required to ensure CF services remain responsive to the evolving health needs of their patients. Partnership with primary care and clearer referral pathways to other specialist services will be essential to delivering effective care in the most appropriate settings. Research to develop effective behaviour change interventions and optimal nutritional targets for patients prescribed CFTR modulator therapies is required to direct clinical practice. Clinical trial number ISRCTN18226594 registration date 09/02/2026

title: Effective child and adolescent mental health care requires integrated and context-sensitive implementation
journal: Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
authors: Bruna Hinnah Borges Martins de Freitas
abstract: Child and adolescent mental health is a major public health priority because of the high prevalence of mental disorders and their long-term consequences (Kieling et al., 2024;Mulraney et al., 2021). In 2019, approximately 293 million people aged 5-24 years were living with a mental disorder, accounting for nearly one-fifth of the years lived with disability in this population (Kieling et al., 2024). Depression and depressive symptoms are also highly prevalent among children and adolescents (Lu et al., 2024). These findings reinforce the need for prevention, early identification, and continuity of care across health, education, social protection, and other settings in which children and adolescents live (World Health Organization and United Nations Children's Fund, 2024).However, findings vary across intervention types and study designs, and the available evidence does not consistently establish longer-term outcomes, functional recovery, sustainability, or costeffectiveness (Eapen et al., 2024;McHugh et al., 2024;Zhang et al., 2023;Kularatna et al., 2022). Implementation also depends on economic feasibility and on the capacity of systems to provide equitable, integrated, and continuous care. Implementation science examines how evidence-based practices can be adopted and sustained in routine care settings, considering the factors that influence their implementation (Williams and Beidas, 2019). Evidence on cost-effectiveness remains limited (Kularatna et al., 2022), while the availability of evidence-based practices does not guarantee their adoption. Professional training alone is often insufficient to sustain changes in practice, particularly when organizational culture, workforce capacity, service fragmentation, weak referral pathways, and discontinuity of care are not addressed (Williams and Beidas, 2019;Carbonell et al., 2024).In this Opinion article, we argue that improving child and adolescent mental health requires moving beyond the identification of effective interventions towards systems capable of selecting, delivering, coordinating, and sustaining appropriate support in routine practice. The article is concerned with the implementation and organization of mental health promotion, prevention, early identification, assessment, treatment pathways, psychosocial support, rehabilitation, and continuity of care; it does not evaluate the clinical efficacy of specific treatments, compare psychopharmacological regimens, or provide treatment protocols for particular diagnoses. Our focus is the service and implementation level: how evidence-informed interventions are made accessible, connected across services, adapted to local circumstances, and sustained around the needs and rights of children, adolescents, and their families.The argument is organized around three interdependent dimensions: (1) the selection and delivery of evidence-based interventions; (2) the organization and coordination of mental health services; and (3) context-sensitive implementation across social, cultural, territorial, and institutional settings. These dimensions are not presented as novel constructs or as an exhaustive taxonomy of implementation science. Rather, they form a pragmatic, child-and adolescent-mental-health-specific lens that connects the intervention itself, the service arrangements through which it is delivered, and the conditions that shape its reach, acceptability, equity, and sustainability.We consider settings across the continuum of care -including schools, primary and community care, specialist outpatient services, hospitals, residential services, and youth-serving systems such as child welfare and juvenile justice -because young people's pathways often cross these boundaries. These settings are included as contexts for access, coordination, transition, and continuity, not as a claim that this article reviews the full range of setting-specific clinical interventions. Populations experiencing substance-use problems or intellectual/developmental disabilities are within scope when considering equitable access and coordinated, developmentally appropriate mental health support; disorder-specific addiction treatment and specialist disability interventions are not the focus. We then discuss implications for practice, service organization, implementation, and public policy.Why these three dimensions? We selected them because they address three connected but analytically distinct implementation questions that recur when evidence is translated into everyday child and adolescent mental health care: what intervention or support is appropriate and deliverable; how services and sectors organize responsibility and continuity around the young person; and under what contextual conditions implementation is feasible, acceptable, equitable, and sustainable. They are mutually dependent rather than sequential or independent.
