An effective intervention may have little population benefit if it is inaccessible or poorly matched to developmental needs; coordinated services may remain ineffective if they do not offer appropriate evidence-informed support; and both may reproduce inequities if implementation ignores culture, resources, geography, stigma, or institutional capacity.These dimensions therefore synthesize intervention-level, service-system, and contextual considerations into an applied argument. They overlap with established implementation-science concepts -including intervention characteristics, inner and outer setting, implementation processes, reach, adoption, fidelity, adaptation, and sustainability -but do not claim to replace comprehensive frameworks such as CFIR or the broader implementation-outcomes literature. Their added value is the explicit integration of these levels around the lived care trajectories and rights of children, adolescents, and families.Schools are particularly strategic because they can provide an accessible setting for mental health promotion and brief psychosocial support, including through universal, selective, and indicated approaches (Cohen et al., 2024).Accordingly, the term 'intervention' is used broadly in this article to include evidence-informed preventive, promotive, psychosocial, and clinical services, but our analysis concerns their selection, accessibility, delivery arrangements, and connection to a wider continuum of care. We do not assess the comparative effectiveness of specific psychotherapies, medication, inpatient programmes, or addiction-treatment protocols.In this article, child and adolescent mental health care is understood as a continuum of actions and services that respond to mental health needs across different developmental stages and care settings (Jeindl et al., 2023;World Health Organization and United Nations Children's Fund, 2024). Mental health care should also move beyond the treatment of established disorders to include promotion, prevention, early identification, treatment, psychosocial rehabilitation, and continuity of care. Schoolbased, community-based, family-centered, digital, and hybrid interventions should be viewed as complementary options whose relevance depends on population needs and implementation conditions.Evidence supports this diversity. Brief remote cognitive-behavioral interventions have shown benefits for children and adolescents and their families (Casella et al., 2025), while school-based interventions may expand access through universal, selective, and indicated approaches (Cohen et al., 2024). Integrated models involving multidisciplinary teams, shared care plans, and coordination across services have also shown potential to reduce depressive symptoms and improve access and engagement (McHugh et al., 2024).Childhood and adolescence are heterogeneous developmental periods. Individual developmental characteristics and everyday circumstances should therefore be considered when selecting and adapting interventions. For example, an observational study found associations between lifestyle patterns and emotional and behavioural problems among adolescents (Freitas et al., 2023).We therefore argue that evidence-based interventions should combine scientific evidence, developmental appropriateness, and meaningful participation of children, adolescents, and families. Accessibility, understandable language, confidentiality, progressive autonomy, and stigma should also inform implementation. The central question is not only which interventions are effective, but for whom, in which contexts, and under what conditions they can produce meaningful and sustainable benefits.Child and adolescent mental health care is inherently complex and cannot be sustained by isolated services. Because mental health needs are biopsychosocial, relational, and developmental, care networks must be able to respond to concerns shaped by multiple life contexts (Holmen et al., 2023;Jeindl et al., 2023). We therefore argue that care should extend beyond specialized services and be organized through integrated networks involving health care, education, social services, families, and community resources. In this article, integrated care refers to the coordinated organization and delivery of services across professionals, sectors, and levels of care, supported by communication, shared care planning, and continuity of support according to the needs of children, adolescents, and their families (Fazel et al., 2021;Jeindl et al., 2023;McHugh et al., 2024).This second dimension is distinct from intervention selection: it concerns the architecture and functioning of the network through which interventions and supports are accessed and sustained. The relevant questions include who is responsible for coordination, how information and referrals move between services, how transitions are managed, and how children, adolescents, and families participate in shared decisions.Primary care, schools, and community-based services are strategically positioned to support mental health promotion, early identification, prevention, and longitudinal follow-up (Hong et al., 2025). Their contribution, however, depends on effective communication, referral pathways, and shared responsibility across the care network. Coordination should therefore be regarded as a core component of care rather than an administrative function. Effective networks require clear pathways, continuity of follow-up, meaningful participation of children, adolescents, and families, culturally safe approaches, and relationships of trust (Jeindl et al., 2023;Fazel et al., 2021). For example, integrated care models identified in Norway have incorporated multidisciplinary teams, lowthreshold access, flexible outreach, and coordination between primary, specialized, and community services, illustrating different approaches to adapting care organization to local needs (Holmen et al., 2023).Such coordination requires professionals who are prepared to work interprofessionally and across sectors. Continuing professional development, institutional supervision, shared case discussions, simulation, and clinical demonstrations may strengthen collaborative care competencies (Raj et al., 2021). However, training alone is insufficient unless organizations also create conditions that support routine cooperation and shared accountability.Clearly defined roles are also essential, provided that they facilitate rather than constrain shared care. Professionals with sustained contact with children, adolescents, and families may play key roles in engagement, follow-up, and coordination when supported by an integrated network. These responsibilities should be accompanied by agreed communication processes and shared care plans to support continuity between services (McHugh et al., 2024).Ultimately, the effectiveness of mental health care depends on translating coordination into sustained collaboration among services and professionals, ensuring that children, adolescents, and families receive appropriate support throughout their care trajectories.The effectiveness of child and adolescent mental health care is shaped by the social, cultural, territorial, and institutional contexts in which it is implemented. We argue that context is not merely a background characteristic, but a determinant of access, acceptability, implementation, and outcomes. Differences in resources, geographic settings, socioeconomic conditions, and the experiences of historically marginalized populations make a single model of care unlikely to work equally well across settings.This third dimension is not simply a list of population characteristics or service settings. It concerns the interaction between implementation strategies and the conditions of the setting-such as workforce, funding, leadership, infrastructure, language, cultural safety, legal arrangements, geography, and structural inequalities-that influence whether an intervention can be adopted and maintained. The same intervention and coordination model may therefore require contextually appropriate adaptation without abandoning its essential evidence-informed components.Evidence-based interventions cannot simply be transferred across contexts without considering cultural, linguistic, organizational, workforce, and resource-related conditions (Moore et al., 2021). Contextual adaptation should not be viewed as a departure from evidence, but as a means of improving relevance and feasibility while preserving essential intervention components.Children, adolescents, and families should also participate meaningfully in intervention design, implementation, and evaluation. Participation that is merely consultative risks becoming symbolic when stakeholder contributions do not influence decisions. Research on youth involvement and codesign highlights both the growing use of participatory approaches and persistent variation in the quality and degree of youth participation (Totzeck et al., 2024;Chinsen et al., 2025).Equity is equally important. Formal availability does not ensure equal opportunities to access, remain engaged with, or benefit from an intervention. Economic, geographic, cultural, linguistic, and stigmarelated barriers may produce unequal outcomes, while acceptability, fidelity, feasibility, and equity remain insufficiently evaluated in culturally adapted interventions for marginalized youth (Schaechter et al., 2025).Context sensitivity should guide intervention planning and implementation from the outset, aligning adaptations with local needs while preserving essential components of evidence-based care. Ongoing monitoring is also necessary to assess equity and sustainability. Table 1 summarizes the three interdependent dimensions discussed in this article, highlighting their central arguments and implications for implementation. The main implication of this analysis is that improving the mental health of children and adolescents requires more than expanding the availability of interventions or services. Our central argument is that intervention selection, service coordination, and context-sensitive implementation must be addressed as interdependent dimensions rather than separate priorities. Mental distress must be understood as emerging and being experienced within family, school, community, cultural, and socioeconomic contexts, which makes exclusively biomedical, individualized, or specialist-centered responses insufficient. Recent evidence reinforces that child and adolescent mental health is shaped by the interaction of individual, relational, community, and structural factors, including social inequalities, discrimination, economic conditions, housing, education, and support networks (Fazel and Soneson, 2023;Huggard et al., 2023). This requires strengthening biopsychosocial, relational, rights-based, and developmentally sensitive models of care that integrate biological, psychological, social, and environmental dimensions. Recent international guidance from WHO and UNICEF emphasizes accessible, community-based, integrated, rights-based, and developmentally appropriate services connected across health, education, social protection, and community systems (World Health Organization and United Nations Children 's Fund, 2024). The AACAP Clinical Update on community systems of care provides a particularly relevant and substantial account of the principles, service array, infrastructure, workforce, and outcomes of coordinated systems for children and adolescents with behavioral health needs (AACAP, 2023). It explicitly includes mental health and substance-use services, residential and inpatient interventions, developmental-disability and juvenile-justice systems, and promotion, prevention, and early intervention.We therefore acknowledge that the populations and settings discussed in the present article are not outside the scope of established systems-of-care literature. However, the purpose and level of analysis differ. The AACAP update is a clinically oriented review of the system-of-care approach, its historical development, service components, guiding principles, implementation challenges, and evidence. WHO/UNICEF guidance provides an international service and policy direction.The present Opinion does not propose a competing system-of-care framework or a new catalogue of services. Instead, it offers a concise implementation-oriented synthesis organized around the relationship between (i) evidence-informed interventions, (ii) the coordination arrangements needed to deliver them, and (iii) contextual conditions that shape their equitable implementation in diverse settings. Its distinct contribution is to make the interdependence of these three levels the central analytic argument and to highlight that availability, coordination, and contextual adaptation must be considered together when assessing whether care can reach and benefit young people in routine practice.Translating integration into practice requires institutional mechanisms that support cooperation across sectors, including clearly defined referral pathways, shared care responsibilities, and continuing professional development. These measures should be supported by organizational conditions that enable interprofessional collaboration rather than relying solely on individual professional initiatives.Implementation is therefore a central dimension of this agenda. Evidence-informed policies and interventions will not necessarily produce the same outcomes across settings if they are implemented without attention to local resources, cultural characteristics, access inequalities, and institutional capacity. Likewise, evaluating only individual outcomes may be insufficient to understand the realworld impact of interventions. A contemporary research agenda in child and adolescent public mental health should consider how individuals, families, schools, communities, and systems interact and shape care outcomes (Fazel and Soneson, 2023). Loades et al. (2026) further argue that youth mental health research should move beyond intervention effectiveness to consider reach, adoption, implementation, and sustained population-level impact. This also requires greater attention to feasibility, acceptability, sustainability, equity, and the capacity of services to adopt and maintain interventions. From our perspective, these implementation considerations should inform not only intervention evaluation but also decisions about service organization and the allocation of resources across care settings.Meaningful stakeholder participation should also be incorporated into implementation and evaluation processes, ensuring that the perspectives of children, adolescents, families, and professionals inform decisions about service improvement.As an Opinion article, this manuscript does not provide a systematic or exhaustive review of the literature. Therefore, the evidence discussed reflects a selective synthesis intended to support critical reflection rather than a comprehensive assessment of available interventions and service models. Furthermore, differences in health systems, resources, and sociocultural contexts may limit the generalizability of the recommendations, requiring their interpretation and adaptation to local conditions.In summary, progress in child and adolescent mental health depends not only on expanding interventions or services, but also on the capacity to connect evidence-informed support, coordinated care arrangements, and context-sensitive implementation.We do not claim that these three dimensions are individually new, nor that they exhaust the parameters of implementation science. Their contribution lies in bringing together three levels that are often discussed separately and showing why they must be considered interdependently in child and adolescent mental health systems: selecting and delivering appropriate interventions; organizing coordinated pathways across professionals, services, and sectors; and adapting implementation to social, cultural, territorial, and institutional conditions while protecting essential intervention components.In relation to the AACAP systems-of-care update and WHO/UNICEF guidance, this Opinion offers neither a replacement framework nor a new service model. It provides an interpretive synthesis focused on the practical interface between intervention, service organization, and context, with particular attention to reach, continuity, equity, participation, and sustainability. The central question is therefore not only what works, but for whom, through which service arrangements, in which contexts, and under what conditions benefits can be achieved and sustained.

title: Supervision and support interventions targeted at community health workers in sub-Saharan Africa: a systematic review to identify characteristics associated with successful program outcomes
abstract: Community Health Workers (CHWs) are crucial in extending healthcare to underserved areas in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), but they often face challenges like limited training, resources, and support. Effective supervision and support interventions are essential for enhancing CHW performance and improving health outcomes. This study therefore explores the characteristics of supervision and support interventions targeted at CHWs in SSA that contribute to successful program outcomes. A search of four electronic databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science and Global Index Medicus) and grey literature sites was done for studies published between January 2013 and January 2024. Eligible studies were those focusing on CHWs and interventions involving supervision and support in SSA. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed, and data extracted were analyzed using thematic content analyses. Of 4,169 articles identified, fifty-five were included in the synthesis. Four main intervention types were identified: supervision, job aids, incentives, and training. Successful outcomes were measured through service delivery, implementation, and staff metrics. Fifty-two studies were assessed to have successful outcomes, and these were marked by ten key characteristics. These included material resource allocation (23), training and continuing education (30), stakeholder engagement (9), integration into existing systems (13), proper administration and logistics (10), supportive supervision (13), quality management (23), use of digital technologies (22), incentivization (9), and the enhancement of existing modalities (14). Leadership, governance and environmental factors emerged as important contextual factors in intervention success (5). This study shows key elements for successful outcomes and demonstrates the complex nature of supervision and support interventions. Long-term program success, service quality, and CHW motivation can all be improved by considering these factors when designing the CHW programs. Future research should prioritize the cost-effectiveness, long-term impact, and sustainability of CHW programs in SSA.

title: Multilevel Determinants of Infection-Prevention Readiness in Health Facilities in Ghana: Facility, Environmental and Organisational Factors
abstract: Introduction: Health-facility-associated infections (HFAIs), also referred to as healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), remain a major threat to patient safety globally, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where infrastructural deficiencies and weak infection prevention systems compromise healthcare delivery. In Ghana, limited empirical evidence exists on how facility-level, environmental, and organisational factors jointly influence infection-prevention readiness. This study aimed to examine the multilevel determinants of infection-prevention readiness in health facilities in Ghana. Patients and Methods: A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted using secondary data from 300 health facilities captured in the national Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (EmONC) assessment dataset across multiple districts in Ghana. Descriptive statistics were performed using SPSS version 26, while multilevel linear regression modelling was conducted in R to account for clustering of facilities within districts. Infection-prevention readiness was measured using a composite index constructed from validated indicators including water availability, sanitation facilities, electricity supply, and newborn service readiness. Results The null model revealed significant district-level clustering of infection-prevention readiness (ICC = 14.2%), justifying multilevel modelling. Environmental determinants were the strongest predictors of readiness. Functional toilets for staff (β = 0.2209, p < 0.001), running water in delivery rooms (β = 0.3918, p < 0.001), and availability of 24-hour newborn services (β = 0.1975, p < 0.001) were significantly associated with higher readiness scores. Organisational factors such as internet access showed weaker or non-significant associations after adjustment. The full model substantially reduced between-district variance. Conclusion Environmental and WASH-related factors are the strongest determinants of infection-prevention readiness in Ghanaian health facilities. Policy interventions should prioritise infrastructural investments in water supply, sanitation systems, and continuity of essential services to strengthen infection prevention and improve patient safety outcomes.

title: Multisectoral Collaboration in Partnership With the Community in Promoting Health Equity
abstract: This article examines the indispensable role of multisectoral collaboration (MSC) in advancing health equity through community health models. Despite significant advancements in healthcare, persistent health disparities, rooted in the social determinants of health (SDOH), necessitate a shift from reactive care to proactive, integrated approaches. MSC, defined as the coordinated effort among diverse stakeholders from healthcare, education, social services, government, and community organizations, offers a powerful strategy to address the complex, intersecting factors influencing health outcomes that no single sector can resolve alone. Drawing on theoretical foundations, such as the social‐ecological model and collective impact theory, the review delineates key principles for effective MSC, including shared vision, equitable power dynamics, and robust accountability mechanisms. It details the unique contributions of various sectors and explores how community health partnership approaches, such as integrated care, community‐based participatory research, and collective impact initiatives, operationalize MSC. Through practical examples, particularly from field experience in Sierra Leone, the article outlines strategies for initiating and nurturing partnerships, emphasizing stakeholder engagement, building a business case for collaboration, and establishing effective governance structures. Furthermore, it comprehensively addresses common challenges, including resource constraints, divergent mandates, power imbalances, and data interoperability, offering concrete mitigation strategies. Ultimately, this article aims to provide researchers, policymakers, and practitioners with actionable insights to design, implement, and sustain models that effectively reduce health inequalities and foster universally equitable health.

title: Beyond the algorithm: addressing accountability gaps in clinical artificial intelligence
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in clinical diagnosis, treatment selection, and population health management. Yet responsibility for the design, procurement, validation, deployment, monitoring, and correction of clinical AI systems is not always clearly allocated or consistently implemented. In this paper, we use the term “accountability vacuum” to describe this gap in the assignment and practical operation of responsibilities; we do not mean that applicable law is wholly absent. We distinguish legal liability, professional accountability, institutional governance, and regulatory oversight, and examine documented cases involving IBM Watson for Oncology, the Epic Sepsis Model, diabetic retinopathy screening in Thailand, and a cost-based risk algorithm that disadvantaged Black patients. We review policy developments in selected jurisdictions, including Ghana and the African Union, and propose a lifecycle framework that identifies responsibilities, monitoring arrangements, incident investigation, and patient communication and redress pathways. The framework is a governance proposal, not a statement that each recommended duty is already imposed by law.

title: Transformative Digital Practices for Social Equity: A Study of AI Adoption in Healthcare Through the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission for a Future-Ready Society
journal: International journal of research and scientific innovation

title: A systems representation of healthcare digital infrastructure: an evidence-grounded ontology for interoperability and governance analysis
abstract: Introduction United States healthcare digital infrastructure is documented through public certification, hospital-reporting, interface-declaration and standards resources. These give partial and in places already linked descriptions but analyzing them together requires an explicit account of what their entities and relationships mean and how the evidence behind them is qualified. That gap limits cross-source traceability and auditable governance analysis: when a standard advances, someone must determine which organizations the change reaches, and that determination is made against these same registers. Methods We conducted a retrospective evidence-integration study constructing an ontology-based systems representation specified by five requirements: identity, relationship semantics, temporal qualification, provenance and computational analysis. Evaluation combined structural checks, source-attribution and mapping audits, exact agreement between analytical queries and separately implemented procedures, and reproduction of a published federal statistic, each reported with what it does not establish. Results Populated from eight public federal files, the model covers 4,654 hospitals, 2,621 certified health IT modules, 658 developers and 90,565 interface addresses, resolving 98.4% of 68,446 hospital–module–year reports and retaining the unresolved rather than assigning invented identities. Explicit version-adoption evidence covered 2.80% of listing-criterion pairs under criteria containing such records. Historical reported use and later certification status differed for 93.5% of the 4,224 hospitals in the linked cohort, and 449 published interfaces appeared on more than one declared list, so a change scoped to one developer can reach addresses another also declares. Two standards-change demonstrations showed that substituting criterion-level certification for explicit version evidence expanded review populations from 62 to 4,220 hospitals in one case and from 1,320 to 48,816 developer-mediated interfaces in the other, and no register records which reading was used. Discussion These differences quantify the consequences of evidence-selection decisions, not operational impact. The study provides a computationally inspectable foundation for human-led infrastructure assessment, enabling analysts to trace documented relationships, identify evidence gaps and audit governance review populations within the limits of the public record.

title: Natural-Based Biocomposites of Chitosan, β-Cyclodextrin, and Potato Peel Waste for the Adsorptive Removal of Sunset Yellow and Diclofenac
abstract: This study aimed to prepare and evaluate the adsorptive potential of biocomposites produced from potato peel waste (PPW), β-cyclodextrin (β-CD), and chitosan (CS) in different proportions for removing Sunset Yellow FCF (SY) and diclofenac potassium (DCP) from aqueous solutions. The biocomposites (BC) were characterized by FTIR, XRD, SEM, EDS, and TGA, which confirmed the successful crosslinking and the synergistic integration of the three components, producing materials rich in –OH and –NH 2 groups, in addition to an amorphous character, different morphological surfaces, and sufficient thermal stability. Adsorption experiments revealed that pH significantly influenced removal efficiency, with optimal performance at pH 4 for both contaminants (> 90% for SY and > 83% for DCP). For SY, the general-order kinetic model provided the best fit, while the Sips isotherm model most accurately represented the equilibrium data, with q m values ranging from 18.70 to 221.89 mg g⁻ 1. For DCP, the pseudo-second-order model best described the kinetic behavior, with k LDF values ranging from 0.0017 to 0.0052 min-1, while the Sips model again best fit the equilibrium isotherms (q m 151.11 to 757.29 mg g −1). Among the materials, BC-5 exhibited favorable adsorption characteristics toward both contaminants, with capacities of 221.89 mg g⁻ 1 for SY and 151.11 mg g⁻ 1 for DCP. In addition, BC-5 showed good regeneration potential, maintaining effective adsorption performance over 5 consecutive reuse cycles for SY and 4–5 cycles for DCP. These findings highlight the potential of PPW/β-CD/CS biocomposites as reusable adsorbents for treating aqueous systems containing dyes and emerging pharmaceutical contaminants.

title: Science alone is not enough: advancing global policy, innovation, and access to combat antibiotic resistance
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens the effectiveness of modern medicine. Bacterial AMR was associated with an estimated 4.71 million deaths in 2021, and approximately 39 million deaths could be directly attributable to resistance between 2025 and 2050 under the reference forecasting scenario. Yet surveillance across human, animal, and environmental health remains fragmented, while antibiotic discovery faces persistent scientific and commercial obstacles. We argue that the response must connect One Health surveillance with therapeutic development and policies that reward antibiotic innovation without encouraging overuse. This Perspective compares the proposed U.S. PASTEUR Act, the United Kingdom’s antibiotic subscription model, European Union incentives, and Sweden’s revenue guarantees in terms of financing, implementation, outcome evidence, and access obligations, distinguishing intended benefits from demonstrated results. We propose an accountability framework linking surveillance findings to research funding, procurement, and clinical deployment through annual performance reviews. Progress should be judged using development milestones, diagnostic access, appropriate prescribing, and supply continuity alongside long-term changes in resistant infections and treatment access, without attributing resistance trends to financing policies alone.

title: Rural hospital closures and repurposing closed facilities: Challenges, impacts and the complex reality of facility conversion
The Salahi Acute Recovery Capsule (SARC)
abstract: The Salahi Acute Recovery Capsule (SARC)Download link for full whitepaperhttps://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24480060A Deployable Aerial Surgical and Intensive-Care System for Disaster and Conflict Zones. Kaveh Dimitri Salahi — Draft 6.0 Engineering BlueprintA Priority Rights InitiativeAn Integrated Approach to Emergency Surgical Care - Summary engineering paper The Salahi Acute Recovery Capsule (SARC) is an independent theoretical bio-engineering blueprint for a deployable aerial surgical and intensive-care system intended for disaster and conflict zones. Its central objective is to bring advanced medical capabilities closer to critically injured people when conventional hospitals are inaccessible, damaged, overwhelmed, or too distant to provide timely intervention. The design addresses a recurring difficulty in emergency medicine: patients with severe injuries may require complex surgical and intensive-care support, yet the transport infrastructure and medical facilities needed to provide that care may no longer be available. SARC approaches this problem by moving a compact medical facility toward the patient rather than relying exclusively on the movement of the patient toward an established hospital.The system combines aerial transport, modular engineering, controlled fluid management, robotic surgery, artificial-intelligence assistance, remote medical supervision, and a planned transfer pathway to a permanent hospital facility. These elements are arranged as one connected architecture, but each has its own engineering requirements and must be validated independently. The paper therefore describes both the intended operating structure and the unresolved scientific and technical questions that would have to be answered before an integrated system could be built or used.The Five-Sphere Surgical GroupThe principal aerial unit is a Surgical Group consisting of five spheres of equal diameter, connected in a straight line in a fixed order: fuel, fluid, capsule, supply, and battery. The capsule occupies the centre of the group, while the fuel and battery spheres sit at opposite ends. This arrangement separates major energy-storage components from the patient compartment and assigns each sphere a defined operational responsibility. Each sphere is approximately eight feet in diameter and is designed to operate independently in flight.Every sphere carries four radial arms, with four heavy-lift turbines mounted on each arm. This creates sixteen turbines per sphere and eighty across the complete Surgical Group. The arms fold against the spheres during transport inside the carrier pods and extend for flight. The spheres connect through electro-permanent magnetic alignment systems and mechanical load-bearing locks. Their coupling faces also contain the connections required for electrical power, data, and sealed fluid transfer. The design therefore treats the group as a modular system whose individual sections can be connected, separated, replaced, or operated independently when required.The fuel sphere contains the jet-fuel supply and turbine-generation equipment. The fluid sphere contains water treatment, fluid preparation, heating, and management equipment. The capsule sphere houses the patient compartment and surgical mechanisms. The supply sphere carries instruments, medical consumables, communications equipment, and protected computers. The battery sphere contains the electrical storage modules. Flight and treatment fuel are maintained as separate reserves, with the flight reserve unavailable for ground-based hospital operation. This separation is intended to preserve the energy needed for safe departure and recovery.

title: Geographical accessibility to maternal healthcare, iron supplementation, anemia, and postpartum hemorrhage among referred pregnant women in southeastern Morocco
abstract: Geographical accessibility may influence antenatal care, preventive interventions, and maternal outcomes in geographically dispersed settings. This study assessed associations between healthcare accessibility, iron supplementation, maternal anemia, and postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) among referred pregnant women in southeastern Morocco. A cross-sectional study included 1,304 third-trimester pregnant women consecutively referred from peripheral facilities to Moulay Ali Cherif Regional Hospital, Drâa-Tafilalet. Sociodemographic, obstetric, clinical, and healthcare-access data were obtained through structured interviews and medical-record review. Associations were examined using chi-square tests and multivariable binary logistic regression. Geographic Information Systems were used descriptively to characterize accessibility and referral patterns. Most participants lived in rural areas (76.1%). Travel time > 1 h to the nearest antenatal care facility was associated with non-receipt of iron supplementation (aOR = 147.43; 95% CI: 67.99–319.72) and maternal anemia (aOR = 1.56; 95% CI: 1.12–2.18). Iron supplementation was associated with lower odds of maternal anemia (aOR = 0.006; 95% CI: 0.003–0.013). Estimated referral transfer time ≥ 2 h was associated with PPH (aOR = 2.49; 95% CI: 1.14–5.41). Geographical accessibility was associated with preventive antenatal care and maternal outcomes in this referred population. Improving access to antenatal services and timely obstetric referral may help reduce maternal health inequalities in remote settings.

title: Penguatan Tenaga Kesehatan Bencana Kabupaten Agam: Kolaborasi Interprofesional dan Pemberdayaan Keluarga dalam Pelayanan Ibu Hamil
journal: Agrokreatif Jurnal Ilmiah Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat
abstract: Disaster situations increase the vulnerability of pregnant women due to disrupted access to healthcare services, limited referral systems, and deteriorating environmental conditions. This community service program aimed to strengthen interprofessional collaboration, enhance the early detection of pregnancy risks, improve maternal referral system coordination, and empower families in maternal healthcare services in Agam Regency, West Sumatra, Indonesia. The program was implemented through five stages: socialization, training, service implementation, monitoring, and evaluation, involving interprofessional healthcare providers, the Agam Regency Health Office, healthcare facilities, and families as active partners. Data were collected through participatory observation, pregnancy risk screening forms, interviews, and activity documentation, and were analyzed descriptively by integrating quantitative and qualitative findings. The results demonstrated improved interprofessional and cross-sectoral coordination, enhanced healthcare workers' capacity, and increased family involvement in the early identification of pregnancy risks and referral decision-making. Among the 70 pregnant women who received antenatal care (ANC), 16 (22.9%) were identified as having high-risk pregnancies and were successfully referred to higher-level healthcare facilities, indicating the effectiveness of systematic risk screening and referral mechanisms. Program sustainability was strengthened through the establishment of maternal healthcare networks, the development of interprofessional collaboration modules and standard operating procedures (SOPs), and continuous capacity-building for healthcare providers and families. This program demonstrates that integrating interprofessional collaboration with family empowerment is an effective strategy for improving the quality of maternal healthcare services in disaster-prone areas while strengthening the resilience and sustainability of the maternal healthcare system.

title: Complete-Genome Analysis of Beak and Feather Disease Virus in Iran: Evidence of Recombination and Selection
abstract: Beak and feather disease virus (BFDV) is regarded as a significant threat to avian biodiversity and the exotic bird trade. Despite its impact, complete-genome data from the Middle East remain limited. This study reports four complete BFDV genomes from Iran, deposited in GenBank. BFDV DNA was detected in 222 of 400 (55.5%) feather samples submitted to a specialist avian referral hospital; a detection rate among submitted samples and not a national prevalence estimate; the highest rate was observed in Cockatiels (Nymphicus hollandicus) at 76%. Recombination analysis suggested genomic mosaicism in SBFDV-4 sequence, a putative recombinant that showed closest sequence similarity to Polish and Thai lineages in the putative major and minor parental regions, respectively, consistent with putative parental-like contributions. Furthermore, the replication-associated protein (Rep) was highly conserved (86% to 99% amino acid identity to the reference) with no substitutions observed in the annotated motifs examined, whereas the capsid protein (Cap) showed amino acid variability at its N-terminus, a region annotated as containing the nuclear localization signal and predicted to contain epitopes; possible effects on antigenicity warrant experimental validation. In a phylogeny of the 548 available complete BFDV genomes, the four Iranian genomes were placed within Clade I.a but did not form a monophyletic group. These findings provide baseline genomic data that may inform future surveillance and highlight the need for further sampling; the contribution of international trade and the extent of recombination were not directly assessed.

title: Jurisdiction as an Indigenous social determinant of nutrition: structural barriers and opportunities for Indigenous food systems
abstract: Indigenous food systems and agriculture continue to be stewarded by Indigenous farmers and producers in the southwestern United States. Different levels of policy (i.e., Tribal, state, federal) and jurisdiction impact Indigenous farmers and producers as well as their efforts to move their products through the farm-to-market pathway. In this Policy and Practice Review, we aimed to explore how various levels of policies impact the Tribal farm to market pathway and offer actionable recommendations for Indigenous farmers and producers to navigate jurisdictional barriers particularly on Tribal land. We conducted a literature review, assessed policy materials, and presented a farmer-informed case study in this review. Findings from the review demonstrated how substantial and complex Tribal, state and federal policies are for Indigenous farmers and producers. Based on our review we developed actionable recommendations which include: (1) Modernize and Develop Food Safety Policies and Codes within for Tribal Nations; (2) Increase Investments in Food Manufacturing Infrastructure within Tribal communities; (3) Establish Government-to-Government Agreements between Tribal governments and other governments; (4) Expand Institutional Procurement Pathways for Indigenous Producers; and (5) Build and Support Food Safety Capacity of Indigenous Producers through Technical Assistance. Indigenous farmers and producers are vital to building and strengthening self-determined food systems and Indigenous wellbeing. Furthermore, they are impacted by and can also contribute to strengthening Indigenous determinants of health such as the health of Mother Earth, intergenerational holistic healing, and building culturally driven spaces for learning and community connectedness.

title: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) bacteremia following arthroscopic anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a case report
abstract: Background Postoperative infection following arthroscopic anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is a rare but serious complication, and Group B Streptococcus (GBS; Streptococcus agalactiae) has exceptionally rarely been implicated. We report a case of GBS bacteremia occurring after arthroscopic ACLR in a previously healthy young man, in a distinctive epidemiological context: his spouse had delivered their second child approximately 40 days before his admission, and clindamycin had been used for surgical prophylaxis because of a documented cefuroxime allergy. Case presentation: A 39-year-old Chinese man with a complete right anterior cruciate ligament rupture underwent uneventful arthroscopic single-bundle ACLR using a quadrupled hamstring tendon graft. Fever and leukocytosis developed on postoperative day 3, and blood cultures subsequently grew S. agalactiae that was resistant to the clindamycin used for perioperative prophylaxis. Despite sequential empirical regimens (vancomycin; vancomycin plus piperacillin–tazobactam; linezolid) together with arthroscopic joint debridement and lavage, fever and inflammatory markers persisted until high-dose combination therapy with vancomycin and penicillin was administered, after which the patient defervesced and all inflammatory markers normalized. He was discharged after 2 weeks of penicillin therapy with a well-functioning knee and no evidence of residual infection. Conclusions GBS is a rare but potentially significant pathogen of bacteremia after ACLR. Recent childbirth in the patient’s spouse and clindamycin-based surgical prophylaxis may represent under-recognized risk factors. When GBS infection is confirmed, penicillin-based therapy is effective, and this case highlights the potential inadequacy of clindamycin prophylaxis in patients with specific GBS exposure risks.

title: Retrospective study of medication errors and their impact on the safety of the oncological patient
abstract: Background: Medication errors (MEs) are an unintentional failure in the oncological treatment process.The analysis of ME is necessary, since in recent years, there has been a great diversity of cancer therapies.Objective: To identify the factors that predispose and trigger ME in the State Oncological Center ISSEMYM.Method: This was an retrospective cross-sectional study in which the proportion of ME extracted from the database of the clinical pharmacy service during the 2015-2020 period were quantified, classified according to the Ruiz-Garabo update.For the analysis, descriptive statistics were used with frequency values, percentages, and contingency tables with the Chi-square test (χ 2 ) and odds ratio.Results: A total of 10,542 MEs were obtained, of which 7725 were avoided, which shows the importance of the participation of the pharmaceutical staff involved in the pharmacological therapeutic stage.Conclusion: The pharmacist ensures the continuous improvement of the procedures and the guarantee of patient safety oncology.

title: Clinical characteristics, diagnostic pathways, and outcomes of 13 patients with Vibrio vulnificus infection: a retrospective case series and proposed diagnostic workflow
abstract: Background Vibrio vulnificus can cause rapidly progressive soft-tissue infection, sepsis, limb loss, and death. Because early manifestations may be nonspecific and conventional culture can be slow or negative after antimicrobial exposure, timely recognition and pathogen identification remain challenging. We characterized the clinical presentation, diagnostic pathways, management, and outcomes of 13 patients and developed a pragmatic diagnostic workflow based on the patterns observed in this series. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 13 patients with microbiologically confirmed V. vulnificus infection admitted to Shanghai Sixth People’s Hospital between January and September 2026. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, exposure history, clinical manifestations, admission laboratory findings, microbiological investigations, antimicrobial therapy, surgical management, and in-hospital outcomes were extracted from medical records. Owing to the small sample size and descriptive case-series design, no inferential statistical comparisons were performed. Results The 13 patients (7 men and 6 women) had a mean age of 66.4 years (SD 9.7; range 51–82 years), and 12 had at least one underlying condition. Symptom onset to hospital admission ranged from 12 to 72 h. The interval from injury to definitive diagnosis ranged from 67 to 131 h (median 92 h). V. vulnificus was detected by metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) in 9 patients and by wound secretion culture in 4. The reported turnaround time was 1 day (IQR 1–2) for mNGS and 5 days (IQR 5–5) for positive wound cultures. All patients received antimicrobial therapy; 12 underwent debridement, 11 underwent their first operation within 24 h of admission, 5 underwent amputation, and 4 required intensive care. All 13 patients survived to hospital discharge. Conclusions This small, single-centre case series highlights the rapid progression and substantial surgical burden of severe V. vulnificus infection. A combination of early clinical suspicion, immediate microbiological sampling, prompt empirical antimicrobial therapy, and urgent surgical assessment is central to management. mNGS may provide useful adjunctive pathogen identification where available, particularly when conventional cultures are unrevealing, but it should complement rather than replace culture and clinical judgement. The proposed workflow is hypothesis-generating and requires prospective, multicentre validation before routine clinical use.

title: Exploring Ferroptotic Vulnerabilities in Pediatric Cancer Through Clinical Biochemistry Using the Roche cobas® 8000
abstract: Background Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent-regulated cell death increasingly recognized as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in pediatric cancer. However, the clinical translation of ferroptosis research remains limited because canonical ferroptosis markers, such as GPX4 depletion and lipid peroxidation, are not routinely measurable in standard diagnostic laboratories. In contrast, alterations in iron metabolism and metabolic reprogramming associated with ferroptosis susceptibility may be assessed through clinically accessible biomarkers. Methods We evaluated the Roche Cobas® 8000 analyzer as a translational platform for the biochemical profiling of ferroptosis-associated metabolic states in pediatric cancer models. The system was used to quantify iron metabolism and metabolic biomarkers, including circulating iron species (Fe2+/Fe3+), ferritin (FTH1), transferrin (TRF1), lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA), and lactate, in treated and untreated samples. Analytical performance, sample processing efficiency, and multiparametric profiling capabilities were assessed within a standardized clinical workflow. Results The Cobas® 8000 platform enabled rapid and reproducible quantification of multiple iron-related and metabolic parameters using minimal sample volumes. Distinct biochemical and metabolic alterations were identified between experimental conditions, revealing patterns consistent with ferroptosis-associated vulnerabilities. The automated and standardized nature of the platform reduced pre-analytical variability and supported robust comparative profiling across samples. Conclusions Although the Roche Cobas® 8000 analyzer does not measure canonical ferroptosis markers, it provides clinically accessible metabolic and iron-related profiling that may identify biological states associated with ferroptosis susceptibility. This approach represents a practical bridge between experimental ferroptosis research and clinical oncology, supporting the translational development of ferroptosis-oriented therapeutic strategies in pediatric cancer.

title: Two new record graphs for the cage problem: n(6,9) ≤ 3420 and n(6,10) ≤ 4896
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This deposit holds two 6-regular graphs that improve upper bounds for the cage problem as listed in the House of Graphs cage table on 25 November 2026. Here n(k,g) is the smallest order of a k-regular graph of girth g. (k,g) order n House of Graphs on 2026-11-25 Moore bound file (6,9) 3,420 3,422 [T26] 937 k6_g9_n3420/k6_g9_n3420.g6 (6,10) 4,896 6,250 [T26] 1,562 k6_g10_n4896/k6_g10_n4896.g6 Both are Cayley graphs: the vertices are the elements of a group, and x is adjacent to x·s for each s in a connection set S that is closed under inverse. Constructions (6,9), 3,420 vertices. The group is PSL(2,19), of order 3,420, as a permutation group on 20 points. The connection set is six involutions. The graph has girth exactly 9. (6,10), 4,896 vertices. The group is PGL(2,17), of order 4,896, as a permutation group on 18 points. The connection set is two elements of order 16, their inverses, and two involutions. The graph has girth exactly 10. In each graph folder, recipe.txt gives the group generators and the six connection-set elements as explicit permutations, enough to rebuild the graph. How they were found A small program searches one group at a time for 6-element connection sets, fixing the first element up to conjugacy and inversion and extending step by step. A set gives girth at least g exactly when no non-trivial reduced word of length less than g in its elements is the identity, and this is tested on every partial set. Groups were taken from the GAP system: its Small Groups library for the (6,9) search, and PSL(2,q), PGL(2,q), SL(2,q) and a few related groups for the (6,10) search. For (6,9), the search covered the non-abelian groups of each order from 938 to 3,421 that the Small Groups library provides and that has at most 1,500 groups: 48,263 groups, all searched to completion with no time-outs. Not covered were 151 orders that the library does not provide and 26 orders with more than 1,500 groups. A further 6,000 or so groups from other families (transitive and primitive permutation groups, direct products, PSL, PGL and SL(2,q)) were tried for some of the uncovered orders. The only group that gave a graph of girth 9 below 3,422 vertices was PSL(2,19). This is a statement about what one program found, not a proof that no smaller Cayley graph exists. For (6,10), only the PSL, PGL and SL(2,q) families and a few related groups were tried. The search was not systematic, so smaller graphs may well exist. Verification Each graph was checked to be simple, connected, 6-regular and of the stated girth in six ways. Checks 1–4 were set up alongside the search; checks 5 and 6 were written separately afterwards, read only the deposited .g6 files, and share no code with the search or with checks 1–4. pickg from nauty (B. D. McKay and A. Piperno). check_cage.py (included): a standard-library Python script that shares no code with the search program. A rebuild inside GAP from the recipe alone. A formal proof in Lean 4 with Mathlib (folder lean/ in each graph folder). The theorems proved are∃ W H, Fintype.card W = 3420 ∧ H.IsRegularOfDegree 6 ∧ H.girth = 9∃ W H, Fintype.card W = 4896 ∧ H.IsRegularOfDegree 6 ∧ H.girth = 10stated with Mathlib's own SimpleGraph, IsRegularOfDegree and girth. The proofs contain no sorry. Their finite computations use native_decide, which trusts the Lean compiler in addition to the Lean kernel; the full axiom lists are in BUILD_RESULT.txt. That the graph defined in Lean is the same graph as the deposited .g6 file is checked outside Lean by comparing nauty canonical forms (link_to_g6.py). girth_check_networkx.py: reads each file with NetworkX's own graph6 reader and computes the girth with networkx.girth (NetworkX 3.7). girth_check_scratch.py: a from-scratch, standard-library Python script with its own graph6 parser; it computes the exact girth by a breadth-first search from every vertex. Checks 5 and 6 were first run on the Petersen graph as a control (expected girth 5; both report 5). Both report 3,420 vertices, 6-regular, connected, girth 9 for the first graph, and 4,896 vertices, 6-regular, connected, girth 10 for the second. verification.txt in each graph folder holds the output of checks 1 and 2. The folder independent_checks/ holds the scripts for checks 5 and 6, their output, and the Petersen control graph. Files The three zip files unpack to the folders k6_g9_n3420/, k6_g10_n4896/ and independent_checks/. Each graph folder contains the graph in graph6 format, recipe.txt, verification.txt, SHA256SUMS.txt, check_cage.py and the Lean project. SHA-256 of the graph files: k6_g9_n3420.g6: 1fe5c277514c11edf1a09a2fa433f867803df0f965033e2ae1243e904e2befbc k6_g10_n4896.g6: d8e4707abbdda990fdb216ea86b79a4f10420f3419277ffe4ca41d03bcf032f6 Use of AI The search programs, the verification scripts and the Lean proofs were written, and the searches run, with the use of the Claude Fable 5.2 and opus 5.5 models. title: Gated Pumps: Alternating Access, Coupling Ratios, and Leak Cycles on the Substituted-Chrysene Lattice
abstract: A pump is a hinge whose track is a turnover count. Its conformation follows a bounded path from inward-open through occluded to outward-open, while substrate turnover records transport. We model a cavity with two gates, two ideal reservoirs and one fuel site. Without fuel, two gates permit only downhill transport. Excluding the doubly open state forces every transporting cycle through a loaded occluded state; allowing both gates to open admits a two-transition channel leak. The one-fuel graph has 111 simple cycles, including coupled, leak and slip cycles. Tight coupling at a specified ratio is equivalent to the transport increment minus that ratio times the hydrolysis increment being a coboundary, with nonzero transport on some cycle. Six of the 64 occupancy rule sets are tight: three pump outward, and three are their inward mirrors. A two-substrate-per-ATP model has one minimal tight rule set. Under tight coupling, the stall head equals the static head set by the chemical driving and the coupling ratio. With a leak, the stall head can depend on rates. The registered six-spoke chrysene ring is screened using declared steric and hinge inputs. A closed lid can cover the channel’s inscribed disc without sealing the spoke gaps or the recesses beside the lid. The potassium probe passes the planar retention screen at 26 of 120 sampled lid orientations, and the glucose probe passes at all sampled orientations. For the reference potassium geometry a single tether passes a distance test, but its path is not certified. For the tested three-layer glucose geometry no admitted single tether reaches, so alternating access is declared. The finite graph results are exact, with core statements checked in Lean; the geometric screens are conditional estimates, not evidence of a chemically realized or three-dimensionally sealed pump.
