title: Accelerating discoveries in pain therapeutics through immersive postdoctoral cross-training in translational research
abstract: 1. We agree. This manuscript is not meant as a formal research study. Rather, this manuscript is a Frontiers Journal Type B Perspective Article. 2. "Bidirectional cross-training" is defined as basic science trainees "interacting with clinicians and observing how pain is assessed, treated..." and clinical research trainees "immersed in laboratory settings..." This sounds nice, and many such programs actually exist.But they are all greatly limited by various practical realities, which is that basic scientists obviously wouldn't and shouldn't be actually treating patients, and clinicians wouldn't and shouldn't be performing laboratory procedures they know nothing about. There are major limitations as to what can be learned simply by "observing" things 2. We added Table 1 to provide examples of cross-training activities.3. The idea of "protected time" seems ideal for nursing schools, but I see serious problems with expanding the model to, say, physicians (who probably wouldn't agree to protect the time) or basic science postdocs (for whom 100% of their time is already "protected").3. We enhanced our description of cross-training, specifying that it would be brief, but long enough for clinical trainees to observe how mechanistic questions are generated, tested, and refined and basic science trainees to have meaningful interactions with people with lived experience of pain (See Section 4, page 10). 4. Many of the citations are poor fits for the points being made. For example, Adams et al., 2024 andPritzlaff et al., 2025 have very little to do with the failure of pain clinical trials; there are direct review papers on documenting this.4. Thank you for catching that error. We replaced Adams et al., 2024 andPritzlaff et al., 2025) with other references (Austin 2021, Wagner et al., 2018, Paul et al., 2010, Thomas et al., 2018) Reviewer 2. Although this piece appears to be the fruits from multidisciplinary retreat in July 2025, as well as interviews with current/former postdoctoral trainees, faculty, and expert mentors, the process is not well described. It may be informative for readers to understand who the stakeholder groups were, how interviewees were selected, whether interviews were formal or informal, what questions were asked, and how the authors determined the "cross-cutting themes."2.We added information about our process (i.e., customer discovery methodology). We also deleted the term "cross-cutting themes" to avoid inferring that we used qualitative methods (See Section 3, page 9).3. Statements such as "a major conclusion" seem tentative. If these were informal consultations rather than qualitative research, that is perfectly reasonable for a commentary-but the manuscript should explicitly describe them as such and avoid methodological language implying formal qualitative analysis.3.We agree and deleted the term "a major conclusion"4. The authors go on to mention -but not flesh out-explicit evaluation metrics of the proposed pathway.4.We added the program's proposed metrics to Figure 1 Houston, TX 77054 Chronic pain, defined as pain that persists or recurs for longer than 3 months (Treede et al., 2019), remains one of the most pressing and persistent public health challenge. It affects nearly one in four adults (Lucas and Sohi, 2024;Yang et al., 2025), and imposes clinical, social, psychological, and economic burdens that diminish quality of life, limit function, and deepen existing health inequities (Austin, 2021;Cohen, Vase and Hooten, 2021;Zajacova, Grol-Prokopczyk and Zimmer, 2021). These effects are particularly pronounced among older adults, individuals living in rural and non-urban communities, and populations with limited access to specialized pain care (Lucas and Sohi, 2024;Sun, Yang and Nahin, 2025;Yang et al., 2025). Yet despite substantial advances in pain science, few therapeutically promising discoveries have moved successfully from basic science to meaningful clinical benefit (Thomas and Wessel, 2018;Austin, 2021).Overcoming these challenges requires investing not only in better therapeutics, but also in a translational pain research workforce prepared to develop, test, and implement therapeutic discoveries that identify people at risk, reduce pain, and address the needs of populations disproportionately burdened by chronic pain (Adams, Wandner and Kolber, 2024;Pritzlaff et al., 2025;National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, 2026). In this perspective, wepropose that such workforce investment should occur in postdoctoral programs through immersive, bidirectional cross-training that integrates basic science, clinical research, protected research time, multidisciplinary mentorship, and sustained engagement with people with the lived experience of pain.The need for immersive bidirectional cross-training emerges from the evolution of the translational continuum. Historically, translational research often began with public health problems or serendipitous observations that moved into accepted practice (Austin, 2021). Over the last century, scientific advances shifted many translational efforts toward laboratory discoveries as starting points for therapeutic development (Austin, 2021). Although this shift expanded opportunities for discovery, it also created a complex pathway from discovery to patient benefit and, at times, separated investigations of disease mechanisms from patients' lived experiences (Rubio et al., 2010). For example, efforts to translate laboratory discoveries in to clinically meaningful therapeutics have identified more than 20 involved steps (Austin, 2021). In pain research, the translation challenge is especially pronounced because of the ceaseless quest to improve and expand basic science models that can account for the biological, psychological, and social variables that shape human pain (Fillingim, 2017;Khera and Rangasamy, 2021;Mouraux et al., 2021) et al., 2010;Thomas and Wessel, 2018;Wagner et al., 2018;Austin, 2021). Against this backdrop, the Cizik Nursing Research Institute at the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston (UTHealth Houston) sought to identify effective translational approaches to accelerate discoveries in pain therapeutics from bench to bedside.In July 2025, the Cizik Nursing Research Institute at UTHealth Houston convened a multidisciplinary retreat, Biobehavioral Approaches to Pain: Urban & Rural Issues. Leaders in translational pain research discussed improved approaches to addressing the persistent problem of chronic pain research, drawing on their experience conducting projects ranging from auricular point acupressure for chronic musculoskeletal pain to studies of mechanisms underlying chronic pain after spinal cord injury. The discussion highlighted the need for basic science models that better account for biological, psychological, and social variables shaping human pain (Fillingim, 2017;Khera and Rangasamy, 2021;Mouraux et al., 2021). The retreat raised two practical questions: What are the gaps in current translational training programs that limit acceleration of scientific discoveries? What support/activities do trainees need to prepare for an academic career that accelerates discoveries from bench to bedside?To answer these questions, we used customer discovery methodology to examine existing translational pain research training programs and explore the trainees' needs (Blank, 2013;Thamjamrassri et al., 2018). Commonly used when launching a new project or business, customer discovery methodology tests assumptions about stakeholders' needs, preferences, and problems by developing hypotheses, identifying interviewees, preparing questions, conducting interviews, organizing findings, revising hypotheses, and repeating the process to identify knowledge gaps and unmet needs (Blank, 2013;Thamjamrassri et al., 2018). We reviewed existing postdoctoral training programs through searches in the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Reporter (https://reporter.nih.gov/) and published literature. We also interviewed 36 national and international stakeholders, including trainees, academic leaders, researchers, industry experts, and people with the lived experience of pain (n=36). Interviews took place by teleconference, email, or in person and were conducted anonymously to protect participants sharing sensitive information. An example of an interview question was "How would you change the training experience to fit trainees' needs?" The authors took interview notes, organized the information, and discussed lessons learned from the discovery process. We defined immersive, bidirectional cross-training as structured learning across basic science and clinical settings, integrated with each trainees' defined translational research project (See Figure 1). Basic science trainees interact with clinicians to observe how pain is assessed, treated, and experienced by patients and families. Conversely, clinical research trainees are immersed in laboratory settings briefly, but long enough to observe how mechanistic questions are generated, tested, and refined (See Table 1). In both directions, these structured experiences are integrated with each trainees defined translational research project rather than offered as an An example of such a bridge program is the UTHealth Houston Cizik School of Nursing's Assistant Professor, Research Track position that supports independent but mentored research for promising early-career investigators. Recognizing the need for early-stage investigators to build a research portfolio for promotion and tenure, the Cizik School of Nursing designed a program that includes mentoring tailored to each investigators' research focus. (Johnson et al., in review).The program provides 80% protected time and mentorship for 3 years to conduct research projects, publish manuscripts, and prepare grant applications. After demonstrating the ability to conduct rigorous research independently and secure external funding, trainees advance to an Assistant Professor, Tenure Track position.Similar institutional bridge programs may be especially useful during the transition from doctoral or postdoctoral training to the early-investigator stage, when challenges in funding and protected time contribute to trainees' departure from academia (Adams, Wandner and Kolber, 2024). Research-intensive nursing doctoral programs are well-positioned to house such translational bridge programs in pain science. Nursing has long served as leaders in pain science, recognizing that pain is influenced by multidimensional, biopsychosocial factors (Jacox, Carr and Payne, 1994), and are uniquely situated to assess and implement novel pain therapies.Trainees, mentors, and people with the lived experience of pain identified three additional Because chronic pain remains a pressing public health challenge, new approaches beyond • Orientation to core laboratory equipment and workflows (pipettes, centrifuges, biosafety cabinet, PCR set-up areas; contamination control);• Pipetting and basic wet-lab technique with quality control (accuracy/precision checks; dilution series; documentation practices);• Perform a BCA protein assay (prepare standards, generate a standard curve, calculate concentrations, interpret variability).• Help patients complete pain surveys;• Experience clinical workflow and pain assessments;• Interact with clinicians to better understand clinical decisions in pain management across a wide variety of pain conditions (e.g., headaches, strokes);• Witness diagnostic and therapeutic treatments (e.g., pharmacotherapy, nonpharmacologic approaches, including various interventional procedures).

title: Drilling it down - Determining the root causes of increased peripheral IV infiltrations and extravasations in paediatric inpatients at London Health Sciences Centre - Children's Hospital
Beyond traditional lipids: evaluating novel lipid-derived indices in premature coronary artery disease: a case control study
abstract: Background/objectives Premature coronary artery disease (PCAD) emerges as an important cardiovascular health concern in younger adults. Its social as well as economic impact cannot be neglected. This study examined the association of Novel lipid-derived indices with PCAD and evaluated their discriminative performance. Methods This retrospective case-control study was conducted at King Saud University Medical City, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and included adults aged 18–50 years. Patients had angiographically confirmed PCAD including acute and chronic coronary syndrome patients and the data obtained from the electronic medical records of the patients from 2015 to 2023, while controls were healthy blood bank donors without known diabetes or hypertension. Novel lipid-derived indices were evaluated including total cholesterol/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (TC/HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol/HDL-C (LDL-C/HDL-C), remnant cholesterol (RC), non-HDL-C/HDL-C (NHHR), and RC/HDL-C. Each marker was examined in a separate logistic regression model adjusted for age, ethnicity, gender, body mass index (BMI), smoking status, and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). Individual-marker discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Results The analysis included 493 patients with PCAD and 427 healthy controls. Per one-unit increase, the adjusted odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) were 1.510 (1.230–1.852) for both TC/HDL-C and NHHR, 1.329 (1.060–1.668) for LDL-C/HDL-C, and 2.228 (1.389–3.574) for RC/HDL-C. For RC, the adjusted odds ratio per 1-mmol/L increase was 2.014 (1.208–3.357). RC/HDL-C had the highest observed area under the curve (AUC), at 0.797 (95% CI: 0.768–0.825), followed by TC/HDL-C and NHHR (both 0.791), RC (0.731), and LDL-C/HDL-C (0.697). Conclusions Among adults 50 years or younger with premature coronary artery disease, TC/HDL-C, LDL-C/HDL-C, remnant cholesterol, NHHR, and RC/HDL-C were associated with PCAD after adjustment for selected cardiovascular risk factors. RC/HDL-C showed the numerically highest discrimination among the evaluated lipid-derived indices, followed by TC/HDL-C and NHHR, but its superiority and incremental clinical value require formal comparison and external validation. Independent validation is needed to confirm the proposed cutoffs and determine whether these indices improve discrimination beyond conventional cardiovascular risk factors. Association between these indices and PCAD encourages further research to confirm clinical applications in order to reduce the risk of incidence as well as the prognosis of detrimental health issues.

title: Long-term renal outcomes and systemic complications in chronic hypoparathyroidism under conventional therapy: a multicenter cohort study
authors: Maria Caroline Alves Coelho Do Amaral
abstract: Purpose To evaluate long-term clinical outcomes and systemic complications in patients with chronic hypoparathyroidism (HP) managed with conventional therapy at tertiary endocrinology centers. Methods This retrospective multicenter cohort study included patients followed at four referral centers in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (2018–2021). Demographic, clinical, laboratory, therapeutic, and complication data were evaluated. Data are presented as n (%) or median (p25–p75). Results Of 113 participants (93.8% women; median age 46 years [37–56]; median disease duration 7.5 years [4–15]), HP was postsurgical in 93.8%, most often for nontoxic multinodular goiter (63.8%). Conventional therapy improved serum calcium and reduced phosphate (both p < 0.001). Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) declined over follow-up (93.1 vs. 81.1 mL/min/1.73 m²; p < 0.001), with chronic kidney disease (CKD) progression in 32.3%. Advanced CKD stages were associated with systemic arterial hypertension (SAH) and diabetes mellitus (DM) (p < 0.001 and p = 0.001). Participants with CKD progression were older (62 vs. 57 years; p = 0.036) and had longer disease duration (12 vs. 7 years; p = 0.025) than non-progressors; osteopenia was also more prevalent among them (24.1% vs. 5.0%; p = 0.018). Conclusion Although conventional therapy promotes adequate metabolic control, clinically relevant complications persist, most notably progressive renal decline affecting nearly one-third of the cohort. CKD progression was associated with older age, longer disease duration, and a higher burden of SAH and DM, indicating a multifactorial process rather than a single cause. These findings underscore the need for rigorous long-term monitoring of renal and cardiometabolic risk in chronic HP, and for prospective, adjusted studies to clarify the specific contribution of the disease and its treatment.

title: From Launch to Institutional Integration: Low-Cost Implementation of an Integrated Addiction Medicine–Psychiatry Bridge Clinic in a Large Academic Health System Using RE-AIM
abstract: Background Hospitalizations and emergency department encounters represent critical opportunities to engage patients with substance use disorders (SUD), yet initiation of evidence-based treatment during these transitions remains inconsistent. Low-barrier bridge clinics have emerged to improve access to rapid treatment and continuity of care; however, limited evidence describes how these programs are implemented, integrated, and sustained within large academic health systems. The Therapeutic Resources and Assistance in Navigation to Services while in Transition (TRANSiT) Bridge Clinic was developed in response to community-identified gaps in addiction and behavioral health care and integrates Addiction Medicine and Addiction Psychiatry within a multidisciplinary transitional care model. Guided by the RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance) framework, we evaluated the implementation, early outcomes, and institutional integration of TRANSiT within a large academic health system. Methods We conducted a mixed-methods implementation evaluation of the TRANSiT Bridge Clinic during the first 18 months following program launch (May 1, 2024–October 31, 2025). We assessed early implementation, adoption, and indicators of maintenance. Quantitative data included referral patterns, patient characteristics, medication initiation, laboratory monitoring, visit completion, and provider survey responses. Qualitative data consisted of open-ended provider survey responses used to assess organizational readiness, provider perceptions, perceived barriers to treatment delivery, and implementation context prior to clinic launch. Results Reach: Over an 18-month period, the clinic served 432 unique patients and received 1,290 referrals, primarily from the inpatient units (66.2%) and emergency department (18.7%). The cohort was predominantly Latino (60.6%) and Medicaid-insured (61.6%), with a high burden of medical and psychiatric comorbidity (e.g., liver disease 18.8%, hypertension 18.3%, anxiety disorders 10.0%). Effectiveness: Fifty-four percent of patients were prescribed medication for treatment, with 69.2% initiated at the first visit. Among patients with alcohol use disorder and follow-up biomarker testing, 51.3% demonstrated improvement. Adoption: Referrals came from multiple hospital campuses, and 95 trainees from multiple graduate medical education programs rotated through the clinic in year one. Pre-implementation provider surveys showed that providers broadly endorsed medication treatment but did not feel prepared to deliver it: 73% of hospitalists reported feeling somewhat or extremely inadequate to provide medication for opioid use disorder. Implementation: The clinic launched using repurposed clinical space and limited new staffing, and brought Addiction Medicine, Addiction Psychiatry, and Infectious Diseases expertise together within a single transitional setting. Maintenance: Early indicators included formal incorporation into the hospital budget, growth in patient and visit volume, faculty recruitment, and service expansion. Conclusions A multidisciplinary bridge clinic integrating Addiction Medicine and Addiction Psychiatry can be implemented within a large academic health system and showed early indicators of sustainability through strategic use of existing clinical, educational, and operational infrastructure. By extending bridge care beyond medication initiation to coordinated management of medical, psychiatric, and social complexity, this model demonstrates a scalable approach for expanding access to evidence-based substance use disorder treatment while addressing community-identified needs.

title: Prevalence of Complementary and Alternative Therapies Use and Associated Factors among Patients with Mental Illness at Mawenzi Regional Referral Hospital, Kilimanjaro, Tanzania: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Background Complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) use is common among people with mental illness worldwide, but data on its prevalence and correlates among this population in Tanzania remain limited. Methods An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 204 patients with mental illness attending the Psychiatric Unit of Mawenzi Regional Referral Hospital, Kilimanjaro, Tanzania, between April and July 2024. Data were collected using a structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire adapted from the NAFKAM International CAM Questionnaire (I-CAM-Q) and analysed in STATA v17 using descriptive statistics and modified Poisson regression to identify factors associated with CAM use. Results The mean age of participants was 44.3 years (SD 14.3) and 59.3% were female. The prevalence of CAM use was 55.9%. The most common types were herbal medicine (41.1%), traditional healers (25.2%), meditation (15.2%) and spiritual healers (15.2%). Male sex was associated with lower CAM use (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] 0.73, 95% CI 0.57–0.93; p = 0.012), while being widowed (aPR 4.83, 95% CI 1.59–14.70; p = 0.006) and employed (aPR 1.42, 95% CI 1.06–1.92; p = 0.020) were associated with higher use. Personal belief (44%) was the leading reason cited for using CAM, followed by cultural belief, cost, lack of access to conventional treatment, and availability of practitioners. Conclusions More than half of patients with mental illness attending Mawenzi Regional Referral Hospital use CAM, most commonly herbal medicine. Sex, marital status and employment status were significant correlates of use. Clinicians should routinely and non-judgementally ask about CAM use to identify potential interactions with conventional psychiatric treatment and to strengthen patient-centred mental health care.

title: Establishing paediatric liver and kidney transplantation in a lower-middle-income country of the WHO European Region: a national health-system analysis, Uzbekistan
abstract: Background and purpose. Uzbekistan is a lower-middle-income country in the WHO European Region with more than 38 million people, of whom 13.8 million are children aged 0–17 years. Until recently, children with end-stage liver or kidney disease depended mainly on transplantation abroad, chiefly in India and Turkey, funded by the state or by families. The National Children's Medical Center (NCMC), Tashkent, established a dedicated paediatric liver and kidney transplantation programme from 2023 and reached full operating capacity in 2026. It is the only centre in the country with a regular, independently staffed paediatric liver transplantation programme; paediatric kidney transplantation is also performed at other national centres, mainly the Republican Specialized Scientific and Practical Medical Center of Surgery named after Academician V. Vakhidov. No published study has described how paediatric transplantation was built in a Central Asian country, how it changed reliance on treatment abroad, or what share of national need it meets. This study addresses that gap to inform national planning. Investigators. Konstantin Semash (principal investigator), Timur Dzhanbekov, Mansur Nasirov (NCMC); Akrom Akhmedov (NCMC; Republican Specialized Scientific and Practical Medical Center of Surgery named after Academician V. Vakhidov). Design. Retrospective study with two linked components: (A) a single-centre cohort of all paediatric liver and kidney transplants at NCMC, and (B) a national analysis of all paediatric transplant recipients in the Ministry of Health transplant recipient registry, combined with national population data, a before–after comparison and a descriptive cost analysis. Study periods: pre-programme era, 2012–2022; Era 1, establishment of the NCMC programme, from the first NCMC transplant to 31 December 2025; Era 2, full capacity, 1 January to 31 December 2026. Setting. Paediatric transplantation at NCMC is almost fully state-funded and uses only living related donors. Participants. Component A: all recipients younger than 18 years who received a liver or kidney transplant at NCMC from the first programme transplant to 31 December 2026; their living donors; and all children referred to NCMC for transplant evaluation in the same period. Follow-up continues to death, last contact, or data lock on 30 June 2027, giving at least 6 months of follow-up for every recipient. Component B: all recipients in the Ministry of Health registry who were younger than 18 years at liver or kidney transplantation, at any centre in Uzbekistan or abroad, up to 31 December 2026. Exclusions: duplicate records (same name, date of birth and organ, or same personal identification number and organ) and patients aged 18 years or older at transplantation. Data sources. Resident population by age, sex, region and year (2015–2026) and live births by region from the State Committee on Statistics (siat.stat.uz); the Ministry of Health transplant recipient registry (14 regional datasets); Ministry of Health payment records for treatment abroad; NCMC medical, outpatient and referral records; NCMC economics department and programme records. Primary outcomes. (1) Transplant rate: transplants in recipients aged 0–17 years per million resident children aged 0–17 years per year, by organ; (2) source of transplantation: number and proportion of paediatric transplants per year performed at NCMC, at other national centres and abroad (by country). Secondary outcomes. Coverage of estimated national need, reported as a range; regional access (transplants per million children aged 0–17 years and liver transplants per 100 000 births, by region of residence); time from referral and listing to transplantation and waiting-list mortality at NCMC; patient and graft survival and Clavien–Dindo grade III or higher complications in recipients and donors at NCMC; deaths, returns to dialysis and proportion alive on immunosuppression in the national registry by centre group, including children transplanted abroad; cost per transplant at NCMC compared with treatment abroad and, for kidney, with dialysis; and programme capacity (staffing, training, funding, monthly volume). Analysis plan. Age at transplantation is calculated from date of birth and operation date (1 July assumed when only the year is recorded); duplicates are removed. Descriptive statistics (medians with IQR, counts with percentages) are disaggregated by sex. Annual counts and proportions by source of transplantation are shown as a time series for 2012–2026. NCMC Era 1 and Era 2 are compared with Mann–Whitney U and Fisher's exact tests. Survival is analysed for the NCMC cohort only, using Kaplan–Meier estimates at 6 and 12 months with 95% confidence intervals and numbers at risk. Rates are given with exact Poisson 95% confidence intervals, and coverage of need under low and high published incidence estimates. Regional rates are mapped. Costs are described, including, for kidney, the number of years after which transplantation costs less than continued dialysis. No multivariable modelling is planned because of sample size. Analyses use R; two-sided p < 0.05. Sensitivity analyses: coverage under low and high incidence estimates; excluding records with year-only operation dates; excluding registry records whose dates could not be verified. Reporting follows STROBE, RECORD and CHEERS 2022. Expected outcomes. We expect to show a shift of paediatric liver and kidney transplantation from abroad to Uzbekistan after the NCMC programme started, regional inequality in access, a remaining gap between transplant activity and estimated national need, and short-term outcomes at NCMC comparable with international benchmarks. The findings will provide the first national description of building a paediatric transplantation service in Central Asia and an evidence base for national policy on scale-up. Anticipated limitations. Deaths occurring before registry enrolment (for example, early post-operative deaths abroad) may not be captured, so registry outcomes are reported descriptively and formal survival analysis is restricted to NCMC. Recent transplants may not yet be entered in the registry; NCMC volumes are taken from NCMC records. Free-text place of transplantation is grouped by predefined rules, and ambiguous entries are verified by the investigators. Missing data are reported per variable, with complete-case analysis and no imputation of outcomes. Ethics. The study follows the Declarations of Helsinki and Istanbul. Approval will be sought from the NCMC Ethics Committee with a waiver of individual consent for retrospective review of routinely collected records. De-identified aggregated data and the data dictionary will be available on reasonable request after publication, subject to Ministry of Health approval. Data status at registration. The Ministry of Health registry and national population data have been obtained, and data cleaning (record selection, deduplication, classification of place of transplantation) has been performed. No analysis of outcomes, survival or costs has been performed at the time of registration. NCMC cohort data collection is ongoing. Timeline. Registration and ethics submission, November 2026; data access request to the Ministry of Health, December 2026; inclusion closes 31 December 2026; follow-up data lock 30 June 2027; analysis and drafting July–August 2027; submission August–September 2027.

title: VALUE BASED CARE IN PRESSURE INJURY PREVENTION
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Role of Value-Based Healthcare in Preventing Pressure UlcersPressure ulcers are a major problem in today’s health care settings, affecting patients in hospitals, intensive care units, long-term care facilities, and community health settings. They can lead to pain, infection, longer hospital stays, decreased quality of life and increased health care costs. Many pressure injuries can be prevented, yet their development remains an important indicator of patient safety and the quality of nursing care.The publication Value-Based Care in Pressure Injury Prevention has been developed to provide an in-depth insight into the concepts, approaches, and cutting-edge tactics relating to the prevention and treatment of pressure injuries. It highlights the need for value-based healthcare that focuses on improving patient outcomes through effective evidence-based interventions and judicious use of healthcare resources.This volume covers basic principles of pressure injuries including skin structure, function, pathophysiology, classification, risk factors and clinical assessment. It also addresses evidence-based prevention, nursing assessments, modern wound care technologies, nutritional monitoring, patient safety measures, quality improvement and teamwork across disciplines.Focus is on healthcare economics, cost-effectiveness, institutional policies, ethical obligations, digital health technologies, and research applications. The volume also delves into the prevention of pressure injuries in critically ill patients, International protocols, Indian medical practices,clinical case analyzes, benchmarking and future developments such as artificial intelligence and personalized healthcare.The chapters are intended to help nursing students, nursing instructors, health care providers, wound care specialists, researchers, and hospital administrators. Pragmatic dialogs, clinical applications and empirically supported suggestions are intended to improve professional expertise and to foster the use of effective preventive measures.This book is mainly intended to cultivate a culture of prevention, not just treatment. It highlights the important contributions of nurses and interdisciplinary healthcare teams to the early detection of risks, regular skin assessments, individualized repositioning, nutritional support, patient education, and continued monitoring of clinical outcomes.It is expected that this book will be an important educational and professional tool to improve patient safety, reduce preventable pressure injuries, maximize healthcare delivery and improve the quality of life of patients.The main aim is to ensure that pressure injury prevention is seen as a shared responsibility and a core element of safe, effective, cost-effective and value-based healthcare.

title: Perceived Quality of Siloed versus Time-Synchronized Data Architectures for AI-Based Digital Mental Health: A Within-Subjects Scenario Study
abstract: Fragmented data architectures may limit how artificial intelligence (AI)-based digital mental health systems combine and communicate multimodal information. This scenario-based study tested whether users perceived the Integrated framework more favorably than the Traditional framework. U.S. adults familiar with digital mental health technologies reviewed standardized descriptions of both conditions and rated system quality, information quality, and perceived transparency and explainability. The constructs covered data quality, portability, response time, accuracy, timeliness, completeness, transparency, and explainability. Paired-samples t tests were supplemented by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Valid paired samples were 277, 267, and 258 for the three constructs, respectively. Ratings favored the Integrated condition for system quality (M = 3.47 vs. 3.38; t (276) = −2.66, P = 0.008, |dz| = 0.16), information quality (M = 3.48 vs. 3.34; t (266) = −4.49, P dz| = 0.28), and perceived transparency and explainability (M = 3.79 vs. 3.65; t (257) = −3.04, P = 0.003, |dz| = 0.19). Nonparametric analyses supported the same conclusions. Absolute paired effect magnitudes ranged from |dz| = 0.16 to |dz| = 0.28. Because participants evaluated descriptions rather than functioning systems and temporal alignment was bundled with integration, the findings identify a modest perceptual advantage rather than causal, technical, or clinical-performance benefits. The results support further user-centered prototype and implementation testing.

title: Layer-wise hybrid binary–stochastic computing architecture for energy-efficient diabetes prediction on FPGA
abstract: Stochastic computing encodes numbers as probabilistic bit streams and reduces multiplication to a single logic gate, which makes it an appealing arithmetic substrate for always-on biomedical inference under severe energy constraints. Its accuracy is bounded by two effects usually treated as global properties of a design: the inverse square-root convergence of stream-based estimates, and the systematic bias introduced when operand streams are correlated. This article proceeds from a different observation, namely, that the accuracy cost of stochastic approximation is not distributed uniformly across the layers of a network, and that precision should be allocated where measurement shows it is required. We define a layer-wise stochastic sensitivity metric that isolates the accuracy attributable to mapping each individual layer into the stochastic domain, and develop a partitioning procedure that converts the resulting profile into a hybrid binary–stochastic assignment while reporting the retained fraction of stochastic computation as an explicit hardware-cost proxy. The methodology is demonstrated on an 8–12–8–4–1 fully connected classifier trained on the PIMA Indian Diabetes dataset under a leakage-free preprocessing protocol. Profiling reveals a strongly concentrated sensitivity distribution, the second hidden layer alone accounting for an 11.9 percentage-point accuracy loss while the output layer is statistically indistinguishable from exact arithmetic, and excluding that layer alone recovers 5.0 percentage points while retaining 58 % of all multiply–accumulate operations in stochastic form. A controlled comparison of independent and shared stochastic number generators demonstrates a correlation-induced error floor that does not diminish with stream length, the implemented bank holding a stochastic cross-correlation of approximately 0.038 independently of length; classifier AUC accordingly remains flat with the generators as implemented but rises toward the exact reference with idealised generators. All four arithmetic partitions were placed and routed for a Xilinx Zynq-7000 device with power annotated from simulated switching activity. The all-stochastic network occupies 5,320 look-up tables and 2,878 flip-flops with no DSP slices, and the selected partition reduces energy per inference by 64 %, to 2.69 μ J at a 1024-bit stream. An all-binary fixed-point baseline is faster and more energy-efficient still, which delimits the regime in which stochastic arithmetic is competitive at this scale and identifies generator cost, rather than stochastic arithmetic itself, as the quantity that must fall for the paradigm to become attractive for compact fully connected classifiers.

title: Quality of life and social networks as factors associated with complementary and alternative medicine use in geriatric anxiety and depression: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Introduction Complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) use is increasingly common in late-life mental health care, yet its clinical and psychosocial correlates remain insufficiently characterized in clinical geriatric psychiatry. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of CAM use in geriatric patients with anxiety and depressive disorders and to identify the independent clinical and psychosocial factors associated with that use. Methods Two hundred eighteen patients aged ≥60 presenting to outpatient clinics or inpatient wards of two psychiatric centres were enrolled through consecutive recruitment between January 2024 and November 2025 in this cross-sectional study. Data were collected using a sociodemographic and clinical information form, the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and the World Health Organization Quality of Life Instrument Older Adults Module (WHOQOL-OLD). Factors associated with CAM use were examined by multivariable binary logistic regression incorporating six covariates: age, HADS-depression score, HADS-anxiety score, WHOQOL-OLD total score, place of residence, and presence of a close acquaintance using CAM. Results At least one CAM modality was used by 28.9% of participants (mean age 69.4 ± 6.4 years), most frequently spiritual healing (46.0%), amulets (31.7%), and herbal therapies (25.4%). In multivariable analysis, absence of a CAM-using acquaintance (OR = 0.141, 95% CI 0.066–0.303, p < 0.001) and urban residence (OR = 0.391, 95% CI 0.192–0.795, p = 0.010) were associated with lower odds of CAM use. Advancing age (OR = 0.902, 95% CI 0.847–0.960, p = 0.001) and higher WHOQOL-OLD score (OR = 0.973, 95% CI 0.953–0.994, p = 0.014) were also associated with lower odds. Neither HADS-depression (OR = 1.003, p = 0.935) nor HADS-anxiety (OR = 0.979, p = 0.673) scores were significantly associated with CAM use. Conclusion Lifetime CAM use was associated with a CAM-using acquaintance, rural residence, younger age, and lower current quality of life; no statistically significant association with HADS scores was detected in this sample. Because CAM use was assessed over the lifetime, temporal sequence cannot be inferred. As herbal preparations, used by a quarter of CAM users, carry herb–drug interaction risks with polypharmacy, clinicians should inquire about CAM use routinely and non-judgementally.

title: Sildenafil 50mg tabs without consulation
Economic evaluation of denosumab in the prevention of skeletal-related events in patients with multiple myeloma in Mexico
abstract: Objectives: To undertake an economic evaluation of denosumab in comparison with a mixed scenario consisted of zoledronic acid or no treatment if there is a contraindication to this agent due to severe renal impairment (Mix ZA/No tx) in patients with multiple myeloma (MM).Methods: The analysis adopted the perspective of the Mexican public health care system as a payer.This is a partitioned-survival five-stages semi-Markov model for a life-time horizon.We evaluated the frequencies of skeletal-related events (SREs) as well as the costs associated to drug acquisition/infusion, routine patient management, medical attention of SREs, treatment of serious adverse events, and anti-myeloma treatment.Results: Denosumab use was more expensive but also more effective, with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios of $13,942 Mexican pesos (MXN) per SRE avoided and $1,893 MXN per additional month of progression-free survival.In general, the model is robust.Conclusions: In patients with MM, denosumab represents a cost-effective intervention in comparison with the Mix ZA/No tx.

title: Deep learning benchmarking for wearable sensor fall detection and multiclass activity recognition
abstract: Wearable sensor-based fall detection is important for protecting older adults, but fair comparison of deep learning methods is hindered by differences in datasets, preprocessing, optimization, and evaluation protocols. This study presents a standardized benchmarking framework in which eight architectures, namely CNN-1D, LSTM, GRU, BiLSTM, CNN-LSTM, a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), a Transformer Encoder, and a Hybrid CNN-Vision Transformer (CNN-ViT), were trained and evaluated under an identical preprocessing pipeline, optimization strategy, and evaluation protocol for binary fall detection and multi-class activity recognition. The benchmark comprises seven public wearable-sensor/multimodal datasets and four public non-wearable vision-based datasets, each evaluated with a stratified 70/30 train–test split. On the primary Ursul (2025) IMU dataset, the Hybrid CNN-ViT achieved the highest test performance (binary: accuracy 95.7%, recall 95.6%, AUC 97.9%; five-class: accuracy 91.3%, AUC 97.4%), followed by the Transformer, and it ranked first in test accuracy on all eleven datasets in the binary task and on all ten datasets with multi-class labels. Because these comparisons derive from a single window-level split without repeated runs, they are reported descriptively. A supplementary reduced-scale verification with three random seeds showed that the Hybrid model matched, but did not significantly exceed, a CNN-only baseline in accuracy, while significantly outperforming a Transformer-only variant on the five-class task and achieving the highest fall-class recall. Because most datasets contain simulated falls performed by healthy adults, the results indicate benchmarking performance rather than clinical reliability. The framework provides a reusable protocol for fairer comparison of future wearable fall-detection models.

title: A Real‐World Comparison of Annualised Bleed Rate Estimates Derived From Patient‐Reported Surveys versus Medical Record Data From US Patients With Haemophilia A
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Annualised bleeding rate (ABR) serves as a central measure for clinical decision-making, regulatory assessment and health technology evaluations in haemophilia. Variability in how real-world bleed events are collected can yield divergent ABR estimates, complicating interpretations of real-world treatment effectiveness and unmet medical need. AIM: This study aims to quantify the differences between ABR estimates using patient-reported outcomes (PROs) versus electronic health record (EHR) data sources in the US. METHODS: This study is a retrospective, observational cohort study using PicnicHealth medical record and Haemophilia Bleed Survey data. ABR was calculated for the same patient using four independent collection modalities; PRO data using Haemophilia Bleed Survey from medical records, bleed rate data, bleed event data and bleed event/rate data combined. RESULTS: Out of 334 patients with confirmed haemophilia A diagnosis in the database, 48 were included in this study. The total median ABR was 4.1, 1.0, 1.3 and 1.3 for PRO data, EHR event data, EHR rate data and EHR event/rate data combined, respectively. A median paired difference of 2.8 bleeds/year (95% CI: 1.8 to 4.2) indicated that across all patients, ABR from PRO data was ∼3 bleeds/per year higher than the total ABR estimates using EHR. CONCLUSION: ABRs calculated using PRO data were consistently higher than those calculated from data collected in routine clinical care. ABR estimates may therefore be influenced by data sources, bleed events and those drawn from PRO data sources may reflect patients perceived burden of bleeding events more accurately than those drawn from EHR.

title: Editorial: Neonatal nutrition under the lens: immunological protection, feeding safety, and public health
abstract: milk-based diets while urging vigilant cardiovascular monitoring and caution regarding the timing of bovine-derived fortifier introduction in micro-preemies.Beyond feeding formulations, the subjective interpretation of feeding intolerance frequently prompts unwarranted feed cessations, significantly delaying the achievement of full enteral feeding (FEF). Addressing this in very preterm infants (<30 weeks' gestation), Maggiora et al. demonstrated that implementing the Rapid Assessment of Feeding Intolerance protocol to replace routine gastric residual aspirations with an objective bedside scoring algorithm significantly accelerated the time to reach FEF, particularly among infants with intrauterine growth restriction. This approach curtailed feed disruptions, preserved early postnatal growth velocity, and lowered central venous access exposure without increasing adverse events. Extending standardized bedside surveillance to surgical cohorts, Xiao et al. showed that a nurse-led feeding tolerance protocol markedly lowered the incidence of FI, reduced abdominal distension and vomiting, and shortened the interval to full feeds in infants recovering from congenital heart disease surgery. By establishing defined clinical parameters and alert thresholds rather than reflexively stopping feeds or modifying formulas, both studies demonstrate that objective symptom interpretation is essential for establishing nutritional autonomy across vulnerable populations.The safety and timing of initiating feeds during acute critical illness were addressed by Yue et al., who retrospectively investigated 94 neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy receiving therapeutic hypothermia. Although infants managed with delayed feeding schedules exhibited greater baseline illness severity, multivariable adjustment confirmed that early minimal enteral feeding did not increase gastrointestinal complications, feeding intolerance, or NEC. Instead, early feeding accelerated full enteral nutrition, shortened parenteral nutrition duration, and decreased hospitalization costs, affirming that early trophic feeding is practical, safe, and cost-effective in hemodynamically stable encephalopathic neonates.Individualized patient-level vulnerabilities were highlighted by Xu et al. in a cohort of 65 preterm twin pairs with birth weight discordance (>20%). Smaller twins faced a significantly higher incidence of NEC across monochorionic and dichorionic gestations, alongside prolonged times to FEF, frequent fasting episodes, and extended hospitalizations. Crucially, multivariable logistic regression revealed that lower gestational age and being small for gestational age (SGA), rather than birth weight discordance itself, were the independent risk factors for NEC, while gestational age, SGA, and being the smaller twin each independently predicted delayed FEF. These findings demonstrate that growth restriction, rather than twin discordance alone, demands customized enteral advancement and heightened clinical vigilance.Broadening the clinical lens to infectious and environmental stressors, Zhu et al. explored metabolic alterations in 139 neonates with PCR-confirmed norovirus infection. After excluding alternate gastrointestinal diagnoses, neonates presenting with gastrointestinal hemorrhage exhibited distinct biochemical disturbances, with lower venous ionized calcium independently predicting the hemorrhagic phenotype. This indicates that monitoring ionized calcium alongside gastrointestinal surveillance may aid in early risk stratification during acute enteric infections. In a large cohort of 1,358 neonates in Botswana, Nakstad et al. analyzed the clinical significance of admission hypothermia (<36.5°C). While admission hypothermia was pervasive, it was not independently associated with early postnatal weight loss, day of nadir, or time to regain birth weight; rather, gestational age remained the primary determinant of growth kinetics, demonstrating that intrinsic developmental maturity governs early growth more decisively than an isolated admission vital sign.Finally, addressing long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, Sinha et al. outlined a PROSPERO-registered protocol following PRISMA and Cochrane guidelines to evaluate how maternal and early-childhood (ages 0-3) iron supplementation affects cognitive development and myelination, integrating clinical outcomes with advanced microstructural neuroimaging (such as diffusion tensor and myelin water imaging) to bridge the gap between early nutritional adequacy and structural brain maturation. We eagerly await the findings emerging from this protocol.In summary, the contributions in this Research Topic illustrate that safeguarding neonatal gastrointestinal integrity and advancing developmental potential require an integrated, objective framework. Hydrolyzed formulas and exclusive human milk regimens minimize mucosal antigenic stress, while standardized clinical scoring systems avoid unwarranted feeding interruptions. Acknowledging that biological immaturity and intrauterine growth restriction, rather than isolated weight discordance or admission temperature fluctuations, govern vulnerability enables clinicians to tailor bedside surveillance effectively. Transitioning from empirical, subjective feeding practices toward protocolized nutritional, hemodynamic, and metabolic monitoring provides a coherent pathway to minimize severe morbidity, shorten hospital stays, and support lifelong developmental health.Author contributions XY: Writing -original draft, Writing -review & editing.

title: Efficacy and safety of Biyuanshu oral liquid for chronic rhinosinusitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is a common chronic inflammatory disease of the nasal and paranasal sinus mucosa that can seriously impair patients’ quality of life. Biyuanshu (BYS) oral liquid is commonly used for rhinitis and sinusitis in clinical practice, but its efficacy and safety in CRS have not been systematically evaluated. Methods This study systematically searched nine Chinese and English databases from inception to 30 June 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating BYS oral liquid alone or in combination with conventional treatment for CRS were included. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the stability of the results. Funnel plots, Peters’s test and Begg’s rank correlation test were used to assess publication bias. The methodological quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and the certainty of the evidence was graded using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Results A total of 19 RCTs involving 2,861 patients were included. Meta-analysis showed that BYS oral liquid significantly reduced nasal symptom scores, including nasal congestion (standardized mean difference [SMD] = −2.47, 95% confidence interval [CI]: −3.84 to −1.10), rhinorrhea (SMD = −1.69, 95% CI: −2.42 to −0.97), and headache (SMD = −2.26, 95% CI: −3.65 to −0.87). It also improved the reported overall effective rate (risk ratio [RR] = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.13 to 1.22). In addition, BYS oral liquid reduced Lund–Mackay computed tomography (CT) scores (mean difference [MD] = −1.70, 95% CI: −2.34 to −1.05) and Sino-Nasal Outcome Test-20 (SNOT-20) scores (MD = −4.50, 95% CI: −5.83 to −3.17). The incidence of adverse events was lower in the BYS oral liquid group than in the control group (RR = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.24 to 0.53). However, all included RCTs were conducted in China, substantial heterogeneity was observed for several outcomes, and the GRADE certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low. Conclusion BYS oral liquid as an adjunctive treatment for CRS may offer additional benefits, particularly in alleviating nasal symptoms. Its potential to improve radiographic findings and quality of life still requires further confirmation, and the available safety data primarily reflect short-term tolerability. Given the limitations of the current evidence, further validation through high-quality RCTs is needed. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261440773, identifier CRD420261440773.

Dye-Selective Photocatalytic Degradation by Hydrothermally Synthesized α-FeOOH: Preferential Activity Toward Malachite Green
journal: Technical Education Science/Giáo dục Kỹ thuật
abstract: In this study, α-FeOOH was successfully synthesized via a hydrothermal method, and its photocatalytic activity was evaluated against five organic dyes, namely Eosin Y, Methylene Blue, Malachite Green, Methyl Orange, and Rhodamine B, under illumination. X-ray diffraction confirmed α-FeOOH to be the only crystalline phase detectable, with crystallite sizes in the nanoscale range. UV–Vis absorption spectra showed that α-FeOOH exhibited excellent photocatalytic selectivity: MG was substantially degraded, with a removal efficiency of >90% after 240 min of illumination, while the other four dyes showed negligible degradation under the same conditions. This selectivity may be associated with differences in the molecular structures, adsorption behaviors, and intrinsic susceptibility of the dye chromophores to oxidative degradation. In particular, the structural characteristics of MG may facilitate oxidative attack on its chromophore compared with the other dyes investigated. These results indicate that α-FeOOH is a promising material for selective photocatalytic systems in the treatment of wastewater containing organic dyes.

title: Clinical outcomes, safety, and biological target engagement of IDH inhibitors in IDH-mutant glioma: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Mutant IDH is a therapeutic target in diffuse glioma, but comparative efficacy and uncontrolled radiographic observations require distinct interpretation. Objective To synthesize clinical outcomes, safety, and target engagement of mutant-IDH inhibitors in glioma. Methods MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through June 10, 2026. Comparative effects, single-arm radiographic proportions, agent-specific safety, and pharmacodynamics were separated. Proportions were analyzed using random-effects binomial logistic-normal models. Registration was retrospective (PROSPERO CRD420261452904). Results 26 reports were included; 13 reports representing 12 underlying studies entered pooled analyses. updated indigo follow-up favored vorasidenib over placebo for progression-free survival (hr 0.35; 95% ci 0.25–0.49) and time to next intervention (hr 0.25; 95% ci 0.16–0.40). in three uncontrolled non-enhancing ivosidenib/vorasidenib cohorts, objective response was 6.3% (5/79; 95% ci 2.7%–14.3%). rano-lgg-restricted disease control was 91.2% (62/68; 95% ci 81.7%–96.0%; prediction interval 62.1%–98.5%); 49/62 classifications were stable disease. ivosidenib adverse-event discontinuation was 2.3% (7/299); vorasidenib any-causality grade ≥3 adverse events were 24.9% (63/253). direct tissue pharmacodynamic evidence chiefly concerned selected perioperative, non-enhancing lower-grade cohorts; plasma or cerebrospinal-fluid measurements did not establish equivalent intratumoral inhibition across disease states. Conclusions Vorasidenib prolongs progression-free survival and delays subsequent intervention in selected patients with non-enhancing grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma previously treated with surgery alone. For other agents and disease settings, evidence remains predominantly uncontrolled, limiting conclusions about treatment-attributable benefit. Agent-specific safety assessment and prospective studies integrating pharmacodynamic and clinical endpoints are needed to refine patient selection, establish treatment sequencing and duration, and determine whether target engagement predicts durable clinical benefit. Systematic review registration http://crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420261452904.

title: A Literature Review: Co-Committed Resources (CCR), the Crisis Inside Disaster Planning
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A county lists fifty contracted buses in its evacuation plan, and a neighboring county lists the same fifty buses in its own. Each plan is sound when read alone. The shortfall appears only when one storm calls both plans at once. The author's November 12, 2026, preprint (Treglia, 2026b) names this condition co-committed resources (CCR) and sets out its remedies. This review has a narrower job. It situates the term in the literature and stakes the claim to it. Co-committed resources are vehicles, people, equipment, supplies, facilities, services, or other capabilities counted as available response capacity by more than one independently developed jurisdictional plan, where no shared record reveals the overlap and nothing guarantees release when several plans call at once. The review asked whether prior work had named or measured the condition, and where each neighboring body of work stops. Searches on November 24 and 25, 2026, covered Scopus, four other scholarly indexes, six preprint and working-paper servers, and grey literature from the United States, the European Union, and Australia. Ten structured Scopus strings returned 358 records, and none used the term. The exact term appeared only in the author's own 2026 preprints. Studies of emergency medical, hospital, and volunteer health personnel measured or described one part of the condition without naming it, and they are credited as precursors. Documented cases fill three gaps: National Guard and reserve members claimed by a state, the federal government, and a civilian employer; a school named as both a shelter and a reunification site; and volunteers registered with more than one system. No study found here counts the same resource across a region's plans. A three-part test marks where the term applies: planning is decentralized, the plans draw on a shared and finite pool, and a shared shock triggers several plans at once. The paper asks that the term be credited when used and invites scholars and practitioners to test and extend it.

title: Bridging the standardisation gap: A lifecycle framework for auto-ID IoT integration with BIM in post-disaster reconstruction
journal: Journal of Information Technology in Construction
abstract: Post-disaster reconstruction places extreme demands on information management. Supply chains fracture, coordination breaks down, and the component data needed to move from temporary housing to permanent rebuilding is rarely retained. Building Information Modelling (BIM) and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies together offer a route to that continuity, yet construction-oriented guidance for staging automatic identification (Auto-ID) device deployment within BIM information management remains absent, and deployments stay fragmented. This study develops a baseline framework for that setting. Its scope is the Auto-ID class of IoT edge devices, principally radio-frequency identification (RFID) and near-field communication (NFC) transponders acting as data carriers, and it excludes environmental and structural sensing. Adopting a Design Science Research (DSR) paradigm, the research proceeds in two empirical stages. Stage 1 is a requirement analysis drawn from a precursor questionnaire of 110 registered architects working on post-disaster housing, which establishes the operational baseline. Stage 2 is an evaluation survey completed by 113 architecture, engineering and construction (AEC) professionals, which assesses the resulting framework. The result is a five-phase technical guideline covering initial engagement, application selection, interoperability, stakeholder alignment and security assurance, with security treated as a gate repeated at each phase. These micro-scale phases are mapped onto the macro-scale disaster management cycle to give an integrated lifecycle model. The study also proposes the Data-to-Design Handover, a mechanism that carries component integrity data from temporary housing units into generative design for permanent reconstruction. Respondents rated all five phases as important in aggregate, with stakeholder alignment rated highest and interoperability lowest, and 68.1% reported that referenceable guidelines would raise their likelihood of adopting Auto-ID solutions. The evaluation is descriptive and perception based. The handover mechanism and the progression towards a mature predictive digital twin are conceptual propositions that were not tested, and the framework awaits implementation in live projects.

title: After the Storm
A prospective longitudinal qualitative study of emotions across nearly a quarter century among firefighter responders to the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing
Inovasi Pupuk Organik untuk Meningkatkan Produktivitas Padi dan Ketahanan Pangan Pascabencana di Kabupaten Cianjur
journal: Agrokreatif Jurnal Ilmiah Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat
abstract: The 2022 Cianjur earthquake affected agricultural activities, including damage to rice fields, disrupted irrigation systems, and reduced agricultural productivity. This community service program aimed to improve farmers’ knowledge and skills in producing and applying organic fertilizer to support sustainable agricultural recovery in the post-disaster period. The program was conducted from May to October 2025 in Bobojong Village, Mande District, Cianjur Regency, involving 50 farmers from local farmer groups. The activities consisted of field observations, educational sessions, demonstrations, and hands-on training in producing solid and liquid organic fertilizers using locally available organic waste. Program effectiveness was evaluated through pre-tests and post-tests consisting of 20 questions covering organic fertilizer sources, composition, benefits, production methods, application, and sustainable agriculture. The average knowledge score increased from 56.3 before the program to 71.3 afterward, representing an improvement of 15 points (26.6%). Participants also gained practical experience in utilizing organic waste as raw material for organic fertilizer production. Furthermore, the activities encouraged farmer groups to explore collective fertilizer production and the use of locally available resources. These results indicate that practical training and educational activities can contribute to improving farmers’ knowledge and skills in organic fertilizer production and application, while supporting greater input independence and sustainable agricultural practices in post-disaster areas.

title: The Relationship Between Depression Levels and Disease Self-Management in Elderly Individuals With Chronic Illnesses Affected by Earthquakes
journal: Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness
abstract: Objective To determine the relationship among depression levels, chronic disease self-management, and its sub-dimensions in elderly individuals with chronic diseases who were affected by the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes. Methods This descriptive and correlational study was conducted among 208 elderly individuals affected by the earthquake, each with at least one chronic disease. Data were collected via face-to-face interviews using the Participant Information Form, the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15), and the Chronic Illness Self-Management Scale. The significance level was set at P < 0.05. Results The mean age of the participants was 71.81 ± 6.19 years. Depression was mild in 42.8%, moderate in 17.3%, and severe in 9.1% of participants. Depression was positively correlated with self-stigma (r = 0.316, P < 0.001) and negatively correlated with coping with stigmatization (r = −0.186, P = 0.007), health care effectiveness (r = −0.351, P < 0.001), and treatment adherence (r = −0.227, P < 0.001), but not with overall chronic disease self-management (r = 0.051, P = 0.463). Conclusion Among older adults with chronic illnesses affected by the earthquake, depression was associated with key domains of disease self-management rather than overall self-management. Early depression screening and holistic nursing interventions are essential in post-disaster care.

title: Extreme weather events and child mental health: a global systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence.
abstract: Background Climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, yet the burden of mental disorders among exposed children has not been quantified globally. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised the global evidence, estimated the pooled prevalence of mental health outcomes in exposed children, and examined sources of heterogeneity. Methods PubMed, PsycINFO and Web of Science were searched for studies reporting clinically relevant mental health outcomes in children (≤ 18 years) exposed to extreme weather events. Prevalence was pooled using robust variance estimation in three-level random-effects models. Univariable meta-regressions with cluster-robust Wald tests examined event type, national income, age, sex and sampling frame. Results 42 studies (140,139 children, twelve countries) on storms, floods and wildfires were included; none examined heat or drought. Pooled prevalence was 17.6% (95% CI 11.2–24.9%, k = 40) for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and 20.2% (95% CI 9.5–33.7%, k = 20) for depression, with high heterogeneity (I²>99%). Girls showed higher PTSD prevalence than boys (difference 2.22 percentage points, 95% CI 0.49–3.95, p = 0.020). PTSD prevalence was lower in population-based than school-based samples (5.0% vs 23.6%, p = 0.002) and in high-income than low- and middle-income countries (10.9% vs 25.5%, p = 0.028). Conclusions Around one in six children exposed to extreme weather events met criteria for PTSD and one in five for depression. The evidence comes mainly from the United States and China: there are no studies from the Middle East and North Africa, only one from Sub-Saharan Africa, and none on heat or drought, even though children in these regions and exposed to these hazards face the greatest climate risk. Child mental health should be built into climate adaptation policy and post-disaster response, and research is urgently needed in under-studied settings. Protocol registration: PROSPERO (CRD42024604257)

title: From Emerging Vectors to Missed Fevers: Why Fragile Health Systems Need Integrated Fever–Vector Preparedness
journal: Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness
abstract: Climate change, urbanization, population mobility, and expanding mosquito vectors are reshaping infectious-disease risks in fragile health systems, where surveillance, diagnosis, and response often remain fragmented. This Policy Analysis argues that preparedness should move beyond isolated pathogen- or vector-specific programs toward an integrated fever-vector model. Undifferentiated fever should serve as the clinical entry point linking environmental intelligence, entomological surveillance, sentinel fever surveillance, tiered laboratory testing, and public health response. Such integration could improve recognition of arboviral infections overlooked in malaria-centered systems, support earlier outbreak detection, and guide targeted vector control and diagnostic preparedness. Somalia and the wider Horn of Africa illustrate the urgency of this shift because climate shocks, displacement, weak laboratory systems, and emerging urban vector-borne risks increasingly converge. The priority is not a more technologically complex system, but a connected and sustainable preparedness architecture capable of linking emerging vectors with febrile illnesses presenting in routine care.

Digital Twin Networks for 6G Wireless Systems: Architecture, Enabling Technologies, AI-Driven Control, and Open Challenges
abstract: The transition to the Sixth Generation (6G) of mobile networks requires proactive and deterministic orchestration to satisfy the stringent key performance indicators of future services, including ultra-reliable low-latency communications, enhanced mobile broadband, and massive machine-type communications. Digital Twin Networks (DTNs) have emerged as a foundational technology to meet these demands, offering real-time and high-fidelity virtual replicas of the physical network. Although the literature explores DTNs conceptually, a gap exists in the coverage of technical classification and computational feasibility evaluations. This survey addresses this gap by formally categorizing state-of-the-art DTN architectures into passive monitoring twins and active control twins. We evaluate their enabling technologies, namely ray-tracing, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, artificial intelligence, and multi-access edge computing. Importantly, we analyze the complexity of ten state-of-the-art frameworks, five reporting complexity expressions, four derived in this survey, and one not derivable, to assess hardware scalability and inference bottlenecks. These architectures are then linked to forthcoming 6G use cases, including smart cities, Industry 5.0, healthcare, and smart grids. Finally, we synthesize crucial unresolved challenges, highlighting graphics processing unit hardware limitations, cyber-physical actuation latency, and the need for a zero-trust security paradigm, offering research directions toward the unified Internet of Everything.

title: Intravenous vs. Oral Iron Therapy in Pregnancy: A Randomized Trial
abstract: Background: Gestational iron deficiency anemia (IDA) remains a critical global public health concern, deeply intertwined with poor maternal-fetal outcomes including preterm birth, low birth weight, and postpartum complications. While traditional oral iron regimens face adherence challenges due to gastrointestinal toxicities, parenteral options like ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) offer accelerated, high-dose correction of iron stores. Objective: To evaluate and compare the therapeutic efficacy, safety profiles, and patient compliance associated with intravenous ferric carboxymaltose versus daily oral ferrous fumarate supplementation in pregnant women diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia. Methods: This randomized controlled trial was conducted at the Department of Obstetrics & Gynecology, Barind Medical College Hospital, Rajshahi, from January 2025 to December 2025. A total of 156 pregnant individuals (16 to 34 weeks of gestation) presenting with a verified diagnosis of IDA (Hemoglobin [Hb] < 11 gm/dL, depleted serum ferritin, and microcytic hypochromic blood films) were enrolled. Participants were randomized into two equal interventions: Group A (oral Ferrous Fumarate 200 mg co-formulated with Folic Acid 0.4 mg, administered twice daily for 6 weeks; n = 78) and Group B (a single total dose of intravenous Ferric Carboxymaltose 1000 mg diluted in 250 mL normal saline infused over 20 minutes; n = 78). The primary outcome measure was the absolute change in Hb concentration 6 weeks post-baseline. Secondary endpoints evaluated patient compliance rates along with the frequency and severity of treatment-emergent adverse experiences, including gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and systemic hypersensitivity events. Data processing was performed using SPSS version 26.0. Results: Both cohorts demonstrated statistical increases in hemoglobin markers from baseline values at the 6-week assessment boundary (p < 0.001). However, the intravenous arm (Group B) achieved a profoundly higher mean hemoglobin elevation (1.664 gm/dL) compared to the oral supplementation cohort (Group A, 1.018 gm/dL). Adverse event charting indicated significantly fewer treatment-related gastrointestinal disruptions and optimized compliance levels within the intravenous group compared to the oral cohort. Conclusion: Intravenous Ferric Carboxymaltose demonstrates clinical superiority over daily oral Ferrous Fumarate in correcting gestational iron deficiency anemia, demonstrating accelerated hemoglobin correction, a more favorable safety index, and enhanced therapeutic adherence. These findings warrant consideration for incorporating targeted IV iron pathways into regional antenatal management guidelines.
